lessons.title: How the Final Works
lessons.readme:
# How the Final Works

This course is a study partner for the CMPE 126 final. It's built from the lectures through Nov 18, plus the labs, quiz reviews and the midterm postmortem. Each chapter is one topic, cut down to what the final tests, and taught the way it was taught in class.

## The final

- **Thu Dec 10, 10:45am to 12:45pm**, on paper, comprehensive (every lecture, Aug 20 through Nov 24).
- True/false, multiple choice, short answer, and **writing C++ by hand**.
- You may bring **one 8.5" x 11" sheet of handwritten notes, both sides**.
- If your final score beats your midterm, it **replaces** the midterm. That puts 30% + 35% = 65% of your grade on this one exam.

## What the midterm rewarded

| Topic | Midterm share |
|---|---|
| Algorithm analysis (Big-O) | 25% |
| Pointers, references, dynamic memory | 23% |
| Recursion | 16% (+5 bonus) |
| Linked lists | 15% |
| Stacks and queues | 11% |
| Inheritance and polymorphism | 10% |

The final covers all of that plus everything after: searching, hashing, sorting, trees, BSTs, heaps, graphs, Dijkstra, and dynamic programming (DP and greedy are quiz-style only).

## How to use this course

Every chapter is a string of small lessons, one idea each, and each one builds on the one before. Most chapters follow a small story on campus, like a boba cafe or the Wellness Center's triage line. There are two kinds of lessons:

- **Quiz lessons** explain an idea, usually with a picture or a traced example, then ask 1 to 3 questions like the ones on the exam.
- **Code lessons** end with an **Assignment** checklist. You fill in the TODOs in real C++17. **Run** checks the basics; **Submit** runs every check, and it also fails on memory leaks and out-of-bounds access, so sloppy pointer code can't sneak by.

Many chapters build one file across several lessons. The code you finished earlier sits at the top of the starter under `// ---- done in earlier lessons ----`, so you can always see the whole thing.

> [!tip]
> The exam has no compiler. After you pass a code lesson, write the same function once more **on paper**, from memory. Anything you miss goes on your notes sheet.

lessons.title: Constructors and Init Lists
lessons.readme:
# Constructors and Init Lists

A brand new object shouldn't start with garbage in it. A **constructor** runs whenever an object is created. It has the class's name and no return type.

```cpp
BobaCafe() : num_drinks_served(0) {
    std::cout << "Boba Cafe Initialized." << std::endl;
}
```

The part after the colon is the **initializer list**. It runs before the body.

![memory, then the init list, then the constructor body](courses/diagrams/0c914b6b-4e70-53ca-b6fe-b15981a27111/steps.svg)

That order matters. By the time the body starts, every member already exists, so `=` in the body is an assignment. For some members that's too late:

- a `const` member can't be assigned
- a reference member must be bound when it's created
- a member whose class has no `Class()` constructor can't be built without arguments

Those three **must** use the list. For class-type members it also saves work, because assigning in the body means building the member first and then overwriting it.

That last case sneaks up on you. The compiler gives you a free `Class()` constructor only until you write **any** constructor of your own. After we write `BobaCooker(int capacity)`, a plain `BobaCooker c;` stops compiling.

> [!warning]
> Members are initialized in the order they're **declared** in the class, whatever order you list them in. Write the list in the same order.

A member can also get a default right where it's declared, like `int cups = 12;` inside the class. Any constructor that doesn't set `cups` in its init list starts it at 12. A member the init list does name gets the list's value instead.

## Assignment

Give the cafe a cooker that starts out full.

1. [ ] Give `BobaCooker(int capacity)` an init list: set `capacity`, start `servings_left` at that capacity, and `refill_count` at 0.
2. [ ] Give `BobaCafe()` an init list: build `bobaCooker` with capacity 3, and start `num_drinks_served` at 0.

The starter won't compile until you do. Read the error first: it's complaining about the two members that have to be in a list.

lessons.title: Destructors
lessons.readme:
# Destructors

When a cafe closes, somebody has to clean up. A **destructor** is the method that runs when an object dies.

```cpp
~BobaCafe() {
    std::cout << "Number of drinks served: " << num_drinks_served << std::endl;
}
```

It's `~` plus the class name, with **no parameters and no return type**, and there's **only one** per class. You never call it yourself. It runs automatically:

- for a local (stack) object, when it **goes out of scope**
- for an object made with `new`, when you **`delete`** it (no `delete`, no destructor)

Locals die in the reverse of the order they were made.

![two cafes constructed and destroyed as their scopes end](courses/diagrams/733bb6c8-4f3b-58c8-8c14-09bd1e430438/life.svg)

If a class owns something, like memory from `new`, the destructor is where it gives that back. Our cafe owns nothing like that, but it does need to update the company's books.

## Assignment

Track every cafe with the static members.

1. [ ] In the constructor, add 1 to `num_open`.
2. [ ] In the destructor, subtract 1 from `num_open`, and add this cafe's `num_drinks_served` to `total_served`.
3. [ ] Complete the static functions `getNumOpen()` and `getTotalServed()`.

lessons.title: Writing a Constructor and Destructor
lessons.readme:
# Writing a Constructor and Destructor

A quiz favorite: you get a class with one private member and two empty boxes, "write the constructor" and "write the destructor." No starter signatures, so every character is yours. Here's the shape to memorize, for a class with a `double` member:

```cpp
class Kettle {
    double liters;
public:
    Kettle(double l) : liters(l) {}                                 // constructor
    ~Kettle() { std::cout << "Kettle cooled." << std::endl; }      // destructor
};
```

**The constructor**

- Its name is exactly the class name. No return type, not even `void`.
- The parameter's type matches the member it fills: a `double` member takes a `double` parameter, not an `int` (an `int` would chop `1.5` down to `1`).
- After the colon goes `member(parameter)`. It's the **member's** name there, not the class name, and no `=`: `liters(l)`, not `Kettle(liters = l)`.
- It still needs a body, even an empty one: `{}`.

**The destructor**

- It's `~` plus the class name, with **empty** parentheses: `~Kettle()`. No parameters, no return type.
- It has **no init list**. Only constructors get a colon list.
- "Prints" means `std::cout << ... << std::endl;`. A destructor can't `return` a value, and returning a string wouldn't print anything anyway.
- You never call it. It runs by itself when the object goes out of scope, or at `delete` for an object made with `new`.

> [!warning]
> Copy the message exactly, punctuation included. `"Kettle cooled."` and `"kettle cooled"` are different output.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Write `Speaker`'s constructor: it takes the volume as a `double` and sets `volume` in an init list.
2. [ ] Write the destructor: it prints `Speaker off.` followed by `std::endl`.

It won't compile until the constructor exists.

lessons.title: Headers and Separate Compilation
lessons.readme:
# Headers and Separate Compilation

The simulator is getting long, and real programs get into the millions of lines. Recompiling all of that after every small edit would be painfully slow. So we split it up:

- a **header** (`.h`) holds the declarations: the interface
- a **source file** (`.cpp`) holds the definitions: the implementation

Each `.cpp` is compiled by itself into an object file. The **linker** then joins those, plus the standard library, into one program.

![two source files compiled separately, then linked](courses/diagrams/306c2ad6-54e8-5851-935e-3c5ffb59b65e/build.svg)

Now change one line in `teabrewer.cpp`:

![after one edit only one object file is rebuilt](courses/diagrams/306c2ad6-54e8-5851-935e-3c5ffb59b65e/edit.svg)

Only that file gets recompiled, then everything is relinked. Besides speed, this lets you ship a library without its source, hides the implementation, and lets people work in parallel once the interfaces are set.

`#include` just pastes the header in. An **include guard** keeps one header from being pasted twice into the same file:

```cpp
#ifndef BOBACAFE_H      // top of bobacafe.h
#define BOBACAFE_H

class BobaCafe { /* ... */ };

#endif                  // bottom
```

`#pragma once` at the top does the same job. Nearly every compiler has it, but it is **not standard** C++.

> [!note]
> The code lessons here keep everything in one header so there's a single file to edit. On paper and in the labs, put method definitions in the `.cpp`.

answers: Two `.cpp` files using the same header
Other files reading the private members

One header pasted twice into the same file
questions.answer: One header pasted twice into the same file

questions.question: What is true of `#pragma once`?
answers: It makes the linker skip unchanged object files
It works like a guard but isn't standard C++
It must go at the bottom of the header file
It is the only standard form of include guard
questions.answer: It works like a guard but isn't standard C++

lessons.title: Is-A and Has-A
lessons.readme:
# Is-A and Has-A

Business is good, so the owner buys a food truck. We need a `MobileBobaCafe`. There are two ways for one class to use another, and one question picks between them: is it an "is-a" or a "has-a"?

![a food truck with an open service window and customers lining up](courses/diagrams/550505c3-2643-5438-b66b-7995a434a907/food-truck.jpg)
*Image: Kurtkaiser, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.*

A food truck is still a cafe: it takes orders and serves drinks. It also has things a shop doesn't, like a propane tank.

![an is-a arrow to the base class and has-a arrows to the members](courses/diagrams/550505c3-2643-5438-b66b-7995a434a907/both.svg)

**Inheritance** is **is-a**. A mobile cafe is a boba cafe, so it gets everything a cafe has and can be treated as one. The existing class is the **base** (parent), the new one is the **derived** (child).

**Composition** is **has-a**. A cafe has a tea brewer, so the brewer is a member. A has-a can also be **many**: a `Menu` that holds a `std::vector<Drink>` member has drinks, and can add, remove and reorder them. A menu is not a kind of drink, so it doesn't inherit from `Drink`, and `Drink` doesn't inherit from `Menu` either.

```cpp
class MobileBobaCafe : public BobaCafe {   // is-a
    float propane_remaining;               // has-a
};
```

A derived class inherits **all** the members, even the private ones. That doesn't mean it can touch them. The `public` after the colon is the **inheritance access specifier**:

| In the base it's… | public inheritance | private inheritance |
|---|---|---|
| public | stays public | becomes private |
| private | inherited, but inaccessible | inherited, but inaccessible |

There's a third level, **protected**: hidden from outside code like private, but usable by derived classes.

> [!tip]
> Lab 8 has a protected `root`. When both classes are templates, the derived one has to write `this->root` or the compiler won't find it.

A class can also inherit from several parents, though we won't need to.

answers: `cash` is not part of a `Cart` at all

lessons.title: Extending the Cafe
lessons.readme:
# Extending the Cafe

A derived class can **extend** its base with new members, and it can customize a method by writing its own.

![a mobile cafe object containing a whole base-class part](courses/diagrams/44b1fab1-a6ae-5fa3-b2bb-8205576019dc/parts.svg)

**Constructors and destructors are not inherited.** The base part gets built first, so call the base constructor in the init list:

```cpp
MobileBobaCafe() : BobaCafe(), propane_remaining(15.0f) {}
```

`BobaCafe()` is optional there, because the base has a default constructor that does what we want. If the base needed an argument, you'd have to write `Base(x)`.

**Reuse the base method by naming it.** The truck's `doOrder` checks the propane, then lets the normal cafe do the real work:

```cpp
return BobaCafe::doOrder(customer_name);
```

Leave off the `BobaCafe::` and the function calls itself.

> [!warning]
> This `doOrder` isn't `virtual`, so it only **hides** the base's version. Which one runs is settled at compile time by the type you call through. A `BobaCafe&` to a truck runs the plain cafe's `doOrder`. We fix that next lesson.

## Assignment

Finish the truck. Making one drink burns 1 unit of propane.

1. [ ] In the constructor's init list, start `propane_remaining` at 15.
2. [ ] `addPropane(amount)`: if `amount` is above 0, add it and return `true`. Otherwise return `false`.
3. [ ] `doOrder(customer_name)`: with 1 unit or less left, return an empty `Drink()`. Otherwise burn 1 unit and return what the base class's `doOrder` returns.

lessons.title: Virtual Functions
lessons.readme:
# Virtual Functions

The cafe now sells hot tea and cold brew. `doOrder` shouldn't care which brewer is plugged in. It should say "add tea" and have the right thing happen. One interface, many types: that's **polymorphism**.

A base-class pointer is allowed to point at a derived object. The question is whose method runs. For a normal method, the **pointer's** type decides, at compile time:

![without virtual the pointer type picks the function](courses/diagrams/be5110e3-6825-5df3-a950-93620046b7fd/plain.svg)

Put `virtual` on the base's method and the **object's** actual type decides, while the program runs. That's called **dynamic dispatch**:

![with virtual the object type picks the function](courses/diagrams/be5110e3-6825-5df3-a950-93620046b7fd/virtual.svg)

```cpp
class TeaBrewerImpl {
public:
    virtual ~TeaBrewerImpl() {}
    virtual void addTea(Drink& drink) { drink.tea_type = "House Tea"; }
};
```

- The same goes for calls through a base **reference**.
- If the object's class didn't override the method, the **nearest base version** runs.
- What matters is `virtual` **in the base**. A derived method with the same signature overrides it, with or without writing `virtual` again. The word `override` only asks the compiler to double-check, and the lecture code leaves it out.
- If you'll `delete` through a base pointer, the base **destructor must be virtual**. Otherwise it's undefined behavior, and usually the derived destructor is skipped.

## Assignment

Make the brewers polymorphic.

1. [ ] Make `TeaBrewerImpl`'s destructor and its `addTea` virtual.
2. [ ] In `ColdBrewTeaBrewerImpl`, override `addTea` to set `tea_type` to `"Cold Brew"`.
3. [ ] Leave `DecafTeaBrewerImpl` empty and watch which version it gets.

lessons.title: Abstract Classes
lessons.readme:
# Abstract Classes

"House Tea" was a silly default. There's no such thing as a brewer in general, only specific kinds. So the lecture's base class refuses to define `addTea` at all:

```cpp
class TeaBrewerImpl {
public:
    virtual ~TeaBrewerImpl() = default;
    virtual void addTea(Drink& workingDrink) = 0;   // pure virtual
};
```

![an abstract brewer with three derived classes](courses/diagrams/70ee0de4-5143-5b33-a703-dd31c084f20c/tree.svg)

| | `virtual` | pure virtual (`= 0`) |
|---|---|---|
| body in the base | yes, a working one | no |
| derived classes | **may** override | **must** override |
| through a base pointer | the object's version runs | the object's version runs |
| makes the class abstract | no | **yes** |

A class with a pure virtual function is **abstract**. You can't create one, but you can have pointers and references to it. A derived class that forgets to override is abstract too.

The payoff: add a Matcha brewer by writing one new class, with no `if` or `switch` to hunt down in `doOrder`. And one list of base pointers can hold every kind of brewer.

Polymorphism comes in two flavors:

- **Dynamic**, at run time: virtual functions.
- **Static**, at compile time: overloaded functions and operators, and templates. An overload is picked by the number and types of the arguments, like `price(int)` and `price(int, int)`.

So the full definition of polymorphism is: **code written against one interface works correctly with several different types, and the right behavior is picked at compile time or at run time from their actual types.** Overloading alone is only the static half. Reusing a base class's members is inheritance, and bundling data with functions behind an interface is encapsulation. Neither is polymorphism.

questions.question: `virtual void f() {}` vs. `virtual void f() = 0;`. Which is true?
answers: Both can be overridden, and both make the class abstract
Only `= 0` uses dynamic dispatch through a base pointer
Both can be overridden; only `= 0` makes it abstract
Only `= 0` can be overridden by a derived class
questions.answer: Both can be overridden; only `= 0` makes it abstract

answers: Creates a derived object behind the scenes

questions.question: Which best describes polymorphism?
answers: Several functions sharing one name with different parameter lists
One interface serving many types, picked at compile or run time
Data and functions bundled together behind a public interface
A derived class receiving the data and methods of its base class
questions.answer: One interface serving many types, picked at compile or run time

lessons.title: Where Variables Live
lessons.readme:
# Where Variables Live

The housing office wants a campus app that tracks every dorm room at Campus Village: how many beds each room has, who's on the waitlist, what each room costs. Before we write any of it in C++, we need a picture of where all that data actually lives while the program runs.

![two green DDR4 RAM sticks with black memory chips](courses/diagrams/4a1adf95-626f-5a68-803a-636473cfbcf3/ram.jpg)
*Image: Dsimic, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.*

That's RAM: a few chips holding billions of bytes. Real hardware is messy: RAM, caches, SSDs, registers. The operating system and the CPU's MMU (memory management unit) hide all of that behind **virtual memory**. Your program gets to pretend memory is one huge array of bytes, and each byte's **address** is just its index in that array.

That big array is split into regions. Here's the layout from lecture, with the highest addresses on top:

![memory regions from high address to low: args, stack, unused, heap, BSS, data, text](courses/diagrams/4a1adf95-626f-5a68-803a-636473cfbcf3/layout.svg)

- **Stack**: local variables, function parameters and local objects. Each function call gets its own chunk, and it's gone the moment the function returns. The stack grows **down**, toward lower addresses.
- **Heap**: anything you make with `new`. It stays until you `delete` it, no matter which function made it. The heap grows **up**.
- **BSS**: globals and statics with no starting value.
- **Data**: globals and statics that do have a starting value.
- **Text**: your compiled code.

The stack and heap grow toward each other into the unused gap in the middle. Everything except the stack and heap lasts for the whole program.

> [!note]
> Real systems shuffle these addresses a bit each run for security (ASLR). The lecture ignores that, and so will we.

As more functions get called, the stack grows toward:

lessons.title: Stack or Heap?
lessons.readme:
# Stack or Heap?

Our app has a `Room` class. Look at where each piece of this code ends up:

```cpp
int main() {
    Room* r = new Room();   // r: stack.  the Room it points to: heap
    Room spare = *r;        // spare: stack (a copy, made by the copy constructor)
    r->print();
    delete r;               // frees the heap Room. r itself is still on the stack
}
```

![r on the stack points to a Room on the heap; spare is a separate Room on the stack](courses/diagrams/f30f5024-bd36-5324-a3d9-a4debd984ba3/pic.svg)

The rule is simple once you see it:

- A variable **declared in a function** is on the stack. That includes a pointer variable like `r` and a whole object like `spare`.
- The thing **`new` creates** is on the heap. `new` hands back its address, and we keep that address in `r`.

`Room spare = *r;` doesn't share the heap Room. It builds a brand new `Room` on the stack and copies the heap one into it. (That copying is done by the **copy constructor**, which gets its own lessons later in this chapter.)

Why use the heap at all? Lifetime. When `main` returns, `r` and `spare` vanish automatically. A heap object stays alive until **you** say `delete`, so a function can create a room record and hand it back to whoever called it.

questions.question: Which of these is still alive after the function that created it returns?
answers: The pointer that held new's result

lessons.title: Pointers: An Address Plus a Type
lessons.readme:
# Pointers: An Address Plus a Type

Addresses alone are too low-level. Code doesn't think in bytes; it thinks in typed things: an `int`, a `Room`, an array. So C++ pairs the two:

**A pointer is an address plus a type.**

```cpp
int beds = 4;          // an int
int* pb = &beds;       // a pointer to an int: holds beds's address
```

![pb holds the address of beds](courses/diagrams/a25600e8-8b36-5576-a4d5-397cd1fe06fb/pic.svg)

`beds` sits at some address, here `0xffd2`. `pb` is its own variable at its own address (`0x2718`), and the value stored inside it is `0xffd2`. The type `int*` tells the compiler what's at the other end, so it knows how many bytes to read and what they mean.

Two operators go with pointers:

| Operator | Name | Example | Gives you |
|---|---|---|---|
| `&x` | address-of | `&beds` | where `beds` lives |
| `*p` | dereference | `*pb` | the thing `pb` points at |

So `*pb` is `4`, and writing through it changes the real variable:

```cpp
*pb = 6;            // beds is now 6
cout << beds;       // 6
```

A pointer can point at a single object, like here, or at the first element of an array, which we'll see soon.

Keep the definition sharp, because quizzes offer look-alikes:

- A pointer is **not** another name for a variable. That's a reference (coming up). A pointer is its own variable holding an address.
- A pointer is **not** tied to the stack. The pointer itself can live on the stack, on the heap, or in global storage, and so can what it points at.
- A pointer frees **nothing** by itself. Memory from `new` stays until you `delete` it.

questions.question: What does the pointer variable `pb` itself store?
answers: A copy of the value in `beds`

questions.question: In one phrase, what is a pointer?
answers: A second name bound to an existing variable
An address paired with the type stored there
A variable that can only exist on the stack
An object that releases its own memory
questions.answer: An address paired with the type stored there

lessons.title: Pointers to Pointers
lessons.readme:
# Pointers to Pointers

A pointer is a variable, so it has an address too. That means you can point at a pointer.

```cpp
int floor = 3;           // an int
int* pf = &floor;        // pointer to int
int** ppf = &pf;         // pointer to pointer to int
int*** pppf = &ppf;      // and one more level
```

![pppf points to ppf, which points to pf, which points to floor](courses/diagrams/e9d6226d-2166-5a53-bbe8-86b71b83e8c0/pic.svg)

Each `*` you apply follows **one** arrow. Count the stars to know where you end up:

| Expression | Follows | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `pf` | nothing | address of `floor` |
| `*pf` | 1 arrow | 3 |
| `*ppf` | 1 arrow | address of `floor` |
| `**ppf` | 2 arrows | 3 |
| `**pppf` | 2 arrows | address of `floor` |
| `***pppf` | 3 arrows | 3 |

A quick check: the stars in the type minus the stars you apply tells you what's left. `pppf` is `int***`; apply two and you have an `int*`, which is an address.

> [!warning]
> `ppf = &&floor;` is **not** legal. C++ reads `&&` as one operator, and even spelled `&(&floor)` it fails: `&floor` gives you a temporary value, not a variable sitting in memory, so it has no address to take. You need the named pointer `pf` in between.

questions.question: Is `int** ppf = &(&floor);` legal C++?
answers: No, `&floor` is a temporary with no address
Yes, but only if `floor` is const
Yes, it gives the same address as `&pf` would
No, because `int**` cannot hold an address
questions.answer: No, `&floor` is a temporary with no address

lessons.title: Swap Through Pointers
lessons.readme:
# Swap Through Pointers

Two students want to trade rooms. The app keeps each student's room number in an `int`, and we want a function that swaps them **in the caller's variables**.

A pointer is how a function reaches back into the caller. Pass the addresses, and the function can write through them:

```cpp
int x = 214, y = 108;
swapPtr(&x, &y);     // afterward x is 108 and y is 214
```

Inside `swapPtr`, `a` and `b` are local pointer variables holding those two addresses. The swap needs a temporary to hold one **value** while the other is copied over:

![swap steps 1 and 2](courses/diagrams/9cad54e5-597c-5c26-83f6-6b68a106922b/a.svg)

![swap step 3 and the result](courses/diagrams/9cad54e5-597c-5c26-83f6-6b68a106922b/b.svg)

Read the pictures from left to right:

1. `int tmp = *a;` saves the value at `a` (214).
2. `*a = *b;` copies 108 into `x`.
3. `*b = tmp;` puts the saved 214 into `y`.

`a` and `b` never change; only the ints they point at do. When the function returns, its frame disappears, and the caller's `x` and `y` keep the new values.

## Assignment

This is the start of `rooms.h`, a small file of room helpers we'll keep adding to.

1. [ ] Complete `swapPtr(a, b)` so it swaps the two ints that `a` and `b` point at.

It should also work when `a` and `b` point at the same int (nothing changes then), and on elements of an array, like `swapPtr(&rooms[0], &rooms[1])`.

> [!warning]
> The mistakes that cost points on paper:
> - **Swapping the pointers instead of the values.** `int* t = a; a = b; b = t;` only trades the two local copies of the addresses. The caller's ints never change. Every assignment that does the work has a `*` on the left.
> - **A temp with no type, or the wrong one.** Write `int tmp = *a;`. Plain `tmp = *a;` doesn't compile, and `int* tmp = *a;` doesn't either.
> - **Saving the address, not the value.** `int* tmp = a;` compiles but gets overwritten by `*a = *b;` (Swap Traps, next).

lessons.title: Swap Traps
lessons.readme:
# Swap Traps

The exam likes to hand you a swap with one line changed. There are two different ways it can go wrong, and you need to tell them apart.

**Trap 1: it doesn't compile.**

```cpp
int* tmp = *a;      // error: *a is an int, tmp is an int*
```

`*a` is a value, not an address. C++ won't put an `int` into an `int*`, so this is a **compile error**, not a wrong answer at run time.

**Trap 2: it compiles but gives the wrong answer.**

```cpp
void swapBad(int* a, int* b) {
    int* tmp = a;   // saves the ADDRESS, not the value
    *a = *b;        // overwrites the value tmp points at
    *b = *tmp;      // reads the new value back
}
```

`tmp` and `a` point at the same int. Once `*a = *b` runs, the old value is gone, so both variables end up holding `b`'s value. With `x = 1, y = 2`, you get `2 2`.

The fix is always the same: save the **value**, `int tmp = *a;`.

> [!tip]
> When you trace pointer code by hand, draw a box for every variable and an arrow for every pointer. Then do one line at a time and cross out the old value in a box when it changes.

questions.question: What happens with `int* tmp = *a;` inside a swap function where `a` is an `int*`?

lessons.title: References
lessons.readme:
# References

Pointers work, but all those `*` and `&` make code noisy. C++ has a second tool: the **reference**.

A reference is **another name for an existing object**. It's not a copy, and it doesn't need dereferencing.

```cpp
int beds = 2;
int& r = beds;     // r is just another name for beds
r = 5;             // beds is now 5
beds++;            // r sees it too: 6
```

![one int with two names](courses/diagrams/36167b4e-c3e9-5769-a4c3-ca4d634e16d0/pic.svg)

How do references compare with pointers? Here's the lecture's table:

| | Pointer | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Declare without initializing | yes | no: `int& r;` won't compile |
| Can be null (`nullptr`) | yes | no, always refers to something |
| Can be re-pointed later | yes | no, stuck to one object |
| Needs `*` and `&` to use | yes | no, works like a normal variable |
| Arithmetic (`p + 1`) | yes | no |
| Multiple levels (`int**`) | yes | no, only one level |

References look less capable, and they are on purpose: they **give up flexibility in exchange for guarantees**. No null checks, no re-binding, cleaner syntax, and more room for the compiler to optimize. The lecture's advice: **prefer references over pointers when you can.**

> [!note]
> `&` means different things in different places. `&i` is address-of. `int& r` declares a reference. `a & b` is bitwise AND, `a && b` is logical AND, and `a &= m` is bitwise AND-assign. Read what's around it.

questions.question: Does `int& r;` (with nothing after it) compile?
answers: Yes, it starts out as null
Yes, it refers to a hidden temporary 0
No, a reference must be initialized
questions.answer: No, a reference must be initialized

questions.question: Which of these can a pointer do that a reference cannot?
answers: Modify the value of the original object
Point at a different object later
questions.answer: Point at a different object later

lessons.title: Pass by Reference
lessons.readme:
# Pass by Reference

Change one character and `square` works:

```cpp
void square(int& i) {    // a reference to the caller's int
    i = i * i;
}
int main() { int i = 5; square(i); cout << i; }   // 25
```

![square refers to main's i](courses/diagrams/ba9e6a38-b7fe-5e41-b102-eb6ea181ca44/pic.svg)

Now `i` inside `square` is **another name for main's `i`**. No copy is made, and the change sticks.

The lecture points out this is **bad style** for a function like `square`: someone reading `square(i)` at the call site has no hint that `i` will change. Modify a caller's variable only when that's clearly the function's job (like a swap).

## const references

Often you want the speed of a reference (no copy of a big object) but promise not to change it. That's `const`:

```cpp
void square(const int& i) {
    i = i * i;          // compile error: i is read-only
}

int square(const int& i) {
    return i * i;       // fine: reads i, returns a new value
}
```

`const T&` is the usual way to pass a big object like a `std::string` or a `vector`: no copy, and the caller knows it won't be changed.

| Parameter | Copies? | Can change caller? |
|---|---|---|
| `int i` | yes | no |
| `int& i` | no | yes |
| `const int& i` | no | no (compile error if you try) |
| `int* p` | copies the address | yes, through `*p` |

answers: It runs but the result is undefined

lessons.title: Returning a Reference
lessons.readme:
# Returning a Reference

Functions can **return** a reference too. Whether that's safe depends on one question: **does the thing outlive the function?**

This one compiles and is safe, even if it looks odd:

```cpp
const int& square(int& i) {
    i = i * i;
    return i;           // i is the caller's variable: still alive after we return
}
int main() { int i = 4; int j = square(i); cout << i << " " << j; }   // 16 16
```

This one is a bug:

```cpp
const int& square(const int& i) {
    int res = i * i;
    return res;         // DANGER: res is a local
}
```

![main holds a reference into square's frame, which no longer exists](courses/diagrams/e5abdbc3-8af2-5906-b791-6d699f8721cd/pic.svg)

`res` lives in `square`'s stack frame. The moment `square` returns, that frame is gone, so the caller gets a reference to memory that no longer holds a valid `int`. That's a **dangling reference**. It might even print the right number once, then break later when another call reuses that stack space.

The rule: **never return a reference or a pointer to a local variable.** A by-value parameter counts as a local too, because it's a copy that lives in the function's frame.

Returning **by value** (`int square(...)`) is always safe: the result is copied out before the frame goes away.

Two wrong explanations show up as options, so rule them out too:

- It **does compile**. A non-const local can be changed (`res += 3;` is fine) and still be returned as a `const int&`. At most the compiler warns you.
- It is **not a leak**. Nothing was made with `new`, so there's nothing to `delete`. The problem is the opposite one: the memory is reclaimed too soon.

questions.question: Which function returns a dangling reference?
answers: `const int& f(int& i) { int r = i*i; i = r; return i; }`
`int f(const int& i) { int r = i*i; return r; }`
`const int& f(const int& i) { int r = i*i; return r; }`
questions.answer: `const int& f(const int& i) { int r = i*i; return r; }`

answers: It leaks memory, because `out` is never deleted
It is safe, because `x` is passed in by reference
Unsafe: it returns a reference to a destroyed local
It fails to compile, because `out` is changed with `-=`
questions.answer: Unsafe: it returns a reference to a destroyed local

answers: Undefined: it returns a dangling reference

lessons.title: const and Pointers
lessons.readme:
# const and Pointers

The room records in our app shouldn't be edited by a function that only prints them. `const` lets the compiler enforce that, and with pointers it can apply in two places: to the **thing pointed at**, or to the **pointer itself**.

The trick from lecture: **read the declaration right to left.**

```cpp
River nile2;                    // an ordinary River
const River nile;               // a const River
const River* nilePc;            // a pointer to a const River
River* const nileCp = &nile2;   // a const pointer to a River
const River* const nileCpc = &nile2;   // a const pointer to a const River
```

| Declaration | Change the River through it? | Re-point it? |
|---|---|---|
| `const River* p` | no | yes |
| `River* const p` | yes | no, and it must be initialized |
| `const River* const p` | no | no |

![three pointer declarations: const on the left of the star locks the River, const on the right locks the pointer](courses/diagrams/9eb4b762-1d30-58b9-897f-611623c9dedb/pic.svg)

A pointer-to-const is the pointer version of `const T&`:

```cpp
void printSquare(const int* pi) {
    *pi = (*pi) * (*pi);     // compile error: can't change an int through a const int*
    cout << *pi << endl;
}
```

> [!tip]
> Find the `*`. A `const` to its **left** protects the object. A `const` to its **right** protects the pointer.

questions.question: `River* const p = &nile;` declares:
answers: A pointer to a const River
A const pointer to a River
A const copy of a River
A const reference to a River
questions.answer: A const pointer to a River

lessons.title: new and delete
lessons.readme:
# new and delete

Each room in the app gets a `Room` record, and the records have to stick around after the function that created them returns. That's exactly what the heap is for.

```cpp
Room* r = new Room();    // allocate one Room on the heap and run its constructor
r->print();
delete r;                // run its destructor and free the memory
```

| | What it does |
|---|---|
| `new T()` | allocates one `T` on the heap, calls its constructor, returns its address |
| `delete p` | calls the destructor of the one object at `p`, frees it |

There are three common ways to end up with a pointer, and only one of them should ever be passed to `delete`:

```cpp
int* p = new int();      // 1. from new: you own it, delete it once
int* r = p;              // 2. a copy of another pointer: same object, don't delete twice
int i;
int* s = &i;             // 3. address of a local: DANGER if it outlives i. Never delete it
```

**Every `new` needs a matching `delete`.** C++ has no garbage collector to clean up after you. (Smart pointers can help, but this class doesn't cover them.)

![before and after delete: r still holds the old address](courses/diagrams/f87429ba-2873-587d-a468-c394aa7d47d7/pic.svg)

> [!warning]
> `delete r;` does **not** change `r`. It still holds the same address, which now points at freed memory. More on that in Dangling Pointers.

questions.question: What does `new Room()` return?
answers: The address of the new Room
A copy of the new Room
The size of a Room in bytes
A reference to the new Room
questions.answer: The address of the new Room

lessons.title: new[] and delete[]
lessons.readme:
# new[] and delete[]

The app also needs a whole block of rooms at once, one per room on a floor. `new` has an array form for that:

```cpp
Room* floor = new Room[4];   // 4 Rooms on the heap, constructor runs 4 times
Room copy = floor[2];        // a stack copy of element 2
floor[3].print();
delete[] floor;              // destructor runs 4 times, block freed
```

![floor on the stack points at element 0 of four Rooms on the heap](courses/diagrams/d5952d36-c464-57a5-9571-bc856fd792f0/pic.svg)

`floor` holds the address of element **`[0]`**, the first Room. Elements sit next to each other in memory, so `floor[2]` is found by stepping two Rooms past that address.

| Allocate with | Free with | Constructors / destructors |
|---|---|---|
| `new T()` | `delete p` | 1 |
| `new T[n]` | `delete[] p` | n |

Mixing them up is **undefined behavior**:

```cpp
Room* floor = new Room[4];
delete floor;      // BAD: should be delete[]
delete[] floor;    // GOOD
```

With plain `delete`, C++ treats it as one object. It won't run all four destructors and won't free the block properly.

> [!note]
> After `delete[] floor;` the variable `floor` still holds the **same address as before**. It isn't set to `nullptr` for you.

answers: `list` must be set to nullptr first
Objects cannot be allocated as arrays

questions.question: After `delete[] scores;`, what does `scores` hold?
answers: The value of its first element

lessons.title: Memory Leaks
lessons.readme:
# Memory Leaks

The housing app runs all semester. If it forgets to free memory, it slowly eats more and more until it crashes. That's a **memory leak**.

A leak happens when you **lose the last pointer** to a heap block before you `delete` it. Once nothing points at it, nothing can ever free it. Three common ways:

- **Reassign** the only pointer: `p = new int[20];` while `p` held the only pointer to an older block.
- **Return** from a function without deleting what it allocated.
- **Overwrite** it with another pointer or `nullptr`.

Trace this one line by line:

```cpp
void f() {
    int* p = new int[8];
    int* q = new int[3];
    int* r = p;       // copies the pointer only: r and p share the 8-int block
    q = p;            // the 3-int block just lost its last pointer
    delete[] r;       // frees the 8-int block, once
}
```

![after q = p, nothing points at the 3-int block](courses/diagrams/42685868-f5b0-5aa5-a673-674351eca401/pic.svg)

`int* r = p;` doesn't make a second block, it just makes a second arrow to the same block. So the 8-int block must be deleted **exactly once**, through either name. The 3-int block is the leak: after `q = p`, no pointer anywhere holds its address.

The lecture's advice: memory bugs are gnarly to track down, so be careful whenever you **copy a pointer**. Code should make it clear who **owns** each pointer (who's responsible for deleting it), and document it when ownership is handed off.

lessons.title: Dangling Pointers
lessons.readme:
# Dangling Pointers

A leak is memory nobody points at. A **dangling** (or **stale**) pointer is the opposite: a pointer to memory that's already gone.

```cpp
Room* floor = new Room[4];
Room copy = floor[2];
delete[] floor;
floor[0].print();     // BUG: floor dangles. It still holds the old address
```

`delete[]` frees the block but leaves `floor` holding the same address. Using it afterward reads or writes memory that may now belong to something else. The program might keep working for a while, which is what makes these bugs so nasty.

Ways to get a dangling pointer:

- Use a pointer after `delete` (above).
- **Delete twice**: `int* q = p; delete p; delete q;` frees the same block twice, which is undefined behavior.
- Keep `&local` after the local is gone, like returning the address of a local variable. (And never `delete` a pointer you got from `&`.)

The habit that helps: after you delete, set the pointer to `nullptr` yourself.

```cpp
delete[] floor;
floor = nullptr;      // now a later mistake is an obvious null pointer, not silent garbage
```

`delete` on a `nullptr` is allowed and does nothing, so this also makes a second accidental `delete` of that same variable harmless (other copies of the pointer still dangle).

answers: `q` is a separate copy of the int
Nothing, each pointer is deleted once
The same block is deleted twice
questions.answer: The same block is deleted twice

lessons.title: C-Style Arrays
lessons.readme:
# C-Style Arrays

Our app stores the number of free beds in each room of a floor. The simplest tool is a built-in **C-style array**:

```cpp
int freeBeds[15];
```

What you get, from lecture:

- **Fixed length**, known when the array is created.
- **Contiguous**: elements sit side by side, from low to high addresses.
- **Indexed from 0**: `freeBeds[0]` through `freeBeds[14]`.
- **No bounds checking**: `freeBeds[15] = 1;` compiles and quietly writes past the end. That's undefined behavior.
- **May be uninitialized**: a local array holds garbage until you fill it.
- Designed for speed and memory efficiency.

## Two dimensions

`int g[2][2]` is an array of rows. You picture a grid, but in memory the rows are laid end to end. That's called **row-major** order:

![a 2 by 2 array as a grid and as four cells in a row](courses/diagrams/a8630619-05db-52f6-9bf1-89c498b31d9d/grid.svg)

So `&g[0][1] < &g[1][0]` is true: everything in row 0 comes before row 1. Going row by row (the inner loop over columns) walks memory in order, which is usually faster.

> [!note]
> The lecture asks you to name the "array features" a language could have: bounds checking, more than one dimension, storing the length, 0 or 1 indexing, initialization. C-style arrays skip most of them in exchange for speed.

answers: A compile error: index out of range

questions.question: In `int g[2][3];`, which element is stored right after `g[0][2]` in memory?

lessons.title: Arrays in Functions
lessons.readme:
# Arrays in Functions

How do you pass the free-beds array to a function? Like this:

```cpp
void report(int len, int array[], int* parray) { ... }

int main() {
    int beds[5] = {2, 1, 0, 3, 1};
    report(5, beds, beds);
}
```

Here's the surprise: in a parameter list, `int array[]` **means** `int* array`. The array isn't copied. `array` is a **local pointer** to the caller's first element, exactly like `parray`.

![array and parray in report both point at beds[0] in main](courses/diagrams/01fc930d-0008-502a-82b0-a070b7b2b0a2/pic.svg)

That has some consequences the exam loves:

- `array == parray` is **true**: both hold the address of `beds[0]`.
- `&array == &parray` is **false**: they're two separate local variables, each in its own spot on the stack.
- `array[i]`, `parray[i]` and `*(array + i)` are all the same element.
- Elements are contiguous, so `&beds[i + 1] == &beds[i] + 1`.
- The function can't know the length. `sizeof(array)` is the size of a **pointer**, so you always pass the length too.
- Writing `array[i] = 0;` changes the **caller's** array. No `&` needed.
- `&beds[2]` is an ordinary `int*` to that one element. Pass it to a function that takes `int*`, and `*p = ...` in there changes `beds[2]` in the caller. It compiles fine.

lessons.title: Searching an Array
lessons.readme:
# Searching an Array

A student asks: "is room 412 still on the open list?" The open rooms are in a C-style array, so we check them one by one. This is **linear search**, and quizzes ask you to write it from scratch:

```cpp
bool hasRoom(const int rooms[], int len, int room) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        if (rooms[i] == room) return true;   // found it: stop right away
    }
    return false;                            // checked every one: it isn't there
}
```

The shape is the whole lesson. `return true` sits **inside** the loop, the moment you find a match. `return false` sits **after** the loop, because you only know the answer is "no" once you've looked at every element.

> [!warning]
> The mistakes graders take points for:
> - **`return false` in an `else` inside the loop.** Then the function gives up after looking at `rooms[0]` alone. `{3, 8}` searched for 8 returns false. Never decide "not found" inside the loop.
> - **No `return false` at all.** Falling off the end of a `bool` function is undefined behavior.
> - **Wrong bounds.** Use `i = 0` and `i < len`. `i < len - 1` skips the last element, and `i <= len` reads past the end.
> - **Asking the array for its length.** A C-style array has no `.size()` or `.length`, and inside the function it's only a pointer. Use the `len` parameter.
> - **A flag declared inside the loop.** If you track `bool found`, declare it **before** the loop. A variable declared inside the loop's braces is gone after the loop.

The worst case is that the room isn't there: all `len` elements are checked, so linear search is O(n).

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `hasRoom(rooms, len, room)`: return `true` if `room` is among the first `len` elements of `rooms`, and `false` otherwise.

lessons.title: Insert Into a Fixed Array
lessons.readme:
# Insert Into a Fixed Array

Campus Village keeps a waitlist of room numbers in a fixed-size array. When a student with priority shows up, they go into a spot in the middle, everyone after them moves back one, and the last one falls off the end.

To open a gap at `idx`, every element from `idx` on has to shift one place to the right. The order matters: **go right to left.** Start by copying the second-to-last element into the last slot, and work back toward `idx`.

Here's inserting 9 at index 1 of `{1, 2, 3, 4}`:

![insert steps 1 and 2](courses/diagrams/aa9e134d-39bd-54e6-8ae4-d8fa81854d42/a.svg)

![insert steps 3 and 4](courses/diagrams/aa9e134d-39bd-54e6-8ae4-d8fa81854d42/b.svg)

```cpp
for (int i = n - 2; i >= idx; i--) arr[i + 1] = arr[i];
arr[idx] = val;
```

Why not left to right? Because each copy would overwrite the next element **before you've moved it**. You end up smearing one value across the rest of the array:

![a left to right shift copies 2 into every slot](courses/diagrams/aa9e134d-39bd-54e6-8ae4-d8fa81854d42/wrong.svg)

The array is full, so the old last element (4) is shifted out and lost. And an index outside `0` to `n - 1` is rejected, with no change at all. (The Lab 2 key calls `abort()` there. Our standalone function returns `false` instead, so it can be tested.)

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `insertAt(arr, n, idx, val)`. Shift right to left, put `val` at `idx`, and return `true`.
2. [ ] If `idx < 0` or `idx >= n`, return `false` and change nothing.

lessons.title: Array Operations Big O
lessons.readme:
# Array Operations Big O

The lecture makes a point worth remembering: **a data structure is defined by both what you can do with it and how fast each operation is.** So let's rate the array.

| Operation | Fast or slow | Big O | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Look up the element at index 5 | fast | O(1) | address = start + 5 × size |
| Change the element at index 7 | fast | O(1) | same math |
| Add to the end | fast, with a caveat | O(1) | only if there's room left |
| Add to the start | slow | O(n) | shift every element right |
| Add to the middle | slow | O(n) | shift everything after it |
| Remove from the middle | slow | O(n) | shift everything after it left |
| Find a value | slow | O(n) | check each one; faster if sorted (binary search) |
| Sort | slow | O(n log n) with a good algorithm | |

The caveat on adding to the end: a fixed array has no room once it's full. A growable array (like `std::vector`) has to copy everything into a bigger one, which you'll see in the analysis chapter.

`insertAt` from the last lesson is O(n): inserting at index 0 shifts n − 1 elements, and that's the worst case. Inserting at the last index shifts nothing, so its best case is O(1).

Why is reading `arr[i]` O(1) for any i?
answers: It checks each element until it gets to i
Its address is computed directly from i
questions.answer: Its address is computed directly from i

lessons.title: The Copy Constructor
lessons.readme:
# The Copy Constructor

Let's fix the shallow copy. We'll use a simpler class for the rest of this chapter: `IntArray`, a floor's bed counts on the heap.

A copy constructor takes the object to copy **by const reference** (by value would need a copy to make a copy, forever). It gives the new object its own array, then copies every element:

```cpp
IntArray(const IntArray& other) : data(new int[other.n]), n(other.n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) data[i] = other.data[i];
}
```

![a and b each point at their own heap array](courses/diagrams/cef9f2c4-b7a0-5add-b7ed-40864953a0cf/pic.svg)

Now the two objects are independent. Changing one doesn't touch the other, and each destructor deletes its own array once.

> [!warning]
> Members are initialized in the order they're **declared** in the class, not the order you list them. `data` is declared before `n`, so `data(new int[n])` would use `n` before it's set. Use `other.n` in the initializer.

## Assignment

The starter's copy constructor is the shallow default, written out.

1. [ ] Make it a deep copy: allocate a new array of `other.n` ints and copy every element into it.

Submit also checks a copy made by passing an `IntArray` **by value**, `IntArray c(b)` syntax, and copying an empty `IntArray(0)`. (Assignment with `=` is the next lesson.)

lessons.readme:
# When the Copy Constructor Runs

The copy constructor runs whenever a **new** object is created as a copy of another one. That happens in more places than you'd think:

```cpp
IntArray b = a;          // 1. creating b from a (even though it uses =)
IntArray c(a);           // 2. same thing, other syntax
show(a);                 // 3. show(IntArray x): passing BY VALUE
return x;                // 4. returning BY VALUE (the compiler may skip this one)
```

It does **not** run here:

```cpp
peek(a);                 // peek(const IntArray& x): a reference, no copy
b = a;                   // b already exists: this is operator=, not the copy constructor
```

That last pair is the classic exam question. The `=` sign doesn't decide it. What matters is whether the object on the left is **being created right now** (copy constructor) or **already exists** (assignment operator, `operator=`).

So passing objects by value isn't free: each call copies the whole array. That's one more reason to pass by `const&` when the function only reads.

questions.question: Which line calls `operator=` instead of the copy constructor? (`a` and `b` already exist.)

lessons.title: The Assignment Operator
lessons.readme:
# The Assignment Operator

`b = a;` when `b` already exists calls `operator=`. The default one copies members too, so it has the same shallow-copy problem, plus a new one: `b`'s old array is never freed.

Our version has four steps. This is straight from the Lab 2 solution:

```cpp
IntArray& operator=(const IntArray& other) {
    if (this == &other) return *this;   // 1. guard against self-assignment
    delete[] data;                      // 2. free what we already own
    n = other.n;                        // 3. reallocate and deep copy
    data = new int[n];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) data[i] = other.data[i];
    return *this;                       // 4. return *this, so a = b = c works
}
```

Here's `c = a;` where `c` held 1 int and `a` holds 3:

![operator= frees the old array, then allocates and copies](courses/diagrams/d80ef973-6ba9-5d53-b7df-2c9f3ff6b8a2/pic.svg)

Why each step matters:

1. **Self-assignment guard.** `a = a` would otherwise delete `a`'s array and then try to copy from it.
2. **Delete first.** Otherwise the old array leaks.
3. **Reallocate.** The sizes may differ, so you can't copy into the old array.
4. **Return `*this` by reference.** `a = b = c` runs as `a = (b = c)`, so `b = c` must give back `b` itself.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Add `operator=` to `IntArray` with all four steps. It must return `IntArray&`.

Tests check self-assignment, assigning to a smaller and a bigger `IntArray`, chaining, that the result is the object itself (not a copy), and that nothing leaks.

lessons.title: The Rule of Three
lessons.readme:
# The Rule of Three

Look at what `IntArray` needed. Because it owns heap memory, it needed:

1. a **destructor**, to `delete[]` the array,
2. a **copy constructor**, so a new copy gets its own array,
3. an **assignment operator**, so `b = a` frees `b`'s old array and deep copies.

That's the **rule of three**: if a class needs any one of these, it almost certainly needs all three. The trigger is usually a raw pointer member that the class owns. The compiler's defaults just copy members, which is fine for `int`s and `std::string`s, and wrong for an owned pointer.

| You write `b = a;` and... | What runs |
|---|---|
| `b` is being created on this line | copy constructor |
| `b` already exists | `operator=` |
| an object goes out of scope or is deleted | destructor |

The labs each wrote part of it. Lab 2's `arrayList` key has the destructor and `operator=`. Lab 4's linked list has the destructor and a copy constructor, which walks the other list and appends a **new** node for each element. By the rule of three, each is still missing one.

Why does `operator=` check `if (this == &other)` first?
answers: To avoid calling the copy constructor

lessons.title: Writing a Class Template
lessons.readme:
# Writing a Class Template

On the exam you may have to write template member functions **outside** the class, the way the lecture and the lab keys do. The syntax has two parts that are easy to forget:

```cpp
template <typename T>                    // 1. repeat this line on EVERY member
T& myArray<T>::operator[](int idx) {     // 2. myArray<T>::, with the <T>
    if (idx < 0 || idx >= allocated_size) {
        abort();                         // bounds check failed: stop the program
    }
    return array[idx];
}
```

Inside the class, `myArray` alone is fine. Outside, the class name is `myArray<T>`, and the compiler only knows what `T` is because of the `template` line right above.

This `operator[]` adds the **bounds checking** C-style arrays don't have. If the index is out of range it calls `abort()` (from `<cstdlib>`), which stops the program on the spot instead of quietly reading garbage.

> [!warning]
> Template code goes **entirely in the header**. The compiler has to see the full definition to generate `myArray<int>` when some `.cpp` file uses it, so you can't hide the member functions in a separate `.cpp`.

## Assignment

The constructor and destructor in `myarray.h` are written outside the class as examples. Until you add the two definitions below, the build stops with "undefined reference".

1. [ ] Below them, define `size()`, outside the class. It returns `allocated_size`.
2. [ ] Define `operator[]`, outside the class. It returns a reference to element `idx`, and calls `abort()` if `idx < 0` or `idx >= allocated_size`.

Tests use both `myArray<int>` and `myArray<std::string>`. Submit also checks that an index of `-1` or `size()` aborts.

lessons.title: Template Rules
lessons.readme:
# Template Rules

Three rules cover almost every template question.

**1. Every member defined outside the class repeats the template line and uses `<T>`.**

```cpp
template <typename T>
int myArray<T>::size() const { return allocated_size; }
```

Forget the `template` line and the compiler doesn't know what `T` is. Forget the `<T>` after the class name and `myArray` is only the template's name, not a type.

**2. Template code lives in the header (`.h`).** The compiler stamps out `myArray<int>` wherever it's used, so it needs the full source there, not just the declarations.

**3. You name the type when you use it**: `myArray<int> a(50);`. Each different type gives a separate generated class.

Our `operator[]` calls `abort()` on a bad index. Don't mix that up with the standard library, which works differently (next lesson):

| | Bad index |
|---|---|
| our `myArray` `[]` | `abort()` |
| `std::vector` / `std::array` `[]` | no check: undefined behavior |
| `std::vector` / `std::array` `.at(i)` | throws `std::out_of_range` |

questions.question: Why must a template class be fully defined in its header?
answers: Template code runs through the preprocessor only
The compiler needs it to generate each `T` version
The linker cannot read code compiled from a `.cpp`
Headers are compiled before any other file
questions.answer: The compiler needs it to generate each `T` version

questions.question: Which is a correct out-of-class definition of `size()` for `template <typename T> class myArray`?
answers: `template <typename T> int myArray::size() const { return allocated_size; }`
`template <typename T> int myArray<T>::size() const { return allocated_size; }`
`template <T> int myArray<typename T>::size() const { return allocated_size; }`
questions.answer: `template <typename T> int myArray<T>::size() const { return allocated_size; }`

lessons.title: STL Containers
lessons.readme:
# STL Containers

You won't hand-write `myArray` in real code. Every C++ compiler ships the **Standard Template Library (STL)**: templated **containers** (data structures), **algorithms**, and **iterators**, all standardized.

| `std::` | What it is | Covered in |
|---|---|---|
| `array` | fixed-size array, like a C array with extras | this chapter |
| `vector` | array that can grow: no fixed capacity, it reallocates when full | analysis |
| `list` | doubly linked list | linked lists |
| `forward_list` | singly linked list, no tail | linked lists |
| `deque` | blocks of arrays: O(1) at both ends and O(1) `[i]` | queues |
| `stack`, `queue` | adapters, built on `deque` by default | stacks and queues |
| `priority_queue` | max-heap | heaps |
| `unordered_map` | hash table with chaining | hashing |
| `map` | red-black tree, keys kept sorted | trees |

None of these are **fundamental types**. The fundamental types are built into the language: `int`, `char`, `double`, `bool`, `float` and so on.

`std::vector` checks bounds only if you ask:

```cpp
std::vector<int> v = {10, 20, 30, 40};
cout << v[2];      // 30, no bounds check
cout << v.at(3);   // 40, bounds checked
cout << v.at(10);  // throws std::out_of_range
```

lessons.title: Walking a List with Iterators
lessons.readme:
# Walking a List with Iterators

The app now keeps the free beds per room in a `std::list<int>`. A linked list has no `[i]`, so how do you loop over it?

With an **iterator**: a generalized pointer. It knows how to point at an element in a container, and how to move to the next one.

```cpp
for (std::list<int>::iterator it = beds.begin(); it != beds.end(); ++it)
    cout << *it;
```

- `begin()` points at the first element.
- `end()` points **one past the last**. It's a stopping marker, so never dereference it.
- `*it` is the element, `++it` moves forward, just like a pointer.

![a list of three with begin on the first node, an iterator on the second, and end one past the last](courses/diagrams/681c676f-8a52-520c-8f26-e23264316043/pic.svg)

Writing out the iterator type is long, so `auto` is common: `for (auto it = beds.begin(); ...)`. For a `const` list you get a `const_iterator`, which can read but not write.

The **range-based for loop** is the same loop with less typing:

```cpp
for (const auto& b : beds) cout << b;    // read each one
for (auto& b : beds) b += 1;             // change each one
for (auto b : beds) b += 1;              // BUG: changes a copy
```

The `&` matters. Without it, `b` is a copy of each element, and changing it does nothing to the list.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `totalFree(beds)`: return the sum of all the elements. Use an explicit iterator loop with `begin()` and `end()`.
2. [ ] Complete `addBeds(beds, k)`: add `k` to every element of the list, using a range-based for loop.

An empty list has a total of 0.

lessons.title: Pointer Tracing Review
lessons.readme:
# Pointer Tracing Review

Time to practice what the exam asks: trace pointer code by hand.

- Draw a box for every variable and write its value inside.
- Draw an arrow for every pointer. A reference is just a second name on an existing box.
- Go one line at a time. `*p = ...` changes the box the arrow points at. `p = ...` moves the arrow.
- Pointer arithmetic moves by **elements**: if `p` points at `a[0]`, `p + 2` points at `a[2]`.

Quick reference:

| Code | Means |
|---|---|
| `int* p = &x;` | p points at x |
| `*p = 5;` | x becomes 5 |
| `int& r = x;` | r is another name for x |
| `r = y;` | x gets y's **value** (r can't be re-pointed) |
| `int** pp = &p;` | `*pp` is p, `**pp` is x |

lessons.title: Memory and Copying Review
lessons.readme:
# Memory and Copying Review

The second half of the chapter, in one place:

- **Stack**: locals and parameters, gone when the function returns. **Heap**: from `new`, gone when you `delete`.
- `new` pairs with `delete`, `new[]` with `delete[]`. After a delete the pointer still holds the old address.
- **Leak**: the last pointer to a block is lost. **Dangling**: a pointer to a block that's gone. **Double delete**: freeing one block twice.
- An array parameter `int arr[]` is a pointer to the caller's first element. Pass the length.
- `insertAt` shifts **right to left**, O(n).
- Copy constructor = a new object made from another (including pass and return by value). `operator=` = an object that already exists. Both must **deep copy** an owned pointer. Rule of three.

lessons.title: The Seven Growth Functions
lessons.readme:
# The Seven Growth Functions

An old legend: a king offers a reward, and the inventor of chess asks for 1 grain of wheat on the first square, 2 on the second, 4 on the third, doubling each time. The last square alone needs 2⁶³ grains, and the board holds 2⁶⁴ − 1 in total. That's centuries of the world's wheat harvest. Growth rate matters more than the starting number.

![a chessboard with 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 grains on its first five squares](courses/diagrams/4e4b1299-6982-56a3-a29b-1352c92cf1ed/wheat-chessboard.jpg)
*Image: McGeddon, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.*

Seven functions show up again and again in this class:

| Function | Name | Lecture example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | constant | index an array |
| log n | logarithmic | binary search a sorted array |
| n | linear | search an unsorted array |
| n log n | n-log-n | heapsort, merge sort, quicksort (average case) |
| n² | quadratic | the insertion sort from the last lesson |
| n³ | cubic | three nested loops over the input |
| 2ⁿ | exponential | naive Fibonacci, Towers of Hanoi, the wheat and chessboard |

![growth curves of log n, n, n log n, n squared and 2 to the n](courses/diagrams/4e4b1299-6982-56a3-a29b-1352c92cf1ed/growth.svg)

At a billion steps per second and n = 1,000,000: n takes 1 ms, n log n about 20 ms, n² about 17 minutes, and n³ about 32 years. 2ⁿ with n = 100 would outlast the age of the universe (13.8 billion years) many times over.

> [!tip]
> Memorize the order: 1 < log n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ. Many exam questions are just "which of these grows faster?"

lessons.title: Doubling the Input
lessons.readme:
# Doubling the Input

Registration traffic doubles every year. If you know an algorithm's growth function, you can predict what doubling does without running anything.

| Function | n → 2n | Why |
|---|---|---|
| log n | adds **one** step | log(2n) = log n + 1 |
| n | doubles | 2n |
| n log n | a bit **more** than doubles | 2n log n + 2n |
| n² | × 4 | (2n)² = 4n² |
| n³ | × 8 | (2n)³ = 8n³ |
| 2ⁿ | **squares** | 2²ⁿ = (2ⁿ)² |

Exponential is the scary one. It doesn't need n to double. It **doubles when n grows by just 1**, since 2ⁿ⁺¹ = 2 · 2ⁿ.

The same trick works for any factor. Triple the input to an n² algorithm and the time goes up 3² = 9 times. Triple it for n³ and it goes up 27 times.

Here's a worked example. A quadratic waitlist report takes 5 seconds on 2,000 students. On 8,000 students, n grew 4 times, so the time grows 4² = 16 times: about **80 seconds**.

lessons.title: Constants and Lower Terms
lessons.readme:
# Constants and Lower Terms

Two rules make growth rates easy to compare: **the highest-order term dominates**, and **constant factors don't change the growth rate**.

Look at how much of n² + 4n + 20 comes from the n² term:

| n | n² | n² + 4n + 20 | n²'s share |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 100 | 160 | 63% |
| 100 | 10,000 | 10,420 | 96% |
| 1000 | 1,000,000 | 1,004,020 | 99.6% |

As n grows, the 4n + 20 stops mattering. So n² + 4n + 20 and n² are both **quadratic**, and 3n + 25 and n are both **linear**.

**But constants still matter for small n.** The lecture compared insertion sort (about n²/4 steps) with merge sort (about 2n log n steps). For small lists, insertion sort is faster, and on the lecture's chart the two curves cross around n = 100 (the chart plots merge sort with a larger constant; the formulas as written cross nearer 44, so the exact spot depends on the constants, which is the point). For a million items at a million steps per second, though, insertion sort takes about **70 hours** and merge sort about **40 seconds**.

So is the AI's waitlist sort bad? It depends. If it only ever sorts small lists, it's fine (though probably still not as good as `std::sort`). With registration-size lists, it's terrible.

lessons.title: Big-Oh: The Definition
lessons.readme:
# Big-Oh: The Definition

"Grows like n" is a good intuition. Big-Oh makes it precise, so you can prove it.

**f(n) is O(g(n)) if there are positive constants c and n₀ such that f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀.**

In words: once n gets big enough (past n₀), a scaled-up copy of g(n) is a **ceiling** for f(n), no matter how big n gets.

**Example: prove 3n + 25 is O(n).** Here f(n) = 3n + 25 and g(n) = n.

1. We need 3n + 25 ≤ c·n for all n ≥ n₀.
2. Try c = 4: we need 3n + 25 ≤ 4n.
3. Subtract 3n from both sides: 25 ≤ n.
4. So it holds for every n ≥ 25. With **c = 4 and n₀ = 25**, the definition is satisfied.

![3n plus 25 and 4n crossing at n equals 25](courses/diagrams/d5b85953-d692-5a8f-9703-ac3fa45dcded/ceiling.svg)

Before n = 25, 3n + 25 is above 4n. That's allowed: Big-Oh only cares what happens from n₀ on.

Any c and n₀ that work are enough. c = 28 with n₀ = 1 also proves it, because 3n + 25 ≤ 28n for every n ≥ 1.

> [!tip]
> Write the definition on your note sheet word for word. A proof is just: pick c, solve the inequality for n, and name n₀.

lessons.title: Disproving Big-Oh
lessons.readme:
# Disproving Big-Oh

To show f(n) is **not** O(g(n)), you have to show that **no** c and n₀ can work. The lecture does it by contradiction.

**Claim: 3n + 25 is not O(1).** Here g(n) = 1, so c·g(n) is just c.

1. Suppose it were. Then some c > 0 and n₀ give 3n + 25 ≤ c for **all** n ≥ n₀.
2. Solve for n: every n ≥ n₀ must satisfy n ≤ (c − 25)/3.
3. But pick any n bigger than both n₀ and (c − 25)/3. It's past n₀, so the inequality must hold, yet it's too big, so it fails.
4. Contradiction. No constant can bound 3n + 25 for all large n. So 3n + 25 is not O(1).

Compare with the proof that 3n + 25 **is** O(n): there, with c = 4, the inequality holds for **every** n ≥ 25 and keeps holding as n grows. Here, whatever c you choose, it breaks once n passes (c − 25)/3.

The same pattern shows n² is not O(n). n² ≤ c·n means n ≤ c, and every n bigger than c breaks it.

Any n that is smaller than (c − 7)/2
Only n = n₀, where the bound starts
Any n bigger than both n₀ and (c − 7)/2
questions.answer: Any n bigger than both n₀ and (c − 7)/2

n² is bigger than n for every n of at least 2

lessons.title: Tight and Loose Bounds
lessons.readme:
# Tight and Loose Bounds

Big-Oh is an **upper bound**: "f(n) is O(g(n))" says f grows **no faster** than g. That means you can rank functions with it:

| | f(n) is O(g(n)) | g(n) is O(f(n)) |
|---|---|---|
| g grows more | Yes | No |
| f grows more | No | Yes |
| same growth | Yes | Yes |

Because it's only a ceiling, some true statements are useless. "4n² is O(n³)" and "6 log n is O(n²)" are both **true**. They're just **loose**. A **tight** bound is more useful.

The lecture's Big-Oh rules: if f(n) is a polynomial of degree d, then f(n) is O(nᵈ). That is:

1. Drop lower-order terms.
2. Drop constant factors.
3. Use the **smallest** class that works: "2n is O(n)", not "2n is O(n²)".
4. Use the **simplest** expression of that class: "3n + 5 is O(n)", not "3n + 5 is O(3n)".

> [!warning]
> On a "which is false?" question, a loose bound is still **true**. Look for the statement where f really grows faster than g. When a question just asks for the run time, it wants the tight bound: the smallest, simplest class (rule 3 and rule 4).

lessons.title: The Analysis Process
lessons.readme:
# The Analysis Process

The registration server checks every pair of a student's requested sections for a time clash:

```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) {
        checkClash(i, j);
    }
}
```

The lecture's five-step process (it used a tournament where every player plays every other, the same loop):

1. **Identify the variable-sized inputs.** Label every parameter or data structure whose size can vary. There can be more than one!
2. **Map the control flow** as a function of those inputs: how many times each loop or recursive call runs.
3. **Find the cost per iteration (or per call).** Primitive operations are O(1). A call to another function costs whatever *its* complexity is.
4. **Combine.** Sequential code adds. Nested loops or recursion use the counts from step 2. Reduce any series to closed form.
5. **Simplify** to the dominant term.

Here: (1) n, the number of sections. (2) The outer loop runs i = 0 … n − 1, and the inner loop runs i times. (3) `checkClash` doesn't depend on n, so it's O(1). (4) 0 + 1 + 2 + … + (n − 1) = **n(n − 1)/2** calls. (5) **O(n²)**.

![six by six grid with the cells below the diagonal highlighted](courses/diagrams/db6e65b2-0976-5d0d-a0fc-d455153dc271/pairs.svg)

Row i has i amber cells, one per `checkClash` call. Six sections means 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15 checks, which is 6 · 5 / 2.

questions.question: A student requests 40 sections (it happens). How many times does `checkClash` run?
Step 1 of the analysis process asks you to:

Find the input that makes it run fastest
Count the lines of code in the function
Pick the constants c and n₀
questions.answer: Identify every input whose size can vary

lessons.title: Checking Every Pair
lessons.readme:
# Checking Every Pair

Let's write the clash checker for real. Each requested section has a start hour, and two sections **clash** if they start at the same hour.

The trick from the last lesson is the loop bound `j < i`. It visits each pair **once**: (1, 0), (2, 0), (2, 1), and so on. It never compares a section with itself, and it never counts the same pair twice in the other order.

| Inner loop | Pairs visited | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| `j < i` | each pair once | none |
| `j < n` | each pair **twice**, plus each section with itself | double counts |

That's n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, so the checker is O(n²).

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `countClashes(start)`. `start[i]` is the start hour of section i. Return how many **pairs** of sections share a start hour.
2. [ ] Use nested loops with `j < i`, so every pair is checked exactly once.

For example, `{9, 10, 9, 13, 10, 9}` has three 9s (3 pairs) and two 10s (1 pair), so the answer is 4.

# Counting Halvings

Searching the course catalog for a section number is slow: it checks every section. But the catalog is **sorted**, so you can use binary search. Look at the middle, then throw away the half that can't contain the key. Each step **halves** what's left.

How many halvings until only 1 item remains? Start with n = 16:

![n goes 16, 8, 4, 2, 1](courses/diagrams/547918e2-e61f-5fab-9194-98e769216485/halvings.svg)

Four halvings, and log₂ 16 = 4. That's no coincidence. After k halvings, n/2ᵏ items are left. Set that to 1 and solve: 2ᵏ = n, so **k = log₂ n**.

That's the justification to write on the exam: "each iteration halves n; after k iterations n/2ᵏ = 1, so k = log₂ n iterations of O(1) work, which is **O(log n)**." It earns partial credit even when the final answer slips.

## Assignment

Lab 3 had this exact helper.

1. [ ] Complete `countHalvings(n)`: while `n > 1`, halve n with integer division and count the step. Return the count.

For example, `countHalvings(16)` is 4, `countHalvings(17)` is also 4 (17 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1), and `countHalvings(1)` is 0.

lessons.title: The Doubling-Loop Trap
lessons.readme:
# The Doubling-Loop Trap

This one was on the midterm, and it fools almost everyone:

```cpp
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i *= 2)
    for (int j = 0; j < i; j++)
        work();
```

The outer loop runs log n times and the inner loop runs "up to n" times, so it's O(n log n)… right? **No.** The inner loop runs **i** times, and i is small most of the time. Add it up:

![bars of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 adding to 31](courses/diagrams/93e2e892-483a-560b-b2a4-abe6d04a9bc8/trap.svg)

1 + 2 + 4 + … + n. With n = 2ᵏ, the geometric series gives 2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1 = 2 · 2ᵏ − 1 = **2n − 1**. That's **O(n)**.

Now compare the inner bound `j < n`. Every row is full:

![five bars of 16 adding to 80](courses/diagrams/93e2e892-483a-560b-b2a4-abe6d04a9bc8/full.svg)

That really is n · (log₂ n + 1), which is **O(n log n)**.

**Write the justification.** "i takes the values 1, 2, 4, …, 2ᵏ with k = log₂ n. work() runs 1 + 2 + … + 2ᵏ = 2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1 = 2n − 1 times, so O(n)." On the midterm, O(n log n) with a solid justification still got partial credit.

lessons.title: More Than One Input
lessons.readme:
# More Than One Input

Step 1 of the analysis process says "there can be more than one input." Take it seriously. Name **every** size that can vary, and keep them separate in your answer.

**Sequential loops add.**

```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += a[i];       // n students
for (int j = 0; j < m; j++) sum += b[j];       // m sections
```

That's O(n + m). You can't call it O(n) because nobody promised m is anywhere near n.

**A grid has rows and columns.** Looping over every cell of a `rows × cols` seating chart is **O(rows · cols)**.

**Calls inside loops multiply.** The lecture's "do it yourself" example:

```cpp
std::vector<std::vector<int>> v = readData();
for (auto& inner : v)
    std::sort(inner.begin(), inner.end());
```

Say there are n inner vectors, each of size k. Each `std::sort` is O(k log k), and it runs n times: **O(n · k log k)**.

> [!warning]
> Don't merge two inputs into one letter. "Let k be the biggest value in v" is a new input, separate from n = the length of v. You'll see that next.

lessons.title: Counting Unique Values
lessons.readme:
# Counting Unique Values

The registrar wants to know how many **different** courses students asked for. Each request is a course number, and course numbers are small non-negative ints.

Lab 3's `func2` does this with a lookup table. Make a `vector<bool>` called `seen` with one slot for every possible value from 0 to the max. Walk the requests once; the first time you meet a value, mark it and count it.

![v is 3 1 3 0 1 3; seen marks slots 0, 1 and 3](courses/diagrams/59808fbc-4361-57c7-af1d-8cb58be01e63/seen.svg)

In the picture, v = {3, 1, 3, 0, 1, 3}. Max is 3, so `seen` has 4 slots. Values 0, 1 and 3 get marked, so the answer is 3. Slot 2 is never used, but it still had to be allocated.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `getMaxVal(v)`: return the largest value. You can assume v isn't empty.
2. [ ] Complete `countUnique(v)`: return 0 if v is empty. Otherwise make `seen` with `maxVal + 1` slots, all `false`, and count each value the first time you see it.

Every value in v is ≥ 0.

> [!warning]
> The table needs `maxVal + 1` slots, not `maxVal`. Values run from 0 **through** maxVal.

lessons.title: Unique Values Big O
lessons.readme:
# Unique Values Big O

Let's run the analysis on `countUnique`, the way the Lab 3 key does.

**Step 1: inputs.** n = the size of v. And **k = the maximum value** in v. That's a second input!

**Steps 2 to 4:**

| Part | Cost |
|---|---|
| `getMaxVal(v)` walks v once | O(n) |
| `vector<bool> seen(maxVal + 1, false)` allocates and clears k + 1 slots | O(k) |
| the loop over v, O(1) per element | O(n) |

**Step 5:** O(n) + O(k) + O(n) = **O(n + k) time**. The `seen` table is extra memory of size k + 1, so it's **O(k) space**.

Why not just say O(n)? Because **we can't assume k is O(n), or the other way around.** Five requests for course 9000 make n = 5 but k = 9000, and then allocating `seen` is the slow part. That's why k is a separate component of the run time.

The trade-off here is common: we spend O(k) memory to make each "have I seen this?" check O(1). Comparing every pair instead would use no extra memory but take O(n²) time.

lessons.title: Counting Sort
lessons.readme:
# Counting Sort

Registration appointments are stored as **minutes after 7:00 a.m.** Priority-registration students go early, so some times are negative. We need them sorted.

Lab 3's `func3` is **counting sort**. Instead of comparing values, it counts them, like `countUnique` does, but it keeps a **count** instead of true/false.

1. Find `minVal` and `maxVal`. The range is `maxVal - minVal + 1` slots.
2. For each value, add 1 to `count[v[i] - minVal]`. Subtracting `minVal` shifts the smallest value to slot 0, which also makes negative values work.
3. Walk the slots in order and write each value back `count[val]` times.

Here's v = {2, −1, 3, 0, 2, −1, 2}, with min = −1 and max = 3:

![v and its count array](courses/diagrams/d9903376-e585-5a55-9e21-1986074e95d1/count.svg)

![count array written back into v in order](courses/diagrams/d9903376-e585-5a55-9e21-1986074e95d1/write.svg)

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `getMinVal(v)`: return the smallest value. You can assume v isn't empty.
2. [ ] Complete `countingSort(v)` so it sorts v ascending, in place, using the three steps above. If v is empty, do nothing.

Values may be negative. `getMaxVal` is already done.

lessons.title: Counting Sort Big O
lessons.readme:
# Counting Sort Big O

Let n be the number of elements and **k = maxVal − minVal**, the range of values.

| Part | Cost |
|---|---|
| `getMinVal` and `getMaxVal` | O(n) each |
| allocate `count` (k + 1 ints set to 0) | O(k) |
| the counting loop over v | O(n) |
| the two nested write-back loops | **O(n + k)** |

Look hard at those nested loops:

```cpp
for (int val = 0; val < range; val++)
    for (int c = 0; c < count[val]; c++)
        v[index++] = val + minVal;
```

The rule "multiply nested loops" would say O(k · n). **That's wrong here**, because the inner bound depends on the outer loop. The outer loop visits k + 1 slots. The inner body runs `count[val]` times, and all the counts **add up to n**: we're just putting the n elements back, not adding new ones. So the total is k + n.

Altogether: O(n) + O(n) + O(k) + O(n) + O(n + k) = **O(n + k) time** and **O(k) space**.

> [!tip]
> When an inner loop's bounds add up to something you know (like n), sum them instead of multiplying.
