lessons.title: Hidden Costs
lessons.readme:
# Hidden Costs

Step 3 of the analysis process says a call to another function costs **its** complexity. Some calls hide a lot of work.

**A size() that walks the list.** The midterm asked about this:

```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < list.size() / 2; i++) {
    // O(1) work
}
```

The loop runs n/2 times. **If** `size()` walks the list to count its nodes (the problem will say so), then it costs O(n), and it's called on **every** check of the condition. That's O(n) · O(n/2) = **O(n²)**, even though it looks linear. If the list keeps a count (Lab 4's `LinkedList`, `std::list`), `size()` is O(1) and the loop is O(n).

**Passing a container by value** copies all n elements: O(n) time and O(n) space, before your function does anything. Our AI-written waitlist sort took `std::list<T> lst` by value, so it copied the whole list going in: O(n) extra time and space before sorting even starts. (Returning it is cheap, because C++ moves a by-value parameter out.) Pass `const&` when you only read.

**Library calls** count too. `std::sort` is O(n log n), and calling it inside a loop multiplies.

**Time and space are separate answers.** Count them separately, because they often differ. `countClashes` from earlier is O(n²) time but O(1) extra space: a couple of loop counters. `countUnique` is O(n + k) time and O(k) space. Sometimes you trade one for the other on purpose, spending memory on a lookup table to save time.

lessons.title: Big-Omega and Big-Theta
lessons.readme:
# Big-Omega and Big-Theta

Big-Oh is a ceiling. It has two siblings.

**Big-Omega, Ω (lower bound).** f(n) is Ω(g(n)) if there are positive constants c and n₀ such that **f(n) ≥ c·g(n)** for all n ≥ n₀. Same definition, inequality flipped: past n₀, a scaled g is a **floor**.

**Big-Theta, Θ (tight bound).** f(n) is Θ(g(n)) **if and only if** f(n) is O(g(n)) **and** f(n) is Ω(g(n)). It's pinned from above and below.

| Statement | True? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 5n + 2 is O(n²) | yes | loose ceiling |
| 5n + 2 is Ω(n) | yes | it grows at least as fast as n |
| 5n + 2 is Θ(n) | yes | both O(n) and Ω(n) |
| 5n + 2 is Θ(n²) | **no** | it isn't Ω(n²) |

These are **separate from best, worst and average case**. Pick the case first, then bound it.

Example: the lecture's swap-based `sort_list` has no early exit. Its inner loop always runs j up to i, so even on an already sorted list it does n(n − 1)/2 comparisons. Its best case is **Θ(n²)**. The shifting insertion sort you'll see in Sorting stops early, so its best case is O(n). Read the loop before you quote a best case.

lessons.title: When an Array Fills Up
lessons.readme:
# When an Array Fills Up

The waitlist is stored in an array, like an array-based stack. What happens when it's full and one more student joins?

A **fixed-size** array just refuses: push throws an exception. Every push stays O(1), but the waitlist has a hard limit.

A **growable** array makes a bigger array, copies everything over, and deletes the old one. That one push costs **O(n)**. The lecture's pseudocode:

```
Algorithm push(o)
    if t = S.length − 1 then
        A ← new array of size …      (S.length + c, or 2 · S.length)
        for i ← 0 to t do
            A[i] ← S[i]
        S ← A
    t ← t + 1
    S[t] ← o
```

There are two strategies for the new size:

- **Incremental:** add a constant c slots.
- **Doubling:** double the size.

Here's doubling, starting from 1 slot:

![array growing from 1 to 2 to 4 to 8 slots, copying each time](courses/diagrams/7117a78f-2645-582f-aa37-439f07c41032/grow.svg)

So what's the run time of push on an array-based stack? The professor's answer was **"it depends."** Fixed-size: O(1). Resizable: O(n) in the worst case, for the push that triggers the copy. The next lessons show why doubling still averages out to O(1).

Always O(n), since every push copies the whole array

lessons.title: Doubling a Full Array
lessons.readme:
# Doubling a Full Array

Let's build the growable waitlist and **count** the copies, so we can see what doubling really costs.

`GrowArray` starts with room for 1 int. It tracks its capacity `cap`, the number of items `n`, and `copies`, the total number of elements copied during resizes.

When `push` finds the array full:

1. Allocate a new array with **twice** the capacity.
2. Copy the n old elements over, adding 1 to `copies` for each one.
3. `delete[]` the old array and point `data` at the new one.

Then store the new item and bump n.

Pushing 8 items resizes at capacities 1, 2 and 4, copying 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 elements. The 9th push doubles again (copying 8), so 9 pushes make 15 copies.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `push(x)`. If the array is full, double its capacity: allocate, copy (counting each copy in `copies`), `delete[]` the old array, and update `data` and `cap`.
2. [ ] Store `x` at the end and update `n`.

Don't grow by a constant. The tests push 100,000 items and check the copy count.

lessons.title: Amortized Analysis
lessons.readme:
# Amortized Analysis

One push can cost O(n). But that's rare. What does a push cost **on average over a long run** of pushes?

**Amortized time** = the total time T(n) for a series of n operations, divided by n. Start with an empty stack in an array of size 1.

**Incremental (add c each time).** For n elements we replace the array k = n/c times, copying c, then 2c, then 3c, up to kc elements (so this one starts with c slots):

T(n) = n + c + 2c + … + kc = n + c · k(k + 1)/2

With k = n/c that's O(n + n²/c²) = **O(n²) total**, so **O(n) amortized** per push.

**Doubling.** For n elements we replace the array k = log₂ n times, copying 1, 2, 4, … elements:

T(n) = n + (1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2ᵏ) = n + 2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1 = n + 2n − 1 = **3n − 1**

The lecture's sum runs up to 2ᵏ = n, so it also counts the resize that happens on the next push. Your GrowArray made 7 copies for 8 pushes, so its real total is n + (n − 1) = 2n − 1. Either way that's **O(n) total**, so **O(1) amortized** per push. It's the same geometric series as the doubling-loop trap.

![copies per resize: doubling makes 4 resizes, growing by 2 makes 7](courses/diagrams/a02a9429-3843-5ce1-89ad-fc2651fe132d/copies.svg)

The right side never stops getting worse: each resize copies more than the last, and they keep coming every c pushes. On the left, resizes get rarer as fast as they get bigger. That's why `std::vector::push_back` is O(1) amortized.

lessons.title: Analysis Review: Loops
lessons.readme:
# Analysis Review: Loops

The exam asks for Big-Oh and sometimes **exact** counts, by hand. For every loop:

- Write down every input that can vary.
- Inner bound independent of the outer index? **Multiply.** Depends on it? Make a table and **sum**.
- Sequential code **adds**.
- Counter multiplied or divided each pass: **log n** passes.
- Doubling outer with `j < i`: 1 + 2 + … + n = 2n − 1, **O(n)**.
- A `break` only leaves the innermost loop.
- A loop whose inner counts add up to n is O(n + k), not O(n · k).

Then simplify to the dominant term, and write one sentence of justification.

lessons.title: Analysis Review: Proofs and Recursion

# Analysis Review: Proofs and Recursion

The rest of the chapter on one page:

- **f(n) is O(g(n))** if there are positive c and n₀ with f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀. To prove it, pick c and solve for n₀. To disprove it, suppose c exists and find an n past n₀ that breaks it.
- **Ω** flips the inequality (floor). **Θ** means both O and Ω.
- Best, worst and average case are a separate choice from O, Ω and Θ.
- Recursion: b calls per call, depth d. b = 1 gives O(d); b ≥ 2 gives O(bᵈ). Depth is n for `n − 1`, log n for `n / 2`. Stack space = depth.
- When the work per call shrinks, add it level by level.
- Growable arrays: doubling is O(1) amortized per push (3n − 1 total); growing by a constant is O(n) amortized.

lessons.title: Why Linked Lists?
lessons.readme:
# Why Linked Lists?

The SJSU card club meets on Thursday nights in the Student Union, and this semester they're writing a deck simulator to study perfect shuffles, just like Lab 4. The simulator puts cards on top of the deck, deals them off, and splits the deck in half thousands of times.

Try storing the deck in an array, with the top card at index 0. Putting a new card on top means **every** other card shifts one slot to make room. With 52 cards that's 52 moves to add one card.

The trouble is that an array is one solid block of memory. Every slot has a fixed neighbor, so making room means moving things.

A **linked list** drops that rule. Each card lives in its own small block called a **node**, and nodes can sit anywhere in memory. Each node holds its data and a pointer to the next node:

```cpp
struct Node {
    int elt;      // the data ("element")
    Node* next;   // the next node, or nullptr at the end
};
```

![an array next to a linked list whose nodes sit at scattered addresses](courses/diagrams/233e412b-2d8e-5cdd-aac7-dac71095bbf0/array.svg)

The list itself is just one pointer, `head`, to the first node. To reach the third card, start at `head` and follow `next` twice. The last node's `next` is `nullptr`, drawn ∅ on the slides. A pointer to the last node, `tail`, is optional.

Putting a card on top now means making one node and changing two pointers. Nothing shifts.

A list is an **abstract data type (ADT)**: it's defined by what its operations do (insert, remove, retrieve), not how they're done. The array list from Lab 2 and the linked list are two implementations of the same List ADT. Over this chapter we'll compare their costs, operation by operation.

> [!note]
> Lab 4's node is a template, `LinkedListNode<T>`, with a constructor. In this chapter we use the plain `int` version from the midterm worksheet.

lessons.title: Nodes and Traversal
lessons.readme:
# Nodes and Traversal

First question from the club: how many cards are in the deck? A linked list has no `.size()` to ask. The only way to learn anything about it is to **walk** it, node by node.

The pattern is a `for` loop with a pointer called `cur`:

```cpp
for (Node* cur = head; cur != nullptr; cur = cur->next) {
    // use cur->elt
}
```

`cur` starts at the first node, and `cur = cur->next` hops to the next one. When it falls off the end, `cur` is `nullptr` and the loop stops. Here's a count of a three-card deck:

![cur walks a three-node list and stops at nullptr](courses/diagrams/248da275-d60a-54e0-bf35-8683a1155840/walk.svg)

Two details make this pattern safe:

- `cur` is a **copy** of `head`. Moving it doesn't move `head`, so the list is unchanged afterward.
- If the list is empty, `head` is `nullptr` and the loop runs zero times. The empty case is handled for free.

Searching works the same way: walk, and stop early as soon as you find what you want. Quiz 4 asked for exactly this, written by hand, under the name `findValue`. The grading rubric took points off for each of these, so check your paper version against the list:

> [!warning]
> - The loop condition is `ptr != nullptr`, not `ptr->next != nullptr` (that skips the last node, and crashes on an empty list).
> - Test the **pointer**, not `*ptr`, and declare it as `Node*`, not `Node`.
> - Compare the **data**: `ptr->elt == val`, never `ptr == val`.
> - The loop must be able to end when `val` isn't there. A `while (true)` with no `nullptr` check never does.
> - `return true` goes inside the loop when you find it; `return false` goes **after** the loop, once every node has been checked. A `return false` inside the loop stops after the first node.
> - The return type is `bool`.

> [!tip]
> On paper, test every list function on three lists: empty, one node, and a few nodes. Most linked list bugs live in the first two.

## Assignment

We'll build the club's deck as a singly linked list of card numbers in `list.h`.

1. [ ] Complete `length(head)`: return the number of nodes. An empty list has length 0.
2. [ ] Complete `contains(head, v)`: return `true` if some node's `elt` is `v`, `false` otherwise.

Neither function should change the list.

lessons.title: Insert at the Front
lessons.readme:
# Insert at the Front

A new card goes on top of the deck. In an array that meant shifting everything. In a linked list it takes three steps, straight from lecture:

1. Allocate a new node.
2. Point the new node's `next` at the current `head`.
3. Update `head` to point at the new node.

![insertFront in three steps: allocate, link to head, move head](courses/diagrams/67504afa-916f-5f17-bb9c-d8d06f3896c9/steps.svg)

What if the list is empty? Then `head` is `nullptr`, so step 2 sets the new node's `next` to `nullptr`, and step 3 makes it the only node. The same three steps work, with no special case.

In C++ the whole thing fits on one line. `new Node{v, head}` fills the fields in order (`elt`, then `next`), so it does steps 1 and 2 together:

```cpp
head = new Node{v, head};
```

**Why `Node*& head`?** The function has to change the caller's `head` variable. With a plain `Node* head`, the function gets a copy of the pointer: it would build the node, point its copy at it, and the caller's `head` would never change. The new node would also leak. The `&` makes `head` a reference to the caller's own pointer.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `insertFront(head, v)` so a new node holding `v` becomes the first node. It must work on an empty list, and it must keep every existing node (don't copy them).

lessons.title: Insert at the Front Big O
lessons.readme:
# Insert at the Front Big O

Count the work in `insertFront`: one `new`, one pointer written into the new node, and one write to `head`. None of that depends on how long the list is. A deck of 3 cards and a deck of 3 million cost the same, so `insertFront` is **O(1)**.

| | Array list | Singly linked list |
|---|---|---|
| insertFront | O(n): shift everything right | O(1) |

That was the first clicker question of the linked list lecture, and it's the main reason to pick a linked list: the front is cheap.

There's one side effect to remember for tracing questions. Each new node goes in front of the last one, so inserting at the front **reverses** the order you inserted in:

```
insertFront 1, then 2, then 3   →   head → 3 → 2 → 1 → ∅
```

The exam likes to hide this inside a loop, where the node is built first and linked in by hand.

lessons.title: Remove from the Front
lessons.readme:
# Remove from the Front

Dealing a card takes it off the top. Removing the first node also takes three steps, and the **order** is the whole lesson:

1. Save the old front: `Node* tmp = head;`
2. Move `head` to the next node: `head = head->next;`
3. Free the old front: `delete tmp;`

![removeFront: save tmp, move head, delete tmp](courses/diagrams/eca44f54-96d1-5db1-827f-96c15e9e8ef7/steps.svg)

Lecture asked which of four snippets is correct. Here's what goes wrong in the other three:

- `head = head->next;` alone moves past the old front but never deletes it. Nothing points to it any more, so it **leaks**.
- `delete tmp; head = head->next;` (with `tmp == head`) frees the node, then reads its `next`. That's reading **freed memory**: it might work today and crash tomorrow.
- `head = head->next; delete head;` deletes the **new** front, the node you meant to keep, and leaks the old one.

The rule behind all three: **grab everything you need from a node before you delete it.**

A one-node list needs no special case: `head->next` is `nullptr`, so `head` becomes `nullptr` and the list is empty. An empty list does need one, though. There's no node to remove, and `head->next` would dereference `nullptr`.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `removeFront(head)`. If the list is empty, return `false` and change nothing.
2. [ ] Otherwise remove the first node, `delete` it, and return `true`. A one-node list ends up with `head == nullptr`.

The tests run with a leak checker, so a node you forget to delete fails the lesson.

# Remove from the Front Big O

`removeFront` does a fixed amount of work: save one pointer, move `head`, delete one node. It never looks past the second node, so it's **O(1)**, for singly and doubly linked lists alike.

An array list pays for it instead. Removing index 0 leaves a hole, and every element shifts one slot left to close it: **O(n)**.

| | Array list | Singly linked | Doubly linked |
|---|---|---|---|
| insertFront | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) |
| removeFront | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) |

Lecture summed it up as "front ops faster vs. ArrayList." The back of the list is a different story, and it's coming up next.

> [!warning]
> On paper, the order of the three lines is worth as many points as the Big O. Save, move, then delete.

lessons.title: Insert at the Back
lessons.readme:
# Insert at the Back

Sometimes a card goes on the **bottom** of the deck. With only a `head` pointer, we first have to find the last node:

1. Start a pointer `cur` at `head`.
2. Follow `next` until `cur->next == nullptr`. Now `cur` is the last node.
3. Allocate the new node (its `next` is `nullptr`) and set `cur->next` to it.

![insertBack: walk cur to the last node, then link the new node](courses/diagrams/ceaabaae-b4ae-508b-965e-50b065987ad0/steps.svg)

Notice the loop condition. We stop when `cur->next` is null, **not** when `cur` is null. If we walked until `cur == nullptr`, we'd have walked off the end, and there'd be no node left to link the new one to.

That condition also explains the special case. If the list is empty, there's no last node at all, and `cur->next` would dereference `nullptr`. So an empty list is handled first: the new node simply becomes `head`.

```cpp
if (head == nullptr) { head = n; return; }
```

The walk visits every node, so this version is **O(n)**. The next lesson shows the classic fix.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `insertBack(head, v)`. If the list is empty, the new node becomes `head`.
2. [ ] Otherwise walk to the last node and link the new node after it.

lessons.title: Insert at the Back Big O
lessons.readme:
# Insert at the Back Big O

Walking to the end costs one step per node, so `insertBack` with only a head pointer is **O(n)**. The midterm asked exactly this: insertBack on a singly linked list without a tail pointer is O(n).

The fix is to keep a second pointer, `tail`, that always points at the last node. Then there's nothing to walk:

```cpp
void insertBack(Node*& head, Node*& tail, int v) {
    Node* n = new Node{v, nullptr};
    if (tail != nullptr) tail->next = n;
    else head = n;   // was empty: n is the first node too
    tail = n;
}
```

That's **O(1)**, and it's Lab 4's `append`. The price is bookkeeping: every operation must keep `tail` correct. The easy one to forget is the empty list. The first node is both the first and the last, so **both** `head` and `tail` must point at it. Removing the last remaining node has to reset both to `nullptr` too.

The same idea works anywhere in the list. If you already hold a pointer `p` to some node, inserting right after it is O(1): `p->next = new Node{v, p->next};`. The midterm asked this one too.

| | Array list | Singly, head only | Singly, head + tail |
|---|---|---|---|
| insertBack | O(1) | O(n) | O(1) |
| insertAfter a node you have | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) |

lessons.title: Remove from the Back
lessons.readme:
# Remove from the Back

Now take the **bottom** card off. This is harder than it looks.

To remove the last node, we have to set the `next` of the node **before** it to `nullptr`. Walking to the last node like `insertBack` does isn't enough: once we're standing on it, there's no way back to its predecessor. And a `tail` pointer doesn't help either, for the same reason. `tail` points at the last node, and nothing points backward.

Lecture's answer is **pointer chasing**: walk two pointers together, one a step behind the other.

1. Start `prev` at `nullptr` and `cur` at `head`.
2. While `cur->next` isn't null: set `prev = cur`, then `cur = cur->next`.
3. Now `cur` is the last node and `prev` is the one before it.
4. Set `prev->next = nullptr` and `delete cur`.

![prev trails one step behind cur](courses/diagrams/efeeb732-df07-58e5-918e-1abef7bd27b4/walk.svg)

![prev is second to last; the last node is unlinked and deleted](courses/diagrams/efeeb732-df07-58e5-918e-1abef7bd27b4/cut.svg)

(The lecture slides call these `tmp2` and `tmp1`.)

There's one special case beyond the empty list. If the list has **one** node, the loop never runs and `prev` is still `nullptr`. There's no previous node to update. Instead, the list becomes empty: set `head = nullptr`.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `removeBack(head)`. If the list is empty, return `false`.
2. [ ] Otherwise walk `prev` and `cur` to the end, unlink the last node, `delete` it, and return `true`.
3. [ ] A one-node list ends up with `head == nullptr`.

lessons.readme:
# Remove from the Back Big O

`removeBack` on a singly linked list walks the whole list to find the node before the last one, so it's **O(n)**.

Keeping a `tail` pointer doesn't change that. It finds the last node instantly, but the work is updating the node **before** it, and there's still no way to reach that node except by walking from `head`. Of the four basic operations, this is the only one that's still O(n) with a tail pointer:

| Singly linked | head only | head + tail |
|---|---|---|
| insertFront | O(1) | O(1) |
| removeFront | O(1) | O(1) |
| insertBack | O(n) | O(1) |
| removeBack | O(n) | **O(n)** |

The array list does this in O(1): just shrink its size by one. Lecture called this "back ops slower vs. ArrayList."

Operations by **position** don't get help from `tail` either. `removeAt(pos)` and `insertAt(pos)` walk from `head` to find the spot, so they're O(n) too. On a quiz that lists groups of operations, cross out any group containing `removeBack` or an `...At(pos)`.

Lecture's advice for this situation: if you need `removeBack` often, **don't use a singly linked list**. A doubly linked list fixes it, because every node also points back to its predecessor. That's a few lessons away.

lessons.title: Clearing a List
lessons.readme:
# Clearing a List

At the end of the night the club puts the deck away. Every node was made with its own `new`, so every node needs its own `delete`. Nothing frees them for us.

The walk looks like traversal, with one twist: you can't use `cur = cur->next` after deleting `cur`, because that reads freed memory. It's the same trap as `removeFront`. So save the next pointer **first**:

1. Save `nx = head->next`.
2. `delete head`.
3. Move on: `head = nx`.
4. Repeat until `head` is `nullptr`.

![clear: save next, delete head, move on](courses/diagrams/ba9d93dd-e56e-52f3-97b7-c33fbcb23a63/steps.svg)

Running the loop on `head` itself (not a copy) has a nice side effect: when it ends, `head` is already `nullptr`, so the caller isn't left holding a pointer to freed memory.

This is exactly what Lab 4's destructor does. The solution key calls it a "deep delete": walk the list and delete each node individually. Use `delete`, not `delete[]`: the nodes were never an array, each was its own `new`.

It's also why `clear()` costs differently. An array list can clear itself in **O(1)** by setting its size to 0, while a linked list must visit and free every node: **O(n)**.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `clear(head)`: delete every node and leave `head` set to `nullptr`. An empty list is fine too.

lessons.title: Deep Copy of a List
lessons.readme:
# Deep Copy of a List

Before the club tries a shuffle, they want to save the current deck so they can compare later. The obvious line doesn't do it:

```cpp
Node* saved = deck;   // copies one pointer, not the list
```

That's a **shallow copy**: two names for the same nodes. Shuffling `deck` rearranges `saved` too, and when both get cleared, every node is deleted twice.

![a shallow copy: two pointers to the same nodes](courses/diagrams/3dd1b674-4dfa-5636-bb20-b5e03dd2c8c6/shallow.svg)

A **deep copy** makes a brand new node for every node, with the same values in the same order. The two lists then share nothing.

![a deep copy: two separate chains of nodes](courses/diagrams/3dd1b674-4dfa-5636-bb20-b5e03dd2c8c6/deep.svg)

To build the copy in order, walk the original and add each new node at the **back** of the copy. Calling `insertBack` for each one would work, but each call walks the whole copy, so the total is O(n²). Instead, remember the copy's last node yourself, the same tail trick from two lessons ago:

1. Start with `first = nullptr` and `last = nullptr`.
2. For each node `p` in the original, make `n = new Node{p->elt, nullptr}`.
3. If `last` is `nullptr`, this is the first node: `first = n`. Otherwise `last->next = n`.
4. Set `last = n`.

Lab 4's copy constructor and the Rule of Three from the arrays chapter come down to this same loop.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `copyList(head)`: return the head of a new list with the same values in the same order. Every node must be new. The copy of an empty list is `nullptr`.
2. [ ] Do it in one pass (O(n)) with a loop. The tests copy a 100,000-node list, too deep for recursion.

lessons.readme:
# A LinkedList Class

Passing `head` around by reference works, but it's easy to get wrong, and the caller has to remember to clear the list. Lab 4 wraps it all in a class that keeps three things together:

![a list with head, tail and count](courses/diagrams/6bd323cc-39c8-5fe8-a31c-48190c9e7f05/cls.svg)

- `head`: the first node
- `tail`: the last node, so `append` (insert at the back) is O(1)
- `count`: the number of nodes, so `getCount()` is O(1) instead of a walk

The constructor starts all three at `nullptr` and 0. The destructor does the "deep delete" from the clearing lesson, so a list cleans up after itself when it goes out of scope.

`append` is the tail-pointer insert from the Big O lesson, plus one more piece of bookkeeping:

![append links the new node after tail, then moves tail](courses/diagrams/6bd323cc-39c8-5fe8-a31c-48190c9e7f05/append.svg)

1. Make the new node.
2. If the list is empty (`tail == nullptr`), the new node is also the head. Otherwise link it after `tail`.
3. Move `tail` to the new node, and add one to `count`.

> [!note]
> In this course the class's methods are written outside the class, like `void LinkedList::append(int v)`, the way the Lab 4 solution key writes them. The copy assignment operator is deleted because Lab 4 didn't ask for one.

## Assignment

The full class declaration is at the top of `linkedlist.h`. Below it:

1. [ ] Complete the destructor: delete every node, with a loop (the tests build a 200,000-node list, too deep for recursion).
2. [ ] Complete `append(v)` in O(1). Handle the empty list, and keep `head`, `tail` and `count` correct.

lessons.readme:
# The LinkedList Copy Constructor

Now the club's "save the deck" idea, as part of the class:

```cpp
LinkedList saved = deck;   // calls the copy constructor
```

If you don't write a copy constructor, C++ writes one that copies each member: `head`, `tail` and `count`. That copies two **pointers**, not the nodes: a shallow copy. When `saved` and `deck` go out of scope, both destructors delete the same nodes, and the program crashes with a double free.

Lab 4 asks for a **deep** copy constructor. The solution key's version is short, because `append` already does the hard part:

1. Start as an empty list.
2. Walk `other`'s nodes and `append` each value.

The cleanest way to "start as an empty list" is to **delegate** to the default constructor:

```cpp
LinkedList::LinkedList(const LinkedList& other) : LinkedList() {
    // head, tail and count are already nullptr, nullptr, 0 here
}
```

That `: LinkedList()` matters. If you write `: head(nullptr), tail(nullptr)` and forget `count`, then `count` starts as garbage, and every `append` adds one to garbage.

The copy's `tail` and `count` come out right automatically, because `append` maintains them.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete the copy constructor. It must make new nodes with the same values in the same order, and the copy's `head`, `tail` and `count` must all be correct.

lessons.title: setHead and equals
lessons.readme:
# setHead and equals

The shuffle lessons later in this chapter rearrange a deck by **relinking** its nodes: no `new`, no `delete`, just new `next` pointers. When that's done, the deck has a new first node, and Lab 4 hands it back with `setHead`:

```cpp
deck.setHead(merge(pile1, pile2));
```

Setting `head` is one line. The catch is that the relinking also moved the last node and maybe changed the length, so `tail` and `count` are now stale. The solution key's `setHead` recomputes both with one walk:

1. Set `head = newHead`.
2. Walk from `newHead` to the end, counting nodes and remembering the last one you saw.
3. Set `tail` to that last node and `count` to the total.

`setHead` doesn't delete or copy anything. The nodes are the same; only the order changed.

Next, `equals` checks whether two lists hold the same values in the same order. The solution key does it in two steps:

1. **Check the counts first.** Different lengths can't be equal.
2. Walk both lists together, comparing `elt`s.

The count check isn't just a shortcut. Because both lists have the same length, the two walks run out of nodes at the same time. Without it, walking a longer list against a shorter one would step past the shorter list's end and dereference `nullptr`.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `setHead(newHead)`: set `head`, then recompute `tail` and `count` by walking from it.
2. [ ] Complete `equals(other)`: return `false` if the counts differ; otherwise compare the elements in order.

lessons.title: Doubly Linked Insert and Remove
lessons.readme:
# Doubly Linked Insert and Remove

Here's lecture's `insertBack` for a doubly linked list with `head` and `tail`, one step per picture:

![doubly linked insertBack in four steps](courses/diagrams/1ed74d3b-1291-5b3e-994c-0e507e75d71a/ins.svg)

```cpp
void insertBack(DNode*& head, DNode*& tail, int v) {
    DNode* n = new DNode{v, tail, nullptr};   // steps 1 and 3: n->prev = tail
    if (tail != nullptr) tail->next = n;      // step 2
    else head = n;                            // was empty: n is the first node too
    tail = n;                                 // step 4
}
```

And here's the payoff, `removeBack`, with no walking at all:

1. Save the old tail, then move `tail` back: `tail = tail->prev`.
2. Set the new tail's `next` to `nullptr`.
3. Delete the old tail.

![doubly linked removeBack in three steps](courses/diagrams/1ed74d3b-1291-5b3e-994c-0e507e75d71a/rem.svg)

Watch the edge case in step 2. If the list had one node, the new `tail` is `nullptr`, and there's no node whose `next` to clear. The list is now empty, so set `head = nullptr` too.

The front operations are **mirror images**: swap `head` with `tail`, and `next` with `prev`, everywhere. `insertFront` makes a node whose `next` is the old head and whose `prev` is `nullptr`, then fixes the old head's `prev`.

## Assignment

`insertBack` is given in `dlist.h`. Write the other three. Each takes `head` and `tail` by reference.

1. [ ] `removeBack(head, tail)`: remove and delete the last node. Do nothing on an empty list.
2. [ ] `insertFront(head, tail, v)`: add a node at the front.
3. [ ] `removeFront(head, tail)`: remove and delete the first node. Do nothing on an empty list.

After every call, all `prev` and `next` pointers must agree, `head->prev` and `tail->next` must be `nullptr`, and an empty list has both `head` and `tail` set to `nullptr`.

lessons.title: Doubly Linked List Big O
lessons.readme:
# Doubly Linked List Big O

With `prev` pointers and a `tail`, every end operation is O(1). Here's lecture's side-by-side:

| | Singly (head + tail) | Doubly (head + tail) |
|---|---|---|
| insertFront | O(1) | O(1) |
| removeFront | O(1) | O(1) |
| insertBack | O(1) | O(1) |
| removeBack | **O(n)** | **O(1)** |
| insert/remove **after** a node you have | O(1) | O(1) |
| insert/remove **before** a node you have | **O(n)**, no prev | **O(1)** |
| memory per element | sizeof(elemType) + 8 | sizeof(elemType) + 16 |

What doesn't change: anything that works by **position**. `retrieveAt(pos)`, `insertAt(pos)` and `removeAt(pos)` still have to walk from an end to find the spot, so they stay **O(n)** in both kinds of list. Holding a pointer to the node is what makes things O(1); knowing its index isn't enough.

> [!tip]
> On the exam, read the setup carefully: "with a tail pointer," "doubly linked," and "you already have a pointer to the node" each change the answer.

lessons.title: Linked Lists in the STL
lessons.readme:
# Linked Lists in the STL

You've been building lists by hand to learn how they work. C++ also ships two:

| Container | What it is |
|---|---|
| `std::list<T>` | doubly linked list, supports everything we've covered |
| `std::forward_list<T>` | singly linked list, **no tail pointer** |

Since `forward_list` has no tail, it doesn't even offer `push_back`: the library won't give you an O(n) operation that looks cheap.

You walk them with **iterators**. An iterator is sort of like a pointer: `begin()` is the first element, `*it` gets what it points at, `++it` moves to the next, and `end()` is one **past** the last element.

```cpp
std::list<int> deck = {12, 7, 30};
for (auto it = deck.begin(); it != deck.end(); ++it) cout << *it << " ";
for (int card : deck) cout << card << " ";   // same thing
```

**When should you use them?** Lecture's answer: when it's convenient and performance doesn't matter much. Linked list nodes are scattered in memory, so walking one causes a **cache miss** at almost every node. In most cases, `std::vector` or `std::deque` are faster, even where the Big O says the list should win.

Linked lists still show up all the time, just not as STL containers. They're often **embedded** in other structures: you might keep a vector of all your shoes and, threaded through it, a list of just the green ones.

questions.question: Which STL container is a singly linked list with no tail pointer?
Why is `std::vector` often faster than `std::list` in practice, even with the same Big O?
answers: Its iterators skip every other element
It never allocates memory on the heap

lessons.title: Linked List vs Array Costs
lessons.readme:
# Linked List vs Array Costs

Here's the whole List ADT in one table, the way lecture laid it out. "Array list" is Lab 2's dynamic array; "pos" is a position (index) in the list.

| Operation | Array list | Singly linked | Doubly linked |
|---|---|---|---|
| insertFront / removeFront | O(n) shift | O(1) | O(1) |
| insertBack | O(1) | O(n), O(1) with tail | O(1) with tail |
| removeBack | O(1) | O(n), even with tail | O(1) with tail |
| retrieveAt / replaceAt / isItemAtEqual(pos) | O(1) | O(n) | O(n) |
| insertAt / removeAt(pos) | O(n) shift | O(n) walk | O(n) walk |
| insertAfter / removeAfter a node you have | O(n) shift | O(1) | O(1) |
| insertBefore / removeBefore a node you have | O(n) shift | O(n), no prev | O(1) |
| clear() | O(1) | O(n) | O(n) |
| memory per element | sizeof(elemType) | + 8 | + 16 |

Three patterns to remember instead of memorizing cells:

1. **Front ops**: lists win. Arrays shift.
2. **Access by position**: arrays win. Lists walk.
3. **Back ops**: a singly linked list loses on `removeBack` no matter what, because nothing points backward.

Notice the two different costs in the `insertAt` row. A linked list never shifts anything, but it has to **walk** to the position first, so it's still O(n). Once you're there, linking in the node is O(1).

Every node needs its own delete

lessons.title: K-th From the End
lessons.readme:
# K-th From the End

A card trick needs the k-th card from the **bottom** of the deck. One way: walk the list once to count its length n, then walk again n − k steps. That's two passes.

The midterm worksheet asked for it in **one pass**, with a hint: think about using two pointers.

The idea is to keep a fixed **gap** between two pointers:

1. Start `lead` and `trail` at `head`.
2. Move `lead` forward k steps. Now it's k nodes ahead of `trail`.
3. Move both one step at a time until `lead` is `nullptr`.
4. `lead` has fallen off the end, and `trail` is still k nodes behind it: exactly the k-th node from the end.

Here's k = 2 on `1 → 2 → 3 → 4`:

![lead starts k ahead of trail; when lead falls off, trail is k from the end](courses/diagrams/de93f8f0-b486-5ac2-a28a-1b281cc55a21/trace.svg)

```
k = 2:   1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → null
         T       L                 start: lead is k = 2 ahead
             T       L             move both one step
                 T       L         lead == null, stop → trail->elt == 3
```

Check the ends: k = 1 means `lead` starts one ahead, so `trail` stops on the last node. k = n means `lead` is already `nullptr` after step 2, so `trail` never moves and returns the first node.

Two pointers walking the same list like this is what lecture calls **pointer chasing**.

## Assignment

These go in `tricks.h`. None of them may change the list.

1. [ ] Complete `kthFromEnd(head, k)` in **one pass** with two pointers. k = 1 is the last element. Assume 1 ≤ k ≤ the length of the list.

lessons.title: Finding the Middle
lessons.readme:
# Finding the Middle

To cut the deck, the club needs its **middle** card. Again, you could count the length and walk halfway: two passes. Here's a one-pass version with two pointers moving at **different speeds**:

- `slow` moves one node per step.
- `fast` moves two nodes per step.

When `fast` reaches the end, `slow` has gone exactly half as far: it's in the middle.

```cpp
while (fast != nullptr && fast->next != nullptr) {
    slow = slow->next;
    fast = fast->next->next;
}
```

The loop condition checks **both** `fast` and `fast->next`, because `fast` jumps two nodes. If `fast->next` were null, `fast->next->next` would dereference `nullptr`.

![slow and fast on five nodes: slow stops on 3](courses/diagrams/3476ec22-db68-5bd0-90ce-c97aa2b79381/odd.svg)

With an even number of nodes there are two middles. This loop stops `slow` on the **second** one:

![on four nodes slow stops on the second middle](courses/diagrams/3476ec22-db68-5bd0-90ce-c97aa2b79381/even.svg)

Speed differences are a powerful trick. The next lesson uses the same two pointers to answer a much harder question.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `middle(head)` with a slow and a fast pointer. Assume the list isn't empty. For an even count, return the **second** middle: `1 → 2 → 3 → 4` gives 3.

lessons.title: Cycle Detection
lessons.readme:
# Cycle Detection

A bug in the shuffle code could point some node's `next` back at an **earlier** node. Then the list never ends: it loops forever, and so does every walk over it. This was the class activity in week 4: write `bool hasCycle(Node* head)`.

The famous answer is **Floyd's cycle-finding algorithm**, the tortoise and the hare. Both start at `head`. Each round, in this order (lecture's):

1. The hare (`fast`) takes **two** steps. If it finds ∅, there's no cycle.
2. If the hare lands on the tortoise, there's a cycle.
3. The tortoise (`slow`) takes **one** step.

Without a cycle, the hare simply reaches the end. With a cycle, both end up going around it, and the hare gains one node on the tortoise every round, so it must eventually land right on it.

Here's lecture's list, `1 → 2 → 5 → 6 → 7 → 8 → 9 → 10`, where 10 points back to 6:

![Floyd rounds 0 to 2 on the lecture list](courses/diagrams/68b55417-5843-5892-a68b-1a05578a7de6/a.svg)

![Floyd rounds 3 and 4: they meet at node 6](courses/diagrams/68b55417-5843-5892-a68b-1a05578a7de6/b.svg)

They meet at node **6**, in round 4. The order of the steps matters for questions like "where do they meet?" If you moved both pointers first and then compared, they'd meet somewhere else (node 8 here).

> [!warning]
> Compare the **pointers** (`fast == slow`), not the values. Two different nodes can hold the same card number, and that's not a cycle.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `hasCycle(head)` with Floyd's algorithm, in lecture's order, using O(1) extra space. An empty list has no cycle, and values may repeat.

lessons.title: Cycle Detection Big O
lessons.readme:
# Cycle Detection Big O

The class activity also asked how much **time** and **memory** your algorithm needs. Here's lecture's analysis of Floyd's.

**Time, no cycle.** The hare moves two nodes per round, so it reaches the end after about n/2 rounds. That's O(n).

**Time, with a cycle.** Once both are in the cycle, the worst case is the hare one step **ahead** of the tortoise, so it has almost a full lap to make up. It gains one node every round, so for a cycle of length c it catches up within O(c) rounds. And c ≤ n, so that's O(n) too.

Both cases: **O(n)** time.

**Memory.** Two pointers, no matter how long the list is: **O(1)** space.

The other answer groups often come up with is to remember every node you've visited, say in a set, and report a cycle when you see one again. That's also O(n) time, but it needs **O(n)** space to hold the visited nodes. Floyd's gets the same answer with two pointers.

lessons.title: Interleaving Two Lists
lessons.readme:
# Interleaving Two Lists

Now the shuffle itself. A **perfect shuffle** splits the deck into two piles and then **interleaves** them: one card from the first pile, one from the second, and so on, like a zipper.

![two piles interleaved card by card](courses/diagrams/732d3c6e-a647-5cfb-b414-f1cd74452875/even.svg)

Lab 4 calls this `merge`, but it doesn't compare anything. It just takes turns. And it doesn't copy cards either: it **relinks** the existing nodes by changing their `next` pointers. Lecture calls that **pointer manipulation**.

The solution key builds the result with a pointer called `last`, the zipper: it always points at the last node of the merged list so far.

1. If `pile1` is empty, the answer is just `pile2`.
2. The first card of `pile1` is the first card of the result. Point `last` at it and advance `pile1`.
3. While both piles have cards: link the next card from the **other** pile after `last`, advance that pile, and move `last` forward. Alternate.
4. When one pile runs out, link the rest of the other one after `last`.

What if the piles aren't the same length? Step 4 handles it, and it's one assignment: the leftover cards are already linked to each other, so attaching the first one attaches them all.

![when pile1 runs out, the rest of pile2 is attached in one step](courses/diagrams/732d3c6e-a647-5cfb-b414-f1cd74452875/uneven.svg)

> [!tip]
> Save a pile's `next` (by advancing the pile pointer) **before** you overwrite anyone's `next`. Relinking first loses the rest of the pile.

## Assignment

The deck code goes in `deck.h`.

1. [ ] Complete `interleave(pile1, pile2)` and return the first node of the result. Take turns starting with `pile1`. When one pile runs out, the rest of the other follows. Either pile may be empty.
2. [ ] Only relink: no `new`, and don't change any `elt`.

lessons.title: Interleaving Big O
lessons.readme:
# Interleaving Big O

How long does interleaving take for piles of length n and m? This was a lecture clicker question.

The loop runs only while **both** piles have cards, so it stops as soon as the shorter one is used up. Each round links one card, so that's at most 2 · min(n, m) rounds, with one pointer change each. Then the leftover cards of the longer pile are attached with **one** assignment, no matter how many there are, because they're already linked to each other.

So the worst case is **O(min(n, m))**, not O(n + m). The long pile's tail is never walked.

Compare that with merging two **sorted** lists, coming up soon. That one has to decide which node goes next by comparing values, and in the worst case it walks both lists almost to the end: O(n + m).

| | Worst case |
|---|---|
| interleave (take turns) | O(min(n, m)) |
| merge sorted lists (compare) | O(n + m) |

You interleave a list of 8 nodes with one of 90,000. Roughly how many `next` pointers change?

lessons.title: The Faro Shuffle
lessons.readme:
# The Faro Shuffle

A **faro shuffle** (perfect shuffle) splits the deck into two **equal** halves and interleaves them perfectly. There are two kinds, depending on which half goes first:

- **Out-shuffle**: the top half goes first, so the top card **stays on top**.
- **In-shuffle**: the bottom half goes first, so the top card becomes the **second** card.

By hand, it's a riffle shuffle where the two halves drop exactly one card at a time, alternating. Real riffles let cards clump; a faro never does.

![two hands riffle shuffling a deck of cards on a table](courses/diagrams/a33e493e-9971-548f-9c64-405f5a1bac73/riffle.jpg)
*Image: Johnny Blood, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.*

![an 8-card deck after an out-shuffle and after an in-shuffle](courses/diagrams/a33e493e-9971-548f-9c64-405f5a1bac73/kinds.svg)

Lab 4's `faro_shuffle` is three moves:

1. **Find the cut.** Walk `pile2` to the last card of the top half.
2. **Split.** Save the card after it, set `pile2->next = nullptr` to end the top half, and point `pile2` at the saved card.
3. **Interleave.** For an in-shuffle, swap the piles first.

The loop in step 1 is easy to get off by one:

```cpp
for (int i = 1; i < count / 2; i++) pile2 = pile2->next;
```

`i` starts at **1**, not 0. `pile2` starts on card 1 and needs to stop on card `count / 2`, the last card of the top half, which is `count / 2 - 1` steps away. Stopping **on** the card before the cut is the point: that's the node whose `next` has to become `nullptr`.

![pile2 stops on card 4, the deck is cut there](courses/diagrams/a33e493e-9971-548f-9c64-405f5a1bac73/split.svg)

In Lab 4 the result went back into the deck with `deck.setHead(merge(pile1, pile2))`. Here we return the new first node instead.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `faroShuffle(deck, count, inShuffle)` and return the first card of the shuffled deck. `count` is the number of cards; assume it's even and at least 2.
2. [ ] Use `interleave` from the last lesson. Only relink: no `new`, no changed values.

lessons.title: Faro Shuffle Facts
lessons.readme:
# Faro Shuffle Facts

Lab 4 used the simulator to answer some surprising questions about a 52-card deck. Perfect shuffles only **simulate** randomness, and sometimes very poorly:

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Out-shuffles to return the deck to its original order | **8** |
| In-shuffles to return the deck to its original order | **52** |
| In-shuffles to **reverse** the deck | **26** |
| Out-shuffles to reverse the deck | **impossible** |

Why can't out-shuffles ever reverse the deck? Look at the definition: an out-shuffle keeps the top card on top. Card 1 is on top before the first out-shuffle, after it, and after every one that follows. A reversed deck needs card 52 on top, so no number of out-shuffles gets there. (The bottom card stays on the bottom too.)

Tracing a small shuffle by hand is a good exam warm-up. Split the deck in half, then take turns. For an in-shuffle the bottom half goes first:

```
deck:        1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
halves:      1 2 3 4 | 5 6 7 8
out-shuffle: 1 5 2 6 3 7 4 8
in-shuffle:  5 1 6 2 7 3 8 4
```

Why can out-shuffles never reverse a 52-card deck?
answers: Each one undoes the one before
They only move the bottom half
The top card always stays on top

lessons.title: Merging Sorted Lists
lessons.readme:
# Merging Sorted Lists

The club sorted the two halves of a deck separately and now wants one sorted deck. That's **merging** two sorted lists, and it was on the midterm review. Unlike interleaving, each step **compares**: the smaller front card goes next.

The lecture version uses two helpers:

- A **dummy** node on the stack, so the merged list always has a node to attach to. Without it, picking the very first node is a special case.
- A pointer `tail`, the zipper: the last node of the merged list so far.

![the dummy node with tail, and the two sorted lists a and b](courses/diagrams/ec35b137-43c9-51a9-97b9-e2fd87aa08c2/start.svg)

Each round, compare `a->elt` and `b->elt`. Link the smaller node after `tail`, advance that list, and move `tail` forward. On a tie, take from `a` (`<=`). Here's lecture's example:

| round | compare | take | merged so far |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 ≤ 2 | 1 from a | 1 |
| 2 | 5 ≤ 2? no | 2 from b | 1 2 |
| 3 | 5 ≤ 4? no | 4 from b | 1 2 4 |
| 4 | 5 ≤ 6 | 5 from a | 1 2 4 5 |
| 5 | 9 ≤ 6? no | 6 from b | 1 2 4 5 6 |
| 6 | 9 ≤ 14 | 9 from a | 1 2 4 5 6 9 |
| 7 | 20 ≤ 14? no | 14 from b | 1 2 4 5 6 9 14 |

Now `b` is empty, so the loop stops, and whatever is left of `a` is attached in one step:

![after b runs out, tail->next = a attaches 20](courses/diagrams/ec35b137-43c9-51a9-97b9-e2fd87aa08c2/end.svg)

The answer is `dummy.next`. The dummy itself is left behind, and since it lives on the stack, there's nothing to delete.

<details>
<summary>Try writing it on paper first, then compare</summary>

```cpp
Node dummy{0, nullptr};
Node* tail = &dummy;
while (a != nullptr && b != nullptr) {
    if (a->elt <= b->elt) { tail->next = a; a = a->next; }
    else                  { tail->next = b; b = b->next; }
    tail = tail->next;
}
tail->next = (a != nullptr) ? a : b;
return dummy.next;
```

</details>

## Assignment

These go in `ops.h`.

1. [ ] Complete `merge(a, b)`: both lists are sorted ascending. Return the first node of one sorted list holding every node of both. Either list may be empty.
2. [ ] Only relink: no `new`, and don't change any `elt`.

lessons.title: Merging Sorted Lists Big O
lessons.readme:
# Merging Sorted Lists Big O

Every round of the merge loop places one node, and the loop runs until **one** list is empty. Then the rest of the other list is attached in O(1).

So the number of rounds depends on the values, not just the lengths. Lecture's question was the **worst** case for lists of length n and m: **O(n + m)**.

The worst case is any input that forces the loop to look at nearly every node of both lists. Lecture's example:

```
a: 1 → 5 → 9 → 20
b: 2 → 50
```

`b` is the shorter list, but its last value, 50, is bigger than everything in `a`. So `b` can't run out until all of `a` has been placed: the loop has to look at every node of both lists.

The best case goes the other way. If every value in `a` is smaller than the first value of `b`, the loop takes all of `a` and stops, and `b` is attached in one step without being walked.

Compare that with interleaving, which never compares, and stops at the shorter list: O(min(n, m)).

lessons.title: Reversing a List
lessons.readme:
# Reversing a List

Lab 4's bonus task: reverse the deck **in place**, with these rules:

1. A single pass.
2. No recursion.
3. Constant space: no array or stack of nodes, and fewer than 5 pointers.

The trick is to flip every `next` pointer to point **backward**, one node at a time. Three pointers do it:

- `prev`: the part already reversed (it starts as `nullptr`, an empty list)
- `cur`: the node being flipped
- `nxt`: the rest of the list, saved before `cur->next` is overwritten

Each step: save `nxt = cur->next`, point `cur->next` back at `prev`, then advance `prev = cur` and `cur = nxt`.

![reversing 1 2 3: the prev list grows as the cur list shrinks](courses/diagrams/3ab2b9c9-a89f-5b8b-afbb-82f8f8437037/steps.svg)

```
start    prev → null                  cur → 1 → 2 → 3 → null
step 1   prev → 1 → null              cur → 2 → 3 → null
step 2   prev → 2 → 1 → null          cur → 3 → null
step 3   prev → 3 → 2 → 1 → null      cur → null, so return prev
```

The order inside the loop matters for the same reason as `removeFront`: once you overwrite `cur->next`, the rest of the list is unreachable unless you saved it in `nxt` first.

At the end, `cur` is `nullptr` and `prev` is the old last node, which is the new head. In Lab 4 that went back into the deck with `deck.setHead(lastNode)`.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `reverse(head)` and return the new first node.
2. [ ] Use a loop: one pass, no recursion, no extra array or stack. Only relink nodes. The tests reverse a 200,000-node list.

# Reversing a List Big O

The loop visits each node once and does a constant amount of work there (one save, one flip, two moves), so reversing is **O(n)** time. It uses three pointers no matter how long the list is: **O(1)** extra space.

Why did Lab 4 forbid recursion? A recursive reverse is short and correct, but every call waits on the call stack until the calls below it return. Reversing n nodes recursively stacks up **n** calls at once: **O(n)** space. With a few hundred thousand nodes, that overflows the stack and the program crashes. The iterative version has no such limit.

(The recursion chapter comes back to this with the lecture's recursive version, as practice tracing recursion on lists.)

When tracing on paper, write out `prev` and `cur` as two lists after each step, like the table in the last lesson. The two lists always hold every node between them: `prev`'s list grows by one and `cur`'s shrinks by one.

lessons.title: Remove Every Other Node
lessons.readme:
# Remove Every Other Node

Here's a pointer manipulation problem from the midterm: thin the deck by removing every **second** card. Keep the 1st, 3rd, 5th, and so on, and delete the rest.

Use `head` itself as the walking pointer. At each kept node:

1. Save the node to remove: `toDelete = head->next`.
2. Link around it: `head->next = toDelete->next`.
3. Free it: `delete toDelete`.
4. Step to the next node to keep: `head = head->next`.

![removing every other node from 1 2 3 4 5](courses/diagrams/5604444a-1284-5fed-ae68-16297358037f/steps.svg)

The loop runs while **both** `head` and `head->next` exist. If `head` is null, we've run off the end. If `head->next` is null, `head` is the last node and there's nothing after it to remove.

The function takes `Node* head` by value, and that's fine here. The first node is always kept, so the caller's `head` never changes; walking the local copy can't hurt it.

Step 2 comes before step 3 for the usual reason: `toDelete->next` has to be read while `toDelete` still exists.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `removeEveryOther(head)`: keep the 1st, 3rd, 5th... nodes, and `delete` every node you remove. An empty or one-node list is left as is.

lessons.title: Insert Before Without the Head
lessons.readme:
# Insert Before Without the Head

Last puzzle from lecture. You're given a pointer `ptr` to some node in a singly linked list, and you must insert a new value **before** it:

```cpp
void insertBefore(Node* ptr, int val);
```

You don't have `head`, so you can't walk to the node before `ptr`. And even with `head`, the walk would be O(n). How can this possibly be O(1)?

Stop thinking about moving **nodes**, and move the **data** instead. Inserting after `ptr` is easy. So:

1. Make a new node right **after** `ptr`, holding a **copy** of `ptr`'s value.
2. Overwrite `ptr`'s value with `val`.

![insert before ptr by copying 3 into a new node after it, then overwriting ptr](courses/diagrams/2f6760e0-49a2-573d-8493-abd5fe714b4c/steps.svg)

The list now reads `1 → 4 → 3 → 5 → 7`. To anyone walking it, 4 was inserted before 3. In reality, the node `ptr` points to now holds 4, and 3 moved into the new node.

```cpp
ptr->next = new Node{ptr->elt, ptr->next};
ptr->elt = val;
```

Two lines, no walking: **O(1)**. (The slide names this function `insertAt(ptr, val)`. It's the same trick.) Lecture calls this the **data copying** technique: in a linked list you can rearrange the data as well as the pointers.

> [!note]
> After the call, `ptr` points at the node holding the **new** value. If the caller cared about `ptr` meaning "the node holding 3," that's no longer true. That's the price of the trick.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `insertBefore(ptr, val)` in O(1) with data copying. Assume `ptr` isn't `nullptr`. It works the same when `ptr` is the last node.

lessons.title: Three Linked List Techniques
lessons.readme:
# Three Linked List Techniques

Lecture gave names to the three moves behind every algorithm in this chapter. Exam questions sometimes ask which one a piece of code uses.

| Technique | What it means | Where you used it |
|---|---|---|
| **Pointer chasing** | two pointers walk the same list, at a gap or at different speeds | removeBack (prev and cur), k-th from the end, middle, Floyd's cycle detection |
| **Pointer manipulation** | change `next` pointers to rearrange existing nodes | interleaving, the faro shuffle, merging, reversing, removeEveryOther |
| **Data copying** | move the values instead of the nodes | insertBefore without the head |

A few habits carry across all of them:

- **Save before you overwrite or delete.** removeFront, clear, reverse and removeEveryOther all depend on reading `next` first.
- **Check the empty list and the one-node list** before anything else.
- **When `fast` jumps two nodes**, check both `fast` and `fast->next`.
- **Relinking doesn't allocate.** If an algorithm only rearranges nodes, there should be no `new` and no `delete` in it.

questions.question: Floyd's cycle detection is an example of which technique?
Reversing a list in place is an example of which technique?

lessons.title: What Is Recursion?
lessons.readme:
# What Is Recursion?

The Spartan Robotics club is building a demo for the engineering open house: a robot arm that solves the Tower of Hanoi puzzle. The arm's planner turns out to be a stack of small recursive functions, so this chapter builds them one at a time.

First, the idea. **Recursion** is when a function solves a problem by calling itself on a **smaller version of the same problem**, until the problem is small enough to answer directly.

Nesting dolls are a good picture of it. Open a doll and you find a smaller doll of the same kind, and so on, until you reach the smallest one, which doesn't open. That last doll is the base case.

![a set of Russian nesting dolls, one opened to show the smaller dolls inside](courses/diagrams/cdf6e4d7-f986-50cf-a5a6-c45628b7e31a/matryoshka.jpg)
*Image: Fanghong, background removed by Gnomz007, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.*

Take power: `power(x, n)` returns xⁿ. Can xⁿ be built from a smaller power? Yes:

```
xⁿ = x * xⁿ⁻¹
   = x * (x * xⁿ⁻²)
   = x * (x * (x * ... (x * x⁰)))
```

xⁿ⁻¹ is the same problem, just smaller. We stop when we reach x⁰, which is 1. That stopping point is the **base case**. Here's the lecture's version:

```cpp
int power_rec(int x, int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 1;              // base case: x⁰ = 1
    return x * power_rec(x, n - 1);    // xⁿ = x * xⁿ⁻¹
}
```

The lecture's recipe for **recursive thinking**:

1. Is the problem small enough? If yes, solve it directly. That's the **base case**, and you need at least one.
2. Otherwise:
   - break it into one or more smaller problems of the same type,
   - solve each one recursively,
   - combine their results into the answer.

Without a base case, `power_rec` would call itself forever, or at least until the program runs out of stack space and crashes.

A base case alone isn't enough, though. For a recursive function to **stop**, two things must both be true:

1. It has **at least one base case**.
2. Every recursive call works on a **smaller problem that moves toward** a base case.

Returning a value is not on that list: a `void` function like Tower of Hanoi stops just fine, and a function that returns a value can still recurse forever.

questions.question: What happens if you delete the base case from `power_rec`?
answers: It returns the right answer anyway

questions.question: In `power_rec`, which line combines the smaller answer into the bigger one?
A recursive function has a base case, yet some calls never stop. Which requirement is it breaking?
answers: It must have a second base case
Calls must move toward a base case
It must return a value on every path
It must call itself exactly once
questions.answer: Calls must move toward a base case

lessons.title: The Call Stack
lessons.readme:
# The Call Stack

How does the computer keep track of all those unfinished calls? With the **call stack**.

Every time a function is called, it gets a **frame** on the call stack holding its parameters and local variables. A `return` removes (pops) its frame and hands the value back to the caller, which was waiting right underneath.

Here's `power_rec(2, 3)`. Each call pushes a new frame on top:

![frames pushed for power_rec(2, 3)](courses/diagrams/d2c5a3a8-9026-5b75-988c-295d8b4c388c/push.svg)

`power_rec(2, 0)` is the base case, so it returns 1 without calling anything. Now the frames come off one at a time, newest first, and each one finishes its multiplication:

![frames popping as each call returns](courses/diagrams/d2c5a3a8-9026-5b75-988c-295d8b4c388c/pops.svg)

The answer, 8, comes out of the very first call, which was the last to finish.

Two things to notice:

- The frames go on and come off in **last in, first out** order. That's exactly a stack, which is the next chapter's data structure.
- While the deepest call runs, **all** the frames are on the stack at once. `power_rec(x, n)` needs n + 1 frames, so it uses **O(n) stack space**. That's why endless recursion crashes: the stack is finite.

questions.question: `power_rec(3, 4)` runs. At the deepest point, how many `power_rec` frames are on the call stack?
Which call **returns first**?

lessons.readme:
# Recursive Power

Time to write some. The robot arm's planner needs to count things like how many positions the puzzle can be in, which is 3ⁿ for n disks. So the first tool is power.

We'll also write **factorial**, the warm-up from Lab 5: n! = n · (n − 1) · … · 1, and 0! = 1. As a recursion:

- base case: `factorial(0)` is 1
- smaller problem: n! = n · (n − 1)!

Factorial is undefined for negative numbers. Lab 5 says to return **-1** for them. Notice that this check has to come **before** the recursion: `factorial(-1)` would otherwise call `factorial(-2)`, then `factorial(-3)`, and never reach 0.

> [!tip]
> Before you write a recursive function, answer the three questions out loud: what's the base case, what's the smaller problem, and how do I combine?

## Assignment

These go in `recursion.h`, which grows through the next few lessons.

1. [ ] Complete `power_rec(x, n)` recursively, the lecture's way: base case `n == 0`, otherwise `x * power_rec(x, n - 1)`. You can assume `n >= 0`.
2. [ ] Complete `factorial(n)` recursively. Return `-1` if `n` is negative.

lessons.title: How Many Base Cases?
lessons.readme:
# How Many Base Cases?

`power_rec` needed one base case. Some problems need more.

Fibonacci, the way this class defines it:

```
f(0) = 1
f(1) = 1
f(n) = f(n - 1) + f(n - 2)   when n > 1
```

That gives 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, … so f(5) = 8.

**What's the minimum number of base cases?** Two. Each call reaches back **two** steps, so with only `f(0)`, the call `f(1)` would ask for `f(0) + f(-1)`, and `f(-1)` never reaches a base case.

**What's the maximum?** There isn't one. You could add `f(2) = 2` as a third base case and the function would still be correct. But the lecture's advice is that an elegant solution uses the **minimum** set of base cases.

**The base case has to be reachable.** Every path of calls must land on one. A step that jumps over it never stops:

```cpp
int count(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 0;
    return 1 + count(n - 2);    // count(3) -> count(1) -> count(-1) -> ...
}
```

Even numbers work. Odd numbers skip right past 0 and recurse until the stack overflows.

> [!warning]
> When an exam asks "for which n does this return?", trace the smallest few n by hand. One of them usually steps past the base case.

questions.question: True or false: adding `if (n == 2) return 2;` as a third base case to the class's Fibonacci makes it return wrong answers.

lessons.title: Tracing Recursive Calls
lessons.readme:
# Tracing Recursive Calls

On the exam you'll be handed a recursive function and asked what it returns. The reliable way is to write each call as a **frame in brackets**, expand until you hit a base case, then collapse from the inside out.

```cpp
int mystery(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;
    return n + mystery(n - 2);
}
```

`mystery(5)`:

```
mystery(5)
-> [5 + mystery(3)]
-> [5 + [3 + mystery(1)]]
-> [5 + [3 + [1]]]          mystery(1) is a base case: returns 1
-> [5 + [3 + 1]]
-> [5 + 4]
-> 9
```

The same trick works on digits. `n % 10` is the last digit, and `n / 10` drops it:

```cpp
int sumDigits(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 0;
    return n % 10 + sumDigits(n / 10);
}
```

```
sumDigits(472)
-> [2 + sumDigits(47)]
-> [2 + [7 + sumDigits(4)]]
-> [2 + [7 + [4 + sumDigits(0)]]]
-> [2 + [7 + [4 + 0]]]
-> 13
```

Don't skip writing the brackets. They're how you avoid losing track of which frame is waiting on which.

lessons.title: Sum of Digits
lessons.readme:
# Sum of Digits

The robot arm's controller reads a move counter, and the club wants a quick checksum of it: the sum of its digits.

You traced this one last lesson. Here are the three questions answered:

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Base case? | `n == 0`: no digits left, the sum is 0 |
| Smaller problem? | `n / 10`, the number without its last digit |
| Combine? | add the last digit, `n % 10` |

The base case is `n == 0` and not `n < 10`. With `n < 10 return 0`, the leftmost digit would be dropped. You could write `if (n < 10) return n;` instead, and that's also correct; it just stops one call earlier.

Quiz 5 offered four base cases for exactly this function. Here's why the other three fail:

| Base case | What goes wrong |
|---|---|
| `if (n < 10) return 0;` | stops one step early and throws away the leading digit: 472 gives 9 |
| `if (n % 10 == 0) return 0;` | tests the **last** digit, so any number with a 0 in it stops there: 4702 gives 2 |
| `if (n == 1) return 1;` | only works when the leading digit is 1 (172 gives 10). Any other leading digit skips past 1 to 0, and `n / 10` keeps giving 0 forever |

Here's `sumDigits(9051)` as frames:

```
[1 + [5 + [0 + [9 + 0]]]] = 15
```

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `sumDigits(n)` in `recursion.h` recursively. You can assume `n >= 0`.

lessons.readme:
# Fibonacci

Fibonacci was the class activity, and Lab 5 asked you to **count** how many times each `fibonacci(n)` gets called. Let's do both.

The code is a direct copy of the definition: two base cases, two recursive calls. Each call that isn't a base case splits into two more, so the calls form a tree:

![call tree of fibonacci(4)](courses/diagrams/a3ab85a8-525b-5020-8ed5-269c6a4186f1/tree.svg)

The green boxes are base cases. Count all the boxes: `fibonacci(4)` makes **9** calls, and the two blue boxes show `fibonacci(2)` computed twice from scratch.

| Call | Times called |
|---|---|
| fibonacci(4) | 1 |
| fibonacci(3) | 1 |
| fibonacci(2) | 2 |
| fibonacci(1) | 3 |
| fibonacci(0) | 2 |
| **total** | **9** |

To count without globals (Lab 5 forbids them), pass a vector by reference into every call and bump `calls[n]` at the start of each one.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `fibonacci(n)` with the class's definition: `f(0) = f(1) = 1`.
2. [ ] Complete `fibonacciCounted(n, calls)`. It returns the same value as `fibonacci(n)`, and every call to `fibonacciCounted(k, calls)` (including base cases) adds 1 to `calls[k]`. The caller passes a vector of `n + 1` zeros. Don't use global or static variables.

lessons.title: Fibonacci Big O
lessons.readme:
# Fibonacci Big O

How slow is the naive `fibonacci`? Look at the total calls:

| n | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| total calls | 3 | 5 | 9 | 15 | 25 |

Each step up multiplies the work by about 1.6. Every call that isn't a base case makes **two** recursive calls, and the depth is about n, so the tree has up to about 2ⁿ circles. The naive version is **O(2ⁿ)**: exponential. `fibonacci(50)` would take minutes.

The waste is obvious from the tree: the same small values get recomputed over and over.

**Memoization** fixes that. Keep a cache (a "memo"). Before computing `fibonacci(n)`, check the cache. If the answer is there, return it immediately with no recursive calls. If not, compute it, store it, then return it.

Now each value from 0 to n is computed only once:

| | Naive | Memoized |
|---|---|---|
| time | O(2ⁿ) | **O(n)** |
| extra space | O(n) call stack | O(n) call stack + O(n) cache |

Memoization trades memory for time. You'll see the same idea again as **dynamic programming** near the end of the course.

lessons.title: Caching Fibonacci
lessons.readme:
# Caching Fibonacci

The robot's planner asks for big Fibonacci numbers, and the naive version is far too slow. Let's add the cache from the last lesson.

Like Lab 5, the cache is **passed in** as a parameter instead of living in a global. Here it's a `vector<long long>` with n + 1 slots, all set to **-1**, meaning "not computed yet". (No Fibonacci number is negative, so -1 can't be confused with a real answer.)

```
fibonacciMemo(n, memo):
    base cases: return 1
    if memo[n] isn't -1: return memo[n]          (already known)
    memo[n] = fibonacciMemo(n - 1) + fibonacciMemo(n - 2)
    return memo[n]
```

Here's the call tree for `fibonacciMemo(5)`. The left branch goes all the way down once and fills `memo[2]`, `memo[3]` and `memo[4]` on the way back up. After that, every right branch is a single lookup:

![call tree of fibonacciMemo(5) with memo lookups](courses/diagrams/d12c19a5-351f-549e-a218-c730db6b2536/tree.svg)

We switch to `long long` because these numbers outgrow an `int` at n = 46.

> [!tip]
> Check the cache **before** recursing. Storing answers you never read saves nothing.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `fibonacciMemo(n, memo)`. It returns the class's Fibonacci number for `n` (`f(0) = f(1) = 1`). `memo` has `n + 1` entries, all `-1` at the start. Store each answer you compute in `memo[n]` and reuse it.

The tests time it: `fibonacciMemo(80, memo)` has to finish instantly.

lessons.title: Fast Power
lessons.readme:
# Fast Power

Back to power. `power_rec` makes n calls, so it's O(n). This was midterm problem 17: do it in **O(log n)**.

The trick is to **halve** n instead of subtracting 1:

| n is… | then |
|---|---|
| even | xⁿ = xⁿᐟ² · xⁿᐟ² |
| odd | xⁿ = x · xⁿᐟ² · xⁿᐟ² |
| 0 | x⁰ = 1 (base case) |

Integer division makes the odd case work: 13 / 2 is 6, and x¹³ = x · x⁶ · x⁶. Check the small ones: x¹ = x · x⁰ · x⁰ = x, and x³ = x · x¹ · x¹.

```
power(x, 13) -> power(x, 6) -> power(x, 3) -> power(x, 1) -> power(x, 0)
```

That's 5 calls instead of 14. With x = 2, the calls go down halving n, then each one squares the answer it gets back:

![power(2, 13) calls going down and values coming back](courses/diagrams/908edf55-d4d9-5031-b305-e7e825114833/calls.svg)

> [!warning]
> Call `power(x, n / 2)` **once** and save it in a variable (`half`). Writing `power(x, n / 2) * power(x, n / 2)` makes two calls per level, and the total work grows back to O(n). The tests time your code to catch this.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `power(x, n)` in O(log n): base case `n == 0`, then `half = power(x, n / 2)`, then return `half * half`, times `x` if n is odd. You can assume `n >= 0`.

lessons.title: Fast Power Big O
lessons.readme:
# Fast Power Big O

Count the calls. Every call to `power` makes **one** recursive call, on n / 2, so n halves each time:

| n | calls |
|---|---|
| 13 | 13, 6, 3, 1, 0: **5** |
| 20 | 20, 10, 5, 2, 1, 0: **6** |
| 1000 | **11** |

That's about log₂ n + 2 calls, each doing O(1) work: **O(log n)** time.

The call stack is the same depth, so it also uses **O(log n) stack space**, compared with O(n) for `power_rec`.

Now the trap from the last lesson. If you call `power(x, n / 2)` **twice**, each call makes two calls on n / 2. The depth is still log₂ n, but the number of calls doubles at every level: 1 + 2 + 4 + … + n, about 2n calls. That's **O(n)**, no better than `power_rec`. Saving the result in `half` is the whole point.

> [!note]
> Midterm-style justification: "each call makes one recursive call, and n halves each time, so the depth is log₂ n and the runtime is O(log n)."

lessons.title: Palindromes with a Helper
lessons.readme:
# Palindromes with a Helper

The club's sign for the demo reads "racecar", and someone wants the robot to check whether words read the same backward. That's the class activity's `isPalindrome`.

The idea: compare the **outermost** pair of characters. If they differ, it's not a palindrome. If they match, the answer is whatever the **inside** gives. Two indices, `b` (begin) and `e` (end), step inward each call:

![b and e step inward on racecar](courses/diagrams/5447ba29-23c5-5fed-89dc-17270e415776/steps.svg)

**Base case: `b >= e`.** When the indices meet (odd length) or cross (even length), every pair has matched.

> [!warning]
> Use `>=`, not `==`. With an even length like "abba", b and e go from (1, 2) straight to (2, 1). They never equal each other, so `==` would run off the ends of the string.

The function the caller sees, `isPalindrome(const string& s)`, only has one parameter. So the lecture adds a **helper** that carries the extra indices, and the public function just starts it:

```cpp
bool isPalindrome(const string& input) {
    return isPalindromeRecursive(input, 0, input.length() - 1);
}
```

Helpers like this show up all over the course: they hide the extra arguments the recursion needs.

## Assignment

This starts a new file, `strings.h`.

1. [ ] Complete `isPalindromeRecursive(input, b, e)`: true if `input[b..e]` is a palindrome.
2. [ ] Complete `isPalindrome(input)` by calling the helper on the whole string. The empty string counts as a palindrome.

# Reversing a String

Lab 5 Task 3: reverse a string recursively. The demo display scrolls the club's name backward, so we need it.

Three questions again:

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Base case? | the empty string reverses to itself |
| Smaller problem? | the string without its first character |
| Combine? | put the first character at the **end** of the reversed rest |

```
reverse("abc")
-> [reverse("bc") + 'a']
-> [[reverse("c") + 'b'] + 'a']
-> [[[reverse("") + 'c'] + 'b'] + 'a']
-> "cba"
```

`s.substr(1)` gives everything after the first character. It's the simplest way to write this, but each `substr` **copies** the rest of the string, so this version is O(n²) for a string of length n. You could avoid the copies with an index helper, like the palindrome. For this lesson the simple version is fine.

lessons.title: Decimal to Binary
lessons.readme:
# Decimal to Binary

The robot arm has a row of LEDs that shows the move number in binary. The class activity wrote exactly this:

```cpp
string dec_to_bin(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return "";
    return dec_to_bin(n / 2) + to_string(n % 2);
}
```

Why does it work?

- `n % 2` is n's **right-most bit** (0 or 1).
- `n / 2` drops that bit: it shifts n right by one.
- The recursive call comes **first** and the bit is added **after**, so the string builds on the way **back up**. The deepest call adds the most significant bit, and the first call adds the least significant one.

| n | n in binary | n % 2 |
|---|---|---|
| 12 | 1100 | 0 |
| 6 | 110 | 0 |
| 3 | 11 | 1 |
| 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 0 | (base case) | |

![dec_to_bin(12) calls going down and strings coming back](courses/diagrams/8a36d47b-2207-55a8-80d7-61497c98a9ee/calls.svg)

> [!note]
> As the professor wrote it, the base case is `n == 0` and it returns the **empty string**. So `dec_to_bin(12)` makes 5 calls (12, 6, 3, 1, 0), and `dec_to_bin(0)` returns `""`, not `"0"`. Answer exam questions about this code as written.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `dec_to_bin(n)` in `strings.h` exactly like the lecture: base case `n == 0` returns `""`. You can assume `n >= 0`.

string dec_to_bin(int n) {

Write the calls going down, n halving each time, until n is 0. Then build the string coming back up, appending each call's `n % 2`:

lessons.title: Is It a Subsequence?
lessons.readme:
# Is It a Subsequence?

The robot logs every move it makes. A demo script lists the moves that **must** happen, in order. Did the log include them all, in that order, possibly with other moves in between? That was the midterm bonus: is `s` a **subsequence** of `t`?

"ace" is a subsequence of "abcde" (a, then c, then e). "aec" isn't: the letters are there, but not in that order.

The professor's first version shrinks both strings with `substr`:

```cpp
bool isSub(const std::string& s, const std::string& t) {
    if (s.size() == 0) return true;     // matched every letter of s
    if (t.size() == 0) return false;    // ran out of t first
    if (s[0] == t[0]) return isSub(s.substr(1), t.substr(1));
    else return isSub(s, t.substr(1));
}
```

If the first letters match, use up one letter of each. If not, skip a letter of `t` and keep looking.

**The order of the base cases matters.** Swap them and `isSub("", "")` returns false, and so does any match that finishes on the very last letter of `t`.

The second version uses **indices** instead of copying strings, with a helper, the same pattern as the palindrome:

| s index | t index | compare | action |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | a, a | match: both move |
| 1 | 1 | c, b | skip t |
| 1 | 2 | c, c | match: both move |
| 2 | 3 | e, d | skip t |
| 2 | 4 | e, e | match: both move |
| 3 | 5 | | s used up: **true** |

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `isSubHelper(s, t, sIndex, tIndex)` recursively: is `s` from `sIndex` on a subsequence of `t` from `tIndex` on? Base cases in this order: `s` used up → `true`, then `t` used up → `false`. The helper must call **itself**.
2. [ ] Complete `isSub(s, t)` by calling `isSubHelper(s, t, 0, 0)`. Don't use `substr`.

lessons.title: Why Index Helpers?
lessons.readme:
# Why Index Helpers?

The midterm solution slide asked: why is the index version more efficient than the `substr` version?

Because `substr` **copies**. `t.substr(1)` builds a brand new string holding everything after the first character. For a string of length n that's O(n) work, in every call.

| Version | work per call | calls | total |
|---|---|---|---|
| `substr` | O(n) copy | up to about n | O(n²) |
| indices | O(1) | up to about n | **O(n)** |

The index version passes the same two strings by `const` reference the whole way down and only moves two integers. No copies at all.

That's the general reason for helpers with index parameters: the palindrome, `isSub`, and (next) the professor's `findLargest` all use one. The public function keeps the simple signature the problem asks for, and the helper carries the bookkeeping.

**Base-case order, once more.** In `isSub`, "s is used up" must be checked **before** "t is used up". When both happen at once, s was fully matched, so the answer is true.
