lessons.title: Bubble Sort Passes
lessons.readme:
# Bubble Sort Passes

On the exam you'll often be asked what the array looks like after a certain number of passes, or what's guaranteed after each one.

Look back at the green part in the last lesson's picture. That pattern has a name: a **loop invariant**, a property that's true at a fixed point of every iteration. For bubble sort:

> After outer iteration i (counting from i = 0), the last i + 1 keys are the i + 1 largest, in sorted order, in their **final** positions.

Notice what's **not** promised: the left part can still be a mess. After pass 1 of the lecture's example, the left side is `3 2 6 7 0 1`.

To trace a pass by hand, keep your finger on the key being carried. It moves right as long as it's bigger than its neighbor. When it meets something bigger, it stops, and the bigger key gets carried instead. So one pass is easy to write down quickly:

- `5 1 8 4 9 2 7 3`: carry 5 past 1, stop at 8. Carry 8 past 4, stop at 9. Carry 9 past 2, 7, 3.
- Result: `1 5 4 8 2 7 3 9`.

Try two passes on paper before you check.

questions.question: Bubble sort (lecture version) on `5 1 8 4 9 2 7 3`. After **two** full passes:
After bubble sort's outer iteration i = 2 (i = 0 is the first), what is guaranteed?
answers: Nothing until the outer loop finishes
The first 3 keys are sorted among themselves but may still move
The last 3 keys are the 3 largest, sorted, in final positions
The first 3 keys are the 3 smallest, in final positions
questions.answer: The last 3 keys are the 3 largest, sorted, in final positions

lessons.title: Bubble Sort Big O
lessons.readme:
# Bubble Sort Big O

Count the work by input. **Comparisons** come from the two loops, and they don't depend on the data at all:

(n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 = **n(n − 1)/2**, which is O(n²), every time.

**Swaps** do depend on the data: a key has to swap once for every key it needs to move past. The farther keys start from their final positions, the more swaps.

| Input | Comparisons | Swaps |
|---|---|---|
| Already sorted (best) | n(n − 1)/2 = O(n²) | 0 |
| Random (average) | n(n − 1)/2 = O(n²) | about n(n − 1)/4 = O(n²) |
| Reverse sorted (worst) | n(n − 1)/2 = O(n²) | n(n − 1)/2 = O(n²): every comparison swaps |

So bubble sort is O(n²) in the best, average **and** worst case.

- **In place?** Yes. A swap only needs one temporary variable: O(1) extra space.
- **Stable?** Yes. It only swaps neighbors, and only when the left one is strictly bigger, so equal keys never pass each other.

> [!note]
> You may have seen a bubble sort that stops when a pass makes no swaps. It's safe to stop: a pass with no swaps found every neighbor pair already in order, and that means the whole array is sorted. That version is O(n) on sorted input. The lecture's version doesn't have that check, so for this class its best case is still O(n²) comparisons.

questions.question: Bubble sort (lecture version) on 6 keys that are **already sorted**. Comparisons and swaps?
Bubble sort on 8 keys in **reverse** order. Comparisons and swaps?
A full bubble sort pass over an array makes **no** swaps. What does that tell you?
answers: The array has no duplicate keys
One more pass is needed to be sure
Only the last key is in its final place

lessons.title: Finding the Minimum
lessons.readme:
# Finding the Minimum

Bubble sort swaps a lot. A big key can be swapped once per step on its way to the end. Could we put each key straight into its final spot with **one** swap?

That's the idea behind **selection sort**. Split the array into a sorted left side and an unsorted right side. Each pass **selects** the smallest key on the unsorted side and swaps it to the front of that side.

Finding the smallest key is a scan. Keep the **index** of the smallest key seen so far in `min`, and update it whenever you find something smaller. Only after the scan is done do you swap, once:

```
min = i
for j = i+1 to size-1
    if A[j] < A[min]
        min = j
swap(A[i], A[min])
```

Here's pass i = 0 on the lecture's example. Blue marks the current `min`:

![selection sort finding the minimum in pass 0](courses/diagrams/8fd8baea-a21f-5c88-97c0-a19e851df76d/scan.svg)

The 0 is now in its final spot, and nothing else moved except the 6 it traded places with.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `selectionPass(A, i)`: find the index of the smallest key in `A[i..size-1]` and swap it into `A[i]`. Use `<`, so the first of several equal minimums wins.

Swap only once, after the scan. Swapping every time you see a smaller key also puts the minimum in front, but it scrambles the rest of the array, and the tests check the whole array after each pass.

lessons.title: Selection Sort
lessons.readme:
# Selection Sort

Run the pass for i = 0, 1, 2, … and the sorted side grows by one key each time:

```
for i = 0 to size-2
    min = i
    for j = i+1 to size-1
        if A[j] < A[min]
            min = j
    swap(A[i], A[min])
```

Here's the whole run on the lecture's example, one row per pass. The green part on the left is finished:

![selection sort after each pass](courses/diagrams/b4f512f3-dc89-54ca-9ff9-5cf793e7f192/table.svg)

At i = 3 the smallest unsorted key is already in place, so it swaps with itself. The pseudocode still calls swap, which is why selection sort does exactly one swap per pass, no matter what.

This gives selection sort its loop invariant, the mirror image of bubble sort's:

> After outer iteration i (from i = 0), the first i + 1 keys are the i + 1 **smallest**, in sorted order, in their **final** positions.

Like bubble sort, it stops at `size-2`: once everything else is in place, the last key has to be the largest.

## Assignment

`selectionPass` is done.

1. [ ] Complete `selectionSort(A)`: call `selectionPass(A, i)` for `i` from `0` to `size-2`.

lessons.title: Selection Sort Big O
lessons.readme:
# Selection Sort Big O

**Comparisons.** Pass i scans the rest of the array no matter what, so it's (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 = **n(n − 1)/2**, O(n²), on every input. Even sorted input doesn't help: the scan can't know the minimum is already in front until it has looked at everything.

**Swaps.** Exactly one per pass, n − 1 in total: **O(n)** on every input.

| Input | Comparisons | Swaps |
|---|---|---|
| Already sorted | O(n²) | O(n) |
| Random | O(n²) | O(n) |
| Reverse sorted | O(n²) | O(n) |

**In place?** Yes. Like bubble sort, only one temporary variable for the swap: O(1) extra space.

**Selection vs. bubble.** Both always make n(n − 1)/2 comparisons. The difference is the swaps:

- **Best case is worse**: on sorted input bubble sort swaps nothing, while selection sort still calls swap n − 1 times.
- **Average and worst case are better**: O(n) swaps instead of O(n²).
- And selection sort is **not stable**. That's the next lesson.

**Can it start early?** Selection sort can't place even its first key until it has scanned **all** of the input: the smallest key might be the last one to arrive. Insertion sort can: each new key is slid into the sorted part as it shows up, like being dealt cards. So when data arrives a piece at a time, insertion sort can be sorting all along, and selection sort has to wait.

questions.question: A large array doubles in size. What happens to selection sort's comparisons and swaps?
Selection sort on 10 keys in reverse order. How many key comparisons and calls to swap?
Scores arrive one at a time, and you want the list kept sorted as they come in. Which sort can do that?

lessons.title: Selection Sort Stability
lessons.readme:
# Selection Sort Stability

Bubble sort only swaps neighbors, so equal keys never cross. Selection sort's swap is **long distance**: it can trade the front key with one at the far end, jumping over everything in between, including an equal key.

The professor's example, with tick marks to tell the two 2s apart:

![selection sort swapping a key past an equal key](courses/diagrams/b8f40d32-c594-5432-a73b-b8df9ee09996/unstable.svg)

The result `1 2" 2'` is sorted, but the two 2s came out in the wrong order. One counterexample is enough: selection sort is **not stable**.

Notice it isn't the comparison's fault. Using `<` so the first equal minimum wins doesn't help, because the damage is done to the key that gets swapped **away** from the front.

> [!tip]
> When a question asks you to trace selection sort with labeled equal keys, track where the key at `A[i]` goes on each swap. That's the one that can jump.

questions.question: Selection sort on `5a 8 5b 1 7` (5a and 5b are equal keys). After **two** passes?
Selection sort (with `<`) on `4a 4b 2`. The final order:

lessons.title: Inserting One Key
lessons.readme:
# Inserting One Key

Selection sort compares O(n²) times even on a leaderboard that's already in order. Can we do better when the data is nearly sorted?

**Insertion sort** is how you sort a hand of cards. The left part is sorted; each pass takes the next key and **inserts** it where it belongs among the keys to its left.

![a fanned-out hand of playing cards, not yet in order](courses/diagrams/3aff566f-934b-5d8d-b940-2289e4fb61d5/hand-of-cards.jpg)
*Image: Jiahui Huang, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.*

Pick up the cards one at a time. Each new card slides left past the bigger cards already in your hand until it reaches its spot, and the cards to its left are always in order.

The professor's version doesn't swap. It saves the new key in `temp`, shifts every bigger key one spot right to open a hole, and drops `temp` into the hole:

```
temp = A[i]
j = i-1
if temp < A[j]
    while j >= 0 and temp < A[j]
        A[j+1] = A[j]
        j--
    A[j+1] = temp
```

Here's pass i = 2 on the lecture's example, where `temp = 3`:

![insertion sort shifting keys to make a hole for 3](courses/diagrams/3aff566f-934b-5d8d-b940-2289e4fb61d5/hole.svg)

Each step is one copy into the hole, and `temp` is written once at the end.

Two details matter. The `j >= 0` test comes **first**, so when `temp` belongs at the very front we stop before reading `A[-1]`. And the `if` guard means a key that's already in place costs one comparison and **no writes** at all.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `insertionPass(A, i)`: insert `A[i]` into the sorted keys `A[0..i-1]` using `temp`, the shifting and the hole, exactly as above. You can assume `i >= 1`.

lessons.title: Insertion Sort
lessons.readme:
# Insertion Sort

Run the pass for every i from 1 to size − 1 (a single key at index 0 is already a sorted hand):

```
for i = 1 to size-1
    temp = A[i]
    j = i-1
    if temp < A[j]
        while j >= 0 and temp < A[j]
            A[j+1] = A[j]
            j--
        A[j+1] = temp
```

The whole run on the lecture's example:

| i | temp | what happens | array after |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 7 | no shift | `6 7 3 2 9 8 0 1` |
| 2 | 3 | shift 7, 6 | `3 6 7 2 9 8 0 1` |
| 3 | 2 | shift 7, 6, 3 | `2 3 6 7 9 8 0 1` |
| 4 | 9 | no shift | `2 3 6 7 9 8 0 1` |
| 5 | 8 | shift 9 | `2 3 6 7 8 9 0 1` |
| 6 | 0 | shift 9, 8, 7, 6, 3, 2 | `0 2 3 6 7 8 9 1` |
| 7 | 1 | shift 9, 8, 7, 6, 3, 2 | `0 1 2 3 6 7 8 9` |

Look at the left part after each row: it's always sorted. That's insertion sort's loop invariant:

> After outer iteration i (insertion starts at i = 1), the first i + 1 keys are sorted **among themselves**.

But they are **not final**. The 0 at i = 6 slides all the way to the front, pushing every key in the sorted part one spot right. Compare that with selection sort, where the left part is both sorted and finished.

Now picture the arcade's leaderboard after one new score comes in. It's already sorted except for one key. Every pass but one stops after a single comparison. That's where insertion sort shines.

## Assignment

`insertionPass` is done.

1. [ ] Complete `insertionSort(A)`: call `insertionPass(A, i)` for `i` from `1` to `size-1`.

On an already sorted leaderboard each pass stops after one comparison, so the tests sort 200,000 sorted scores and expect it to be quick.

lessons.title: Insertion Sort Big O
lessons.readme:
# Insertion Sort Big O

**Best case: already sorted.** Each pass makes one comparison (`temp < A[j]` is false) and moves on. That's **n − 1 comparisons** in total, O(n), and the `if` guard means **no writes into A at all**.

**Worst case: reverse sorted.** Every new key has to travel all the way to the front. Pass i shifts i keys, so it's about n(n − 1)/2 comparisons and shifts: **O(n²)**.

Counting exactly with the professor's guarded code: on `5 4 3 2 1`, pass i does 1 comparison for the `if` plus i for the while loop (the loop ends on `j >= 0`, not on a comparison). That's 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = **14** comparisons. Without the `if` it would be 10, which is why the exam cares which version you trace.

- **In place?** Yes, only `temp`.
- **Stable?** Yes. It stops shifting at the first key that isn't **strictly** bigger (`temp < A[j]`), so a key never jumps over an equal one. Using `<=` there would break that.

Excellent best case, more data movement than selection in the worst case, and stable.

> [!warning]
> Read the loop before quoting a best case. The analysis lectures also show a swap-based "insertion sort" whose inner loop always runs from the start up to i with no early exit. That one is Θ(n²) even on sorted input.

lessons.title: Simple Sorts Compared
lessons.readme:
# Simple Sorts Compared

You now have three O(n²) sorts. They look alike on a Big O sheet, but they behave differently, and the exam likes to ask exactly where.

| | Comparisons | Swaps: sorted / random / reverse |
|---|---|---|
| Bubble (lecture version) | always n(n − 1)/2 = O(n²) | 0 / n(n − 1)/4 / n(n − 1)/2 |
| Selection | always n(n − 1)/2 = O(n²) | O(n) every time, one per pass |
| Insertion | O(n) sorted, O(n²) reverse | shifts: 0 / O(n²) / O(n²) |

The loop invariants, after outer iteration i (bubble and selection start at i = 0, insertion at i = 1):

| Sort | What's guaranteed |
|---|---|
| Bubble | the **last** i + 1 keys are the largest, sorted, **final** |
| Selection | the **first** i + 1 keys are the smallest, sorted, **final** |
| Insertion | the **first** i + 1 keys are sorted among themselves, **not** final |

All three are in place with O(1) extra space. Bubble and insertion are stable; selection is not.

How to pick between them:

- Data is **nearly sorted**? Insertion sort, the only one with an O(n) best case.
- **Swaps are expensive** (big records)? Selection sort, which never does more than n − 1.
- Bubble sort is the easiest to remember, and that's about it.

questions.question: 1,000 scores, **already sorted**. Which simple sort makes the fewest key comparisons?
1,000 scores in **reverse** order. Which simple sort moves keys around the least?
answers: They all move keys about equally

questions.question: "The first i + 1 keys are sorted among themselves, but a smaller key may still be placed in front of them." Which sort?

lessons.title: Merging Sorted Arrays
lessons.readme:
# Merging Sorted Arrays

O(n²) is fine for a few hundred scores. On a whole semester of games it isn't. To do better we need a new idea, and it starts small.

The arcade has two cabinets, and each one keeps its own leaderboard already sorted. To build one combined board, we don't need to sort from scratch. We can **merge**:

1. Look at the front of each list.
2. Take the smaller one and append it to the output.
3. When one list runs out, copy the rest of the other. That costs **no** comparisons.

```
merge(A, B):
    S = empty
    while A and B are not empty
        if A.first() <= B.first()
            S.insertLast(A.removeFirst())
        else
            S.insertLast(B.removeFirst())
    copy the rest of A, then the rest of B, into S
```

Here's `merge([2, 5, 8], [3, 6, 9, 13])`. Blue is each list's front, red is already used, amber is what was just taken:

![merge steps 1 and 2](courses/diagrams/6355c68e-d711-5b6e-87a6-f6a013a94020/m1.svg)

![merge steps 3 and 4](courses/diagrams/6355c68e-d711-5b6e-87a6-f6a013a94020/m2.svg)

![merge step 5 and the leftovers](courses/diagrams/6355c68e-d711-5b6e-87a6-f6a013a94020/m3.svg)

Five comparisons, then 9 and 13 are copied over for free.

**On paper** (Quiz 7), merge works on plain arrays with three indexes: `i` into A, `j` into B, `k` into the output S. The skeleton is given and you fill in the two branches:

```cpp
while (i < lenA && j < lenB) {
    if (A[i] <= B[j]) {
        S[k] = A[i];   // copy A's front into S
        i++;           // and move past it in A
    }
    else {
        S[k] = B[j];
        j++;
    }
    k++;               // already in the skeleton, after the if/else
}
while (i < lenA) S[k++] = A[i++];
while (j < lenB) S[k++] = B[j++];
```

> [!warning]
> - Write into **S**. Nothing gets swapped or written back into A or B; there's no `temp`.
> - Each branch advances only the index it read from: `i++` with A, `j++` with B. Forgetting it copies the same key forever.
> - Don't add your own `k++` inside a branch when the skeleton already has one after the if/else, or every other slot of S is skipped.

Why `<=` and not `<`? On a tie it takes from A first, and A's keys came first originally. That's what will make merge sort **stable**.

You've seen this before: it's the linked list merge from the Linked Lists chapter, but on vectors.

## Assignment

1. [ ] `merge(a, b)`: both are sorted ascending. Return a new sorted vector with every key from both. Use `<=` so ties take from `a` first.

lessons.title: Counting Merge Comparisons
lessons.readme:
# Counting Merge Comparisons

Every comparison in merge sends one key to the output. The leftovers at the end go over without any comparisons. So the number of comparisons depends on **when one list runs out**.

Say the two lists hold n keys in total, n/2 each.

**Fewest: n/2.** Every key in one list is smaller than every key in the other, like `1 2 3 4` and `5 6 7 8`. Each comparison takes from the first list; after 4 comparisons it's empty, and `5 6 7 8` is copied over for free.

**Most: n − 1.** The lists interleave all the way to the end, like `1 3 5 7` and `2 4 6 8`. Every key but the very last one needs a comparison to leave.

| A | B | Comparisons |
|---|---|---|
| `1 2 3 4` | `5 6 7 8` | 4 (= n/2) |
| `1 3 5 7` | `2 4 6 8` | 7 (= n − 1) |
| `2 5 8` | `3 6 9 13` | 5 |

Either way, merge is **O(n)**: it touches each key once. That one fact is what merge sort's whole analysis is built on.

To count on paper, walk the merge and make a tally mark every time you compare two fronts. Stop tallying the moment either list is empty.

lessons.title: Merge Sort
lessons.readme:
# Merge Sort

Merging is fast, but it needs two sorted lists. Where do they come from? From merge sort itself. That's the classic **divide and conquer** approach:

- **Divide:** split S into two halves S1 and S2, about n/2 keys each.
- **Recur:** merge sort S1 and S2.
- **Conquer:** merge the two sorted halves.

```
mergeSort(S):
    if S.size() > 1
        (S1, S2) = partition(S, S.size()/2)
        S1 = mergeSort(S1)
        S2 = mergeSort(S2)
        S = merge(S1, S2)
    return S
```

(The lecture's `partition` here just means "split in half". It has nothing to do with quicksort's partition later.)

The base case is a list of 0 or 1 keys, which is already sorted. The lecture shows it with playing cards: K 10 J 2 5 7 Q 4. Here they are as numbers (J = 11, Q = 12, K = 13). The top half of the picture splits, the bottom half merges back up:

![merge sort splitting into single keys and merging back](courses/diagrams/e2795fa2-a450-5045-b50a-215f8d561b5a/tree.svg)

Notice that all the real sorting happens in merge. Splitting just cuts the list without looking at any keys.

## Assignment

`merge` is done.

1. [ ] `mergeSort(S)`: return a sorted copy of `S`. If it has 0 or 1 keys, return it as is. Otherwise copy the first `size/2` keys into `S1` and the rest into `S2`, sort each recursively, and return `merge` of the two.

A vector can be built from part of another: `vector<int> S1(S.begin(), S.begin() + half);`

lessons.readme:
# Merge Sort by Hand

On paper, merge sort is a tree. Draw it in two halves, just like the picture in the last lesson:

1. **Split down.** Cut each list in half (the left half gets `size/2` keys) until every piece has one key. No comparisons happen here.
2. **Merge up.** Merge neighboring pieces back together, level by level, until one sorted list is left.

A shortcut for questions about the last step: right before the final merge, the two halves are simply the **left half sorted** and the **right half sorted**. You don't have to trace the whole tree to know what they are.

For `6 7 3 2 9 8 0 1`:

| Level | Pieces |
|---|---|
| split | `6 7 3 2` · `9 8 0 1` |
| split | `6 7` · `3 2` · `9 8` · `0 1` |
| merge pairs | `6 7` · `2 3` · `8 9` · `0 1` |
| merge 4s | `2 3 6 7` · `0 1 8 9` |
| merge 8 | `0 1 2 3 6 7 8 9` |

Count comparisons in the final merge with the tally method from Counting Merge Comparisons: `2 3 6 7` with `0 1 8 9` takes 0, 1, then 2, 3, 6, 7 one comparison each, and 8 9 are leftovers. That's 6.

lessons.title: Merge Sort Big O
lessons.readme:
# Merge Sort Big O

Let T(n) be the time to merge sort n keys, and c a constant. A list of 1 key costs T(1) = c. Otherwise we sort two halves and merge, and merging costs about cn:

```
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn
     = 2[2T(n/4) + cn/2] + cn  = 4T(n/4) + 2cn
     = 4[2T(n/8) + cn/4] + 2cn = 8T(n/8) + 3cn
     ...
     = 2ᵏ T(n/2ᵏ) + kcn             after k steps
```

Stop when the pieces have one key: n/2ᵏ = 1, so k = log₂ n. Plug that in:

T(n) = n · T(1) + cn log₂ n = cn + cn log₂ n = **O(n log n)**

Picture it as the tree from Merge Sort: log₂ n levels, and every level merges all n keys once.

Merge sort always splits in half and always merges everything, so it's **O(n log n)** in the best, average **and** worst case. No input is bad for it. A nearly sorted array doesn't get **fewer splits** either: splitting is by position, not by value, so the tree has the same log₂ n levels whatever the keys are. And for n a power of 2, doubling n to 2n adds exactly **one** more level.

But on arrays it moves a lot of data. Every key is copied at every level, about n log n copies whatever the input, which gives it bigger constants and worse cache behavior than quicksort.

- **In place?** No. On arrays it needs **O(n)** extra space to hold the merged results.
- **Stable?** Yes, thanks to `<=` in merge.

Good (not best) best case, excellent worst case, stable, needs extra memory.

O(n) sorted, O(n log n) reversed

answers: The number of levels of recursion
The cost of the two recursive calls
The cost of merging the two halves

lessons.title: Partitioning Around a Pivot
lessons.readme:
# Partitioning Around a Pivot

Merge sort is O(n log n) every time, but on arrays it needs O(n) extra memory and copies every key at every level. Could we split the work so nothing needs merging afterward?

That's **quicksort**, the other divide and conquer sort. Merge sort does its real work **after** the recursive calls, in merge. Quicksort does its real work **before** them, right inside the array. Put another way: merge sort has an easy divide (cut in half by position) and a hard combine (merge); quicksort has a hard divide (partition) and an easy combine (nothing to do). The lecture describes it like this:

- **Divide:** pick a key p, called the **pivot**, and partition S into
  - **L**: keys less than p
  - **E**: keys equal to p
  - **G**: keys greater than p
- **Recur:** sort L and G.
- **Conquer:** join L, E and G.

Once the array is arranged as L, then the pivot, then G, the pivot is in its **final** sorted position. Everything smaller is to its left, everything bigger to its right. Nobody ever has to move it again.

Here's the lecture's array, partitioned around its last key, 6:

![an array before and after partitioning around 6](courses/diagrams/cd2d5906-c2c7-5abb-9bdd-86d96c7e52c0/leg.svg)

Neither L nor G is sorted yet. That's fine: recursion will handle them. And "join" costs nothing, because L, the pivot and G are already side by side in the array.

The professor's partition puts keys **equal** to the pivot in L along with the smaller ones. We'll write it next.

questions.question: A partition of 8 keys puts the pivot 50 at index 3. Which of these **must** be true?
answers: 50 is the median of the 8 keys

questions.question: Where does each sort do its main work?
answers: Merge sort after its recursive calls, quicksort before them
Merge sort before its recursive calls, quicksort after them
questions.answer: Merge sort after its recursive calls, quicksort before them

lessons.title: Lomuto Partition
lessons.readme:
# Lomuto Partition

There are many ways to partition. The class uses the **Lomuto** scheme: the pivot is the **last** key, and one scan from `lo` to `hi - 1` builds `[keys ≤ pivot] [pivot] [keys > pivot]`.

The index `i` marks where the next key ≤ pivot will go. Everything before `i` is already known to be ≤ pivot. When `j` finds another small key, swap it to `i` and move `i` up:

```
Partition(S, lo, hi)
    pivot = S[hi]
    i = lo
    for j = lo to hi-1
        if S[j] <= pivot
            swap S[i] with S[j]
            i++
    swap S[i] with S[hi]
    return i
```

Here's the lecture's trace on `7 3 8 0 9 2 1 6`:

![Lomuto partition traced step by step](courses/diagrams/c3b154bb-e743-5f7d-9c7a-33d2703a968a/trace.svg)

When the loop ends, `S[lo..i-1]` is L, and `S[i..hi-1]` is G. The last swap trades the pivot with the first key of G, which drops the pivot right between them.

It scans the array once, so partition is **O(n)**: exactly hi − lo comparisons.

## Assignment

1. [ ] `partition(S, lo, hi)`: Lomuto, exactly as above, pivot = `S[hi]`. Return the pivot's final index. Only touch `S[lo..hi]`.

The tests check the whole array afterward, so follow the steps exactly; another partition scheme would leave the keys in a different order.

# Partition by Hand

Partition traces are an exam favorite. Keep a little table: the array, `i`, `j`, and what happened. A few things to check yourself against:

- `i` only moves when a key ≤ pivot is found, so `i` always equals lo plus the number of keys ≤ pivot seen so far.
- A swap where `i == j` swaps a key with itself. It still counts as a step, but nothing moves.
- The final swap puts the pivot at index `i`, and that's the return value.
- The return value is lo plus the number of keys (other than the pivot itself) that are ≤ the pivot. You can use that to double-check your answer before you trace.

Try these on paper first, then check.

lessons.title: Quicksort
lessons.readme:
# Quicksort

With partition done, quicksort is three lines. After partition the pivot is final, so sort what's left of it and what's right of it:

```
QuickSort(S, lo, hi)
    if lo >= hi
        return
    p = Partition(S, lo, hi)
    QuickSort(S, lo, p - 1)      // L
    QuickSort(S, p + 1, hi)      // G
```

Start it with `lo = 0` and `hi = n - 1`. A range with 0 or 1 keys is already sorted, which is the `lo >= hi` base case.

Divide is partition, recur sorts L and G, and there's nothing left to conquer: the keys were swapped in place and the pivots are already where they belong.

Here's the whole run on `7 3 8 0 9 2 1 6`. Each row is one level of recursion, shown after its partitions. Green keys are final, and ∅ is an empty range:

![quicksort recursion on 7 3 8 0 9 2 1 6](courses/diagrams/eda1499e-9cd4-577e-9528-4f083c570e80/tree.svg)

Notice the recursive calls skip the pivot: `p - 1` and `p + 1`, not `p`. Including it would hand the same range back to quicksort when the pivot is the largest key, and the recursion would never end.

## Assignment

The leaderboard is a `vector<int>`, and `partition` is done.

1. [ ] `quickSort(S, lo, hi)`: sort `S[lo..hi]` in place, as above. Keys outside that range must not change.

lessons.title: Quicksort Big O
lessons.readme:
# Quicksort Big O

Let T(n) be quicksort's time on n keys, and P(n) the time for partition, which is O(n). If L ends up with k keys, G has the other n − k − 1 (the pivot is in neither):

**T(n) = T(k) + T(n − k − 1) + P(n)**

So everything depends on k, which depends on how good the pivot was.

**Perfect split.** The pivot lands in the middle every time: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + P(n). That's merge sort's recurrence, so **O(n log n)**. Here's an input where last-key pivots happen to split perfectly every time:

![quicksort splitting perfectly: a tree about log n deep](courses/diagrams/135c6d8e-c494-55cf-b17d-3dede3f27818/balanced.svg)

The recursion is a tree about log₂ n levels deep, and each level partitions about n keys in total.

**Typical split.** Splits don't need to be perfect. Even lopsided ones like 25/75 still give a tree O(log n) deep, so the **average case** is **O(n log n)** too. Quicksort also walks memory in order, which is cache-friendly, so in practice it's usually faster than merge sort.

**Space.** Swaps are O(1), so the lecture calls quicksort **in place**. But each level of recursion waits on the call stack, so it uses **O(log n)** stack space on good splits.

**Stable?** No. Partition swaps keys long distances across the array.

What about a bad split? That's the next lesson.

answers: The number of swaps partition made
The index of the last key
The number of keys that went into L
questions.answer: The number of keys that went into L

lessons.title: Quicksort Worst Case
lessons.readme:
# Quicksort Worst Case

Now try **already sorted** input with the last key as pivot. The pivot is always the **largest** key, everything goes into L, and G is empty. Instead of a tree we get a **chain** that's O(n) deep:

![quicksort on sorted input makes a chain](courses/diagrams/750f48ce-8151-52fe-ad47-e9ef69e427a8/chain.svg)

The recurrence becomes T(n) = T(n − 1) + P(n). Partition at depth k does n − k comparisons (it never compares the pivot with itself):

(n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 = **n(n − 1)/2** comparisons = **O(n²)**

With the last key as pivot, these all hit the worst case:

- **Sorted:** the pivot is always the largest; all of it goes to L.
- **Reverse sorted:** the first pivot is the smallest, so L is empty and the final swap sends the old first key (the largest) to the end. The next pivot is the largest, and so on: still a chain.
- **All keys equal:** a special case of sorted. Every key is ≤ the pivot, so all go to L.

A chain also means the recursion stack is **O(n)** deep, not O(log n).

The cruel part: a leaderboard that's already mostly sorted, a very common real input, is exactly what breaks it.

lessons.title: Random Pivots
lessons.readme:
# Random Pivots

The arcade's leaderboard is almost always nearly sorted, the exact input that wrecks last-key quicksort. The lecture calls quicksort "usually randomized" for this reason. The fix is to stop picking a predictable pivot.

**Pick the pivot at random** from `[lo, hi]`, swap it into `S[hi]`, then run the same Lomuto partition.

A random key is rarely near the minimum or maximum, so splits are usually reasonably balanced, around 25/75 or better. Here's the same sorted input as before, with random pivots:

![quicksort with random pivots on sorted input makes a tree](courses/diagrams/692dafe8-8e4e-5995-8ee2-524a0756e3d4/tree.svg)

A tree again, not a chain. That means:

- the recursion is expected to be O(log n) deep
- every level does O(n) comparisons
- so **O(n log n) expected on every input order**

No input is bad any more, only unlucky pivot choices, and getting unlucky over and over is extremely unlikely.

What about **median-of-three** (take the middle value of the first, middle and last keys)? It makes a bad pivot less likely, especially on sorted input, but some inputs can still drive it to O(n²). That's why `std::sort` also keeps a heapsort fallback, which we'll see soon.

> [!note]
> The lecture's claim is about the **order** of the input. Lomuto puts every key equal to the pivot into L, so an array of all equal keys is still a chain no matter which one you pick. A three-way partition that keeps a separate E group (like the L/E/G description) fixes that.

## Assignment

1. [ ] `randomPartition(S, lo, hi)`: choose a random index `r` in `[lo, hi]` (for example `lo + std::rand() % (hi - lo + 1)`), swap `S[r]` with `S[hi]`, and return `partition(S, lo, hi)`.
2. [ ] `randomQuickSort(S, lo, hi)`: quicksort that uses `randomPartition`.

The tests sort 200,000 already sorted scores and expect it to finish quickly.

lessons.title: Sorting Algorithms Compared
lessons.readme:
# Sorting Algorithms Compared

Put this table on your notes sheet.

| Sort | Best | Average | Worst | Extra space | Stable |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bubble | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | ✔ |
| Selection | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | ✘ |
| Insertion | **O(n)** | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | ✔ |
| Merge | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | **O(n)** | ✔ |
| Quick | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | **O(n²)** | O(1) + O(log n) stack | ✘ |
| Heap | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(log n) stack | ✘ |

- **In place** means rearranging inside the array with O(1) extra space for swaps. Bubble, selection, insertion and quick are in place; merge sort on arrays is not.
- **In-core vs. out-of-core**: the data fits in RAM, or it doesn't (sort chunks from disk, then merge).
- Space complexity still **counts the recursion stack**, so quicksort is O(log n) space even though the lecture calls it in place.

> [!warning]
> Heapsort (coming up in the Heaps chapter) only moves keys inside the array, and the Nov 12 slides said "in place: O(1)". On Nov 17 the professor crossed that out: the sift-down from class is recursive, so heapsort and buildHeap use **O(log n)** stack space. Only a loop version of sift-down makes them O(1).

lessons.title: Quicksort or Merge Sort?
lessons.readme:
# Quicksort or Merge Sort?

For big data you'll almost always pick one of the two O(n log n) sorts. The lecture's rule of thumb:

**Choose quicksort when:**

- you're sorting **arrays in memory**. It's in place and cache-friendly, so it's usually faster in practice;
- stability doesn't matter;
- expected O(n log n) is good enough. With random pivots, O(n²) is unlikely on any input.

**Choose merge sort when:**

- you need a **stable** sort;
- you need a **worst-case** O(n log n) guarantee;
- the data is a **linked list**. Merge only relinks nodes, so it needs no extra array, and quicksort's jumping around by index is slow on a list.

The C++ standard library gives you both, as you'll see next: `std::sort` is quicksort-based, and `std::stable_sort` is merge-based.

| Situation | Pick |
|---|---|
| a million ints in a vector, fastest wins | quicksort |
| records sorted by one field, ties keep their order | merge sort |
| a singly linked list | merge sort |
| a hard real-time system that can never hit O(n²) | merge sort (or heapsort, if memory is tight) |

lessons.title: Sorting with the STL
lessons.readme:
# Sorting with the STL

In real code you'd never hand-write a sort. `<algorithm>` has two:

```cpp
std::sort(v.begin(), v.end());          // fast, NOT stable
std::stable_sort(v.begin(), v.end());   // stable
```

`std::sort` uses **introsort** (introspective sort, which changes strategy depending on how it's doing):

- **Quicksort** does most of the work, with a **median-of-three** pivot: the middle value of the first, middle and last keys. On random data that makes a bad pivot less likely.
- **Heapsort** takes over if the recursion gets too deep, so the O(n²) case can't happen.
- **Insertion sort** finishes small partitions (under 16 keys), where it beats quicksort.

So `std::sort` guarantees **O(n log n) comparisons in the worst case** (since C++11), works in place, and is **not stable**. `std::stable_sort` is based on **merge sort**.

Both sort ascending using `<`. To sort another way, pass a comparison as a third argument: a function (often a lambda) that returns true when its first argument should come **first**:

```cpp
std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b) { return a > b; });   // descending
```

The comparison must be **strict**: use `>` or `<`, never `>=` or `<=`. With `>=`, a key "comes before" an equal key and also after it, which breaks the sort's assumptions.

## Assignment

Time to post the leaderboard. Each `Entry` has a player tag and a score, and the vector starts in the order the games finished.

1. [ ] `rankBoard(board)`: sort it by score, **highest first**. Players who tied must stay in the order they finished in, so use `std::stable_sort` with a strict comparison.

# Simple Sorts Review

The exam asks you to trace these sorts by hand, so practice that here. Work each one on paper, one comparison at a time, and write the array after every pass.

Quick reference:

- **Bubble:** pass i compares neighbors `A[j]`, `A[j+1]` for j = 0 to n − 2 − i, swapping if left > right. After pass i the last i + 1 are final.
- **Selection:** pass i swaps the smallest key in `A[i..n-1]` into `A[i]`. After pass i the first i + 1 are final. One swap per pass.
- **Insertion:** pass i (from 1) saves `A[i]` in temp, shifts bigger keys right, drops temp in the hole. The first i + 1 are sorted among themselves.

Before you pick an answer, check it against the invariant. After two selection passes, the first two keys must be the two smallest. After one bubble pass, the last key must be the largest.

lessons.title: Merge and Quicksort Review
lessons.readme:
# Merge and Quicksort Review

Last round: the two divide and conquer sorts, traced by hand.

- **Merge:** compare the fronts, take the smaller (ties from the left list). Leftovers cost no comparisons.
- **Merge sort:** split until single keys, then merge back up. Right before the final merge, the halves are the left half sorted and the right half sorted.
- **Lomuto partition:** pivot = last key. `i` is where the next key ≤ pivot goes. The final swap puts the pivot at `i`, which is returned.
- **Quicksort:** partition, then recurse on `lo..p-1` and `p+1..hi`. The pivot is never part of either call.

For partition questions, count first: the return value is lo plus the number of other keys ≤ the pivot. Then trace to get the array.

questions.question: How many key comparisons does it take to merge `1 4 6` with `2 3 8 9`?

lessons.title: Binary Trees
lessons.readme:
# Binary Trees

A group of students is building **Spartan Maps**, a campus map for SJSU. The first feature is the search box: type a few letters, and it suggests matching buildings. With hundreds of names and abbreviations, scanning a list on every keystroke is O(n). Over this chapter we'll build a structure that finds things by walking **one path** instead: a binary search tree. First, plain binary trees.

A **binary tree** is either **empty**, or it has a special node called the **root**, plus a **left subtree** and a **right subtree**, which are binary trees themselves. That definition is recursive, and so is almost every function we'll write.

![a binary tree with its root and leaves marked](courses/diagrams/21abf81f-05da-5781-8607-921a61666258/parts.svg)

The root is drawn at the top, a left child to the left, a right child to the right. A node at the bottom with **no children** is a **leaf**. In C++ each node holds its data and two pointers:

```cpp
template <typename T>
struct BinaryTreeNode {
    T info;
    BinaryTreeNode<T>* left;     // nullptr if no left child
    BinaryTreeNode<T>* right;    // nullptr if no right child
};
```

The tree itself is just a `BinaryTreeNode<T>* root`, the same way a linked list is just a `head` pointer. Lab 8's version adds a constructor, `BinaryTreeNode(const T& _info) : info(_info), left(nullptr), right(nullptr) {}`. Our exercises use a plain `int` version called `TreeNode`.

Binary trees show up everywhere: expression trees, yes/no decision trees, tournament brackets, BSTs, heaps, `std::map`, Huffman compression, and the trees built by Dijkstra's and Prim's algorithms.

A tournament bracket is a binary tree turned on its side. The final, at the far right, is the root. Every match is a node whose two children are the matches (or players) that fed into it, and the 16 starting players are the leaves:

![a 16-player single elimination tournament bracket](courses/diagrams/21abf81f-05da-5781-8607-921a61666258/bracket.png)
*Image: Matthewbeckler, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.*

questions.question: In a linked list, `head` points at the first node. What plays that role in a binary tree?
A node has a right child but no left child. What is stored in its `left`?
answers: A pointer to its right child

lessons.title: Tree Vocabulary
lessons.readme:
# Tree Vocabulary

The exam uses these words exactly, so let's pin them down on one tree.

![a tree with each level labeled at the left; leaves 4, 8, 7 and 9 in green](courses/diagrams/7c695de3-2353-5095-91a2-21c9b09f690c/levels.svg)

- The **level** (or **depth**) of a node is the number of branches (edges) from it up to the root. The root is level 0.
- The **height** of a tree is the largest depth of any node. This tree has height 3. A one-node tree has height 0, and in this class an **empty** tree has height **−1**.
- A **leaf** has no children: 4, 8, 7 and 9 here.
- An **internal** node has at least one child: 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6. Note that 5 has only one child, and it still isn't a leaf.
- A binary tree is **acyclic**: following child pointers never brings you back to a node.

Two shapes get special names:

- **Perfect**: every internal node has 2 children and all leaves are on the same level.
- **Complete**: every level is full except maybe the last, and the last level fills from the left with no gaps. Heaps (next chapter) use this one.

> [!tip]
> "Level" counts edges, not nodes. If you count nodes instead, every answer comes out one too big.

lessons.title: Perfect and Skewed Trees
lessons.readme:
# Perfect and Skewed Trees

How tall can a tree with n nodes be? It depends entirely on its shape, and that will decide how fast our search box is.

**The fullest shape: perfect.** Count the nodes level by level. Each level holds twice as many as the one above:

| Level | Nodes |
|---|---|
| 0 | 2⁰ = 1 |
| 1 | 2¹ = 2 |
| 2 | 2² = 4 |
| … | … |
| k | 2ᵏ |

Add them up: 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2ᵏ = **2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1**. So a perfect tree of height 3 has 15 nodes. Turned around, n nodes can be packed into a height of only ⌊log₂ n⌋. That's the **best** case.

**The thinnest shape: skewed.** If every node except the bottom one has only one child, the tree is a chain, also called **degenerate** or **skewed**. Each node is one level deeper, so the **worst-case height is n − 1**.

![a perfect tree next to a skewed chain](courses/diagrams/37010bd9-3120-5521-8085-b1110e7e0ea1/shapes.svg)

A skewed tree is really a linked list wearing a tree costume. Keep that picture in mind: it comes back when a BST gets built from sorted input.

lessons.title: Tree Traversals
lessons.readme:
# Tree Traversals

To print every building in the tree, we need to **visit** each node exactly once. Recursion gives three natural orders, and they differ only in **when** you visit the root compared to its two subtrees:

| Order | Steps |
|---|---|
| **Pre-order** | visit root, traverse left, traverse right |
| **In-order** | traverse left, visit root, traverse right |
| **Post-order** | traverse left, traverse right, visit root |

The left subtree always goes before the right one. Here are the visit numbers on our small tree:

![pre-order and in-order visit numbers](courses/diagrams/b0d45bda-aa29-5099-b50a-0e1377ea7eef/pre_in.svg)

![post-order visit numbers](courses/diagrams/b0d45bda-aa29-5099-b50a-0e1377ea7eef/post.svg)

A quick way to check yourself: pre-order always **starts** with the root, and post-order always **ends** with it.

**One walk, three orders.** All three traversals make the **same** trip: down the left side of every subtree before its right side, touching each node three times, as in the dashed path below. The only difference is which touch counts as the visit. Pre-order visits a node when the walk passes it on the **left**, in-order when it passes **underneath**, post-order when it passes on the **right**:

![a dashed path circling the tree counterclockwise from the root, with a dot on the left, bottom and right of each node](courses/diagrams/b0d45bda-aa29-5099-b50a-0e1377ea7eef/walk.svg)

Follow the amber dots along the path and you read 1 2 4 5 3 6; the blue dots give 4 2 5 1 3 6; the green dots give 4 5 2 6 3 1. That's a fast way to do traversals by hand on an exam.

There's also a fourth order, **level order**: level 0, then level 1, and so on, left to right (1 2 3 4 5 6 here). It isn't recursive. It uses a queue, just like breadth-first search in the Graphs chapter.

> [!warning]
> Trace one subtree **completely** before moving on. After visiting 2 in pre-order, you finish 2's whole subtree (4, 5) before going anywhere near 3.

```

    1   6    14
```

lessons.title: Traversals in Code
lessons.readme:
# Traversals in Code

The three traversals are each four lines of code. Here's the lecture's in-order, which prints instead of saving:

```cpp
template <typename T>
void inorder(BinaryTreeNode<T>* root) {
    if (root == nullptr) return;     // an empty subtree: nothing to visit
    inorder(root->left);
    cout << root->info << " ";
    inorder(root->right);
}
```

The `nullptr` check is the **base case**. Every leaf calls the function twice more on its two empty children, and those calls return right away.

To get pre-order or post-order, move the visit line: above both calls for pre-order, below both for post-order. That's the whole difference.

Lab 8's traversals don't print. They take a `vector<T>& arr` and add each value to the **end** of it, so the grader can check the order. We'll do the same. Pass the vector by reference so every recursive call adds to the same one.

## Assignment

Spartan Maps keeps its buildings in a tree of `TreeNode`s. Write the three traversals so the app can list them.

1. [ ] `preorder(t, out)`: root, left, right.
2. [ ] `inorder(t, out)`: left, root, right.
3. [ ] `postorder(t, out)`: left, right, root.

Each one appends `info` to the end of `out` as it visits a node, and does nothing for an empty tree.

lessons.title: Expression Trees
lessons.readme:
# Expression Trees

A binary tree can also hold **structure**, not just data. An arithmetic expression is a good example. Here is `2 * (3 + 4 - (5 - 6))`:

![the expression tree for 2 * (3 + 4 - (5 - 6))](courses/diagrams/e46120d2-7159-5bce-97c7-fddf834656fd/expr.svg)

- Each **operator** is an internal node, and its two operands are its children.
- Each **number** is a leaf.
- No parentheses are needed: the shape alone says what gets computed first. An operator happens after the operators below it.

Each traversal reads the same tree in a different notation:

| Traversal | Notation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-order | prefix | `* 2 - + 3 4 - 5 6` |
| In-order | infix | `2 * 3 + 4 - 5 - 6` |
| Post-order | postfix | `2 3 4 + 5 6 - - *` |

Look at the in-order line. It drops the parentheses, so it no longer means the same thing. That's why compilers and stack calculators like **postfix**: you can evaluate it left to right with a stack and never need a parenthesis. You did exactly that in the Stacks chapter.

> [!tip]
> To build the tree from an expression, find the operator that happens **last**. It becomes the root, and the two sides become its subtrees.

lessons.title: Counting Nodes and Leaves
lessons.readme:
# Counting Nodes and Leaves

Spartan Maps wants a stats line: how many buildings are in the tree, and how many sit at the bottom as leaves.

Almost every binary tree function has the same recipe:

1. **Base case:** handle the empty tree (`nullptr`).
2. **Recursive case:** ask the left and right subtrees the same question, then combine their answers with this node.

Here it is for a function we won't need, the sum of all keys:

```cpp
int sumTree(TreeNode* t) {
    if (t == nullptr) return 0;                       // empty: nothing to add
    return t->info + sumTree(t->left) + sumTree(t->right);
}
```

Counting nodes is the same shape, adding 1 per node instead of `info`.

Counting leaves needs one more case. A node is a leaf only when **both** children are `nullptr`. A node with one child is internal, so it isn't counted; its child might be.

![a tree with its leaves marked](courses/diagrams/bcd240ef-eaa4-502f-80c1-4f347dd40041/leaves.svg)

Lab 8's `BinaryTree` also has `isEmpty()`, which is just `root == nullptr`.

## Assignment

1. [ ] `countNodes(t)`: the number of nodes in the tree. An empty tree has 0.
2. [ ] `countLeaves(t)`: the number of nodes with no children. An empty tree has 0.

lessons.title: Tree Height
lessons.readme:
# Tree Height

Height will decide how fast every BST operation is, so let's compute it.

The recipe is the same as last lesson. The height of a tree is one more than the height of its **taller** subtree, because the deepest node lives down one of the two sides:

```
height(t) = 1 + max(height(left), height(right))
```

What about the base case? A single node has height 0, and its two subtrees are empty. For the formula to give 1 + max(?, ?) = 0, an empty tree must have height **−1**. That's why the lecture and Lab 8 define it that way.

![subtree heights](courses/diagrams/9562a2fc-cb78-5307-9a28-233a647fb510/heights.svg)

Notice that the deepest path here goes **right**. A function that only follows the left side, or that picks a side by which child exists, gets this tree wrong. Always ask both sides.

> [!warning]
> Don't return 0 for an empty tree. Then a single node would have height 1, and every answer would be one too big.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `height(t)`: the largest depth of any node. An empty tree is −1, and a single node is 0.

lessons.title: Deep Copy of a Tree
lessons.readme:
# Deep Copy of a Tree

The Spartan Maps team wants to try a change on a **copy** of the tree without touching the live one. What does copying a tree mean?

```cpp
BinaryTree<int> a;
BinaryTree<int> b = a;
```

A **shallow copy** just copies the value of `root`. Now both trees point at the **same** nodes. Change a key through `b` and `a` changes too. Worse, when both destructors run, each one deletes the same nodes, and the second delete is undefined behavior, usually a crash.

A **deep copy** walks the whole tree and makes a **new** node for every node, linked into the same shape. The two trees share no memory at all.

![shallow copy: a.root and b.root point at the same three nodes; deep copy: b.root points at its own three new nodes](courses/diagrams/fe60de6f-43b5-55e5-b408-073436f138f8/shallow_deep.svg)

The recursion is short. To copy a tree: make a new root with the same `info`, whose left child is a copy of the left subtree and whose right child is a copy of the right subtree. An empty tree copies to `nullptr`.

```
copy of (1, L, R)  =  new node 1, left = copy of L, right = copy of R
```

The lecture's ADT calls this `copy(const BinaryTree& other)`, and points out that it's **not** the copy constructor. In Lab 8 your copy constructor and assignment operator can call it. Remember that assignment must handle `a = a` safely: copying a tree onto itself must not destroy it first.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `copyTree(t)`: return a deep copy of `t`. Every node must be newly allocated, with the same keys in the same shape. A copy of an empty tree is `nullptr`.

lessons.title: Destroying a Tree
lessons.readme:
# Destroying a Tree

Every node came from `new`, so every node needs a `delete`, or the program leaks. Lab 8's destructor must "free every node in the tree."

The order matters. Once a node is deleted, you can't read its `left` and `right` pointers any more, because they're gone with it. So delete the **children first**, then the parent. That's a **post-order** traversal where "visit" means `delete`:

![the order nodes are deleted](courses/diagrams/e8e000ff-a0af-53f0-9c26-9076bfa89681/order.svg)

The root is deleted last, after everything below it is already gone.

Take the pointer **by reference** (`TreeNode*& t`) and set it to `nullptr` at the end. Then the caller's `root` doesn't dangle: it correctly says the tree is empty, and calling `destroy` a second time is harmless.

> [!warning]
> Deleting the parent **first** and then following `t->left` reads freed memory. It often seems to work on your laptop. Our grader runs AddressSanitizer, which catches it every time, and so does a careful exam grader.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `destroy(t)`: delete every node in post-order (both children before the parent), then set `t` to `nullptr`. Destroying an empty tree does nothing.

lessons.title: Binary Tree Big O
lessons.readme:
# Binary Tree Big O

Look back at everything we've written: traversals, `countNodes`, `countLeaves`, `height`, `copyTree`, `destroy`. Each one calls itself once on every node and does a constant amount of work there. So each is **O(n)**.

| Function | Time | Why |
|---|---|---|
| any traversal | O(n) | visits each node once |
| countNodes, countLeaves, height | O(n) | asks every node once |
| copyTree | O(n) | one `new` per node |
| destroy | O(n) | one `delete` per node |

**Searching** is the interesting one. The lecture's ADT has `search(x)`: is x anywhere in the tree? In a plain binary tree there's no rule about **where** a key goes. 42 could be in the left subtree, the right subtree, or anywhere. So a search must check **every** node: **O(n)**, even if the tree is perfectly shaped.

That's the problem with plain binary trees for Spartan Maps. The fix is to add an ordering rule, so a search can rule out a whole subtree at each step (about half of what's left, if the tree is balanced). That's a **binary search tree**, and it's next.

**Space.** The recursion keeps one call per level on the stack, so the extra space is O(h). That's O(log n) for a balanced tree, but O(n) for a skewed one.

answers: O(h) where h is the height

lessons.title: Binary Search Trees
lessons.readme:
# Binary Search Trees

Here's the rule that turns a binary tree into something you can search fast. In a **binary search tree (BST)**, the key in each node is:

- **larger** than every key in its left subtree, and
- **smaller** than every key in its right subtree.

Written recursively: a BST is empty, or a root with subtrees LT and RT, where **every key in LT < root's key < every key in RT**, and LT and RT are BSTs themselves.

![a BST next to a tree that breaks the rule](courses/diagrams/77551e4c-8794-5422-b075-2e68e786b588/rule.svg)

The rule is about the **whole subtree**, not just the children. In the right-hand tree, 55 is fine compared to its parent 30. But it's in 50's **left** subtree, and 55 > 50. So that tree is not a BST, even though every parent-child pair looks right.

Two things follow from the rule:

1. **In-order prints the keys sorted.** In-order visits the left subtree (all smaller), then the root, then the right subtree (all larger). For Spartan Maps, that's an alphabetical list of buildings for free.
2. **Search can skip a whole subtree at each step.** If the key you want is smaller than this node, it can't be on the right. We'll build that next.

> [!note]
> The lecture's rule uses strict < and >, so a BST holds no duplicate keys. Lab 8's insert simply ignores a key that's already there.

questions.question:
```
       60
      /  \
    35    80
   /  \   /
  20  45 58
```
Is this a BST?
answers: No: 58 is in 60's right subtree but 58 < 60
No: 80 needs two children to be valid
Yes: each child is in order with its parent
No: 45 must be the left child of 35
questions.answer: No: 58 is in 60's right subtree but 58 < 60

answers: In the order they were inserted

lessons.title: Is It a BST?
lessons.readme:
# Is It a BST?

Before trusting a tree, Spartan Maps wants to check that it really follows the BST rule.

The tempting check is "left child < node < right child" at every node. Last lesson showed why that isn't enough: 55 passed its parent's test but broke its grandparent's.

The fix is to carry the limits down. Every node has a **range** of keys it's allowed to hold, set by its ancestors:

- The root can be anything.
- Going **left** from a node with key k, everything must be **< k**, so k becomes the new upper limit.
- Going **right**, everything must be **> k**, so k becomes the new lower limit.

![allowed ranges carried down the tree](courses/diagrams/69d0d159-2e35-56dd-ab68-08ec9242656a/ranges.svg)

55 has to be between 30 and 50, and it isn't. Caught.

```cpp
bool between(TreeNode* t, long lo, long hi) {
    // true if t is a BST whose keys are all strictly between lo and hi
}
```

Start with the widest range, `LONG_MIN` to `LONG_MAX`. They are `long`s so they sit outside every `int` key.

> [!tip]
> Another correct way: do an in-order traversal and check that every key is bigger than the one before. Either way passes.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Make `isBST(t)` return true exactly when `t` follows the BST rule: every key is strictly greater than all keys in its left subtree and strictly less than all keys in its right subtree. An empty tree is a BST. A repeated key is not allowed.

You can finish the `between` helper, or replace it with your own approach.

lessons.title: BST Search
lessons.readme:
# BST Search

Now the payoff. To search a BST, start at the root and compare:

- key **==** this node's key: found it, return true.
- key **<** this node's key: it can only be in the **left** subtree, so go left.
- key **>** this node's key: it can only be on the **right**, so go right.
- you walked off the tree (`nullptr`): it isn't there, return false.

Here's `search(34)` on the lecture's tree. Blue nodes are compared; the green one is the match.

![search 34 walks 33, 49, 39, 34](courses/diagrams/08560a30-3ced-58bc-b2ea-247f081cfd65/search34.svg)

Four comparisons, and the 21, 10, 28, 65 and 80 nodes are never touched. Each step throws away a whole subtree.

The lecture writes it as a loop with a `cur` pointer:

```
search(key):
    cur = root
    while cur != nullptr
        if key == cur->info      return true
        else if key < cur->info  cur = cur->left
        else                     cur = cur->right
    return false
```

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `search(root, key)`: return true if `key` is in the BST. Follow **one path** down from the root, as above. The tests time a large tree, so a search that looks in both subtrees is too slow.

lessons.title: BST Search Big O
lessons.readme:
# BST Search Big O

Search follows a single path from the root down. It does one comparison per level, and the path can't be longer than the tree is tall. So search is **O(h)**, where h is the height.

What is h? That depends on the shape, which depends on the order the keys arrived in:

![a bushy BST next to a chain](courses/diagrams/3f01a399-9576-53f4-a25b-4f8c79045fe1/shapes.svg)

| Shape | Height | Search |
|---|---|---|
| balanced | about log₂ n | O(log n) |
| a chain | n − 1 | O(n) |

So the honest answer to "what is the **worst-case** search time in a BST with n nodes?" is **O(n)**. A BST is only O(log n) **if it stays balanced**. For a million buildings, that's the difference between about 20 steps and about a million.

Compare with a plain binary tree, which is O(n) no matter what shape it has. In a BST the shape is everything.

questions.question: A BST holds 1,000 keys and you know nothing about its shape. In the worst case, how many nodes does one search visit?

```
          40
         /  \
       20    60
      /  \     \
    10    30    70
         /
       25
```
How many nodes does `search(26)` compare against before it returns false?

lessons.title: BST Insert
lessons.readme:
# BST Insert

New buildings open, and Spartan Maps needs to add them. Where does a new key go?

Search for it. If it's not there, the search walks off the tree at exactly the spot where it **would** have been. Put it there. So **new nodes are always added as leaves**, and nothing else in the tree moves.

Here's `insert(50)` on the lecture's tree:

![insert 50 becomes the left child of 65](courses/diagrams/e22d1689-978f-50b1-9ed0-4f5d17b1a7ad/insert50.svg)

The lecture's insert is a loop, like search, with one special case for an empty tree:

```
insert(key):
    if root == nullptr:  root = new node(key); return
    cur = root
    while true
        if key < cur->info
            if cur->left == nullptr:  cur->left = new node(key); return
            cur = cur->left
        else if key > cur->info
            (the same on the right)
        else
            return            // duplicate key: do nothing
```

Since search is O(h) and adding the leaf is O(1), insert is **O(h)** too.

> [!note]
> Lab 8's BST is a template that must work for any `T` with only `<` and `==`. So don't write `key > cur->info`. Write `cur->info < key`, which means the same thing.

## Assignment

lessons.title: Insert Order and Tree Height
lessons.readme:
# Insert Order and Tree Height

The same keys can build very different trees. It all depends on the order they arrive in.

![sorted inserts make a chain; shuffled inserts make a bushy tree](courses/diagrams/f9d31fac-8b6c-56c0-a1dd-76d909d2b484/orders.svg)

**Sorted input.** Each new key is larger than everything already in the tree, so it always goes right. No node ever gets a left child. Height = n − 1 = 6, and search is O(n). Sorted input is common in real life: IDs, timestamps, a file that's already sorted. The Spartan Maps building list is close to alphabetical, which is why Lab 8 **shuffles** the names before inserting them.

**Shuffled input.** Early keys land near the middle and split the rest into two groups, so both sides fill in. Height = 3, close to log₂ 7 ≈ 2.8.

**On average.** If keys arrive in random order, an average search visits about 2 ln n ≈ **1.39 log₂ n** nodes, so search, insert and remove are O(log n) on average. That counts the **nodes an average search visits**, not the height. For n = 1,000,000:

| Insert order | Average search visits about |
|---|---|
| perfectly balanced | 20 nodes (log₂ n) |
| random | 26 nodes (≈ 1.39 log₂ n) |
| sorted | 500,000 nodes (n/2) |

Random order costs only about 30% more than perfect balance. Sorted order is a disaster.

lessons.title: BST Remove: Leaf
lessons.readme:
# BST Remove: Leaf

A building closes, and its name has to come out of the tree. Removing is the hardest BST operation, because the tree must still follow the BST rule afterward. The lecture splits it into **three cases**, by how many children the doomed node has. Start with the easy one.

**Case 1: the node is a leaf.** Nothing hangs below it, so just cut it off: set the **parent's** pointer to it to `nullptr`, then free the node.

Here's the lecture's `delete(34)`. 34 is the left child of 39:

![removing leaf 34](courses/diagrams/fad31dc7-a3d7-5811-bda5-aa6b63c30935/del34.svg)

So the answer is `39->left = nullptr; free 34`. The details count on the exam:

- It's the parent's **left** pointer because 34 was a **left** child. Setting the wrong side would cut off 45's whole subtree.
- Just freeing 34 without touching 39 leaves 39 pointing at freed memory: a dangling pointer.
- You can't copy anything into 34's spot. There's nothing to copy.

To change the parent's pointer you have to **know** the parent. A loop has to remember it as it walks down. Two lessons from now we'll use a trick that avoids tracking it.

questions.question:
```
        60
       /  \
     40    80
    /  \     \
  30    50    90
```
50 is a leaf. What should `remove(50)` do?

lessons.title: BST Remove: One Child
lessons.readme:
# BST Remove: One Child

**Case 2: the node has exactly one child.** Its child (and everything under it) still needs a home. The child's whole subtree was on the correct side of the parent already, so it can simply move up one level: **relink the parent's pointer to the node's only child**, then free the node.

Here's the lecture's `delete(47)`. 47 is the right child of 45, and 47's only child is 46:

![removing 47, which has one child](courses/diagrams/9a90b498-859d-5ccd-b8f4-4179b5c56551/del47.svg)

The answer is `45->right = 46; free 47`. It's `right` because 47 was 45's **right** child. Which side the **only child** is on (46 is a left child) doesn't matter. That's the part students mix up.

Why is this safe? Everything under 47 was bigger than 45, because it was all in 45's right subtree. So 46 is bigger than 45, and it can sit in 45's right pointer.

| Case | What to do |
|---|---|
| 1: leaf | parent's pointer = `nullptr`, free the node |
| 2: one child | parent's pointer = the only child, free the node |

Notice that case 1 is really case 2 where the "only child" is `nullptr`. Our code will handle both with the same two lines.

questions.question:
```
      60
     /  \
   40    80
     \
      52
     /
    45
```
What should `remove(52)` do?

lessons.title: Remove Leaves and One-Child Nodes
lessons.readme:
# Remove Leaves and One-Child Nodes

Time to code cases 1 and 2. Both need to change the **parent's** pointer. Instead of tracking the parent, here's a trick: walk down **recursively**, passing the pointer **by reference**.

```cpp
void remove(TreeNode*& t, int key)
```

When you call `remove(t->left, key)`, the `t` inside that call isn't a copy. It **is** the parent's `left` pointer. So writing `t = something` rewires the parent directly. At the top, `t` is the caller's `root`, so even removing the root works with no special case.

```cpp
if (key < t->info) remove(t->left, key);       // t becomes parent->left
else if (t->info < key) remove(t->right, key); // t becomes parent->right
```

Once `t` points at the node to remove, cases 1 and 2 are the same two lines:

```cpp
TreeNode* old = t;
t = (t->left != nullptr) ? t->left : t->right;   // the only child, or nullptr for a leaf
delete old;
```

Save the node in `old` **before** overwriting `t`, or you lose the only pointer to it and can't delete it.

Case 3 (two children) gets the next lesson. For now, call `removeTwoChildren(t)`, which does nothing yet.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `remove(t, key)`:
   - an empty tree: the key isn't there, do nothing
   - go left or right recursively to find the key
   - two children: call `removeTwoChildren(t)`
   - otherwise (a leaf or one child): point `t` at the only child (or `nullptr`) and delete the node

It must be O(h). The tests only remove nodes with zero or one child.

lessons.title: BST Remove: Two Children
lessons.readme:
# BST Remove: Two Children

**Case 3: the node has two children.** Now there's no single child to move up. Which key could take the node's place and keep the rule?

It has to be bigger than everything left of it and smaller than everything right of it. Two keys qualify: the node's **neighbors in sorted order**. For 49 below, the sorted keys are … 46, **47**, 49, **58**, 65 …, so 47 (the largest in the left subtree) or 58 (the smallest in the right subtree) could replace it. Both keep a valid BST.

**The class rule uses the left side:** q = the **largest key in the left subtree**. To find it, go **left once, then right until there is no right child**. Copy q's key into the node, then remove q.

![finding q, the largest key in 49's left subtree](courses/diagrams/6920b100-532e-5a21-9b5f-b97ffacd80b1/find_q.svg)

![copy 47 into the node](courses/diagrams/6920b100-532e-5a21-9b5f-b97ffacd80b1/copy_q.svg)

![remove the old 47 with case 2](courses/diagrams/6920b100-532e-5a21-9b5f-b97ffacd80b1/remove_q.svg)

Step 3 is always easy. q was found by going right until there was **no right child**, so q has at most a left child. **Removing q is always case 1 or case 2.**

> [!warning]
> Either neighbor gives a valid tree, but when the exam asks "which tree results?", use the class rule, the largest key in the **left** subtree, unless the question says otherwise. The successor's tree is a typical wrong answer.

Why would anyone pick the other side? If equal keys are allowed, they all go one way, so you replace from that side. And always taking from the left tilts the tree over time, so some implementations alternate or pick randomly.


Insert 50, 20, 70, 10, 30, 60, 80, 25 into an empty BST. Then `remove(20)` and `remove(50)`, using the class rule. What is the result in pre-order?

lessons.title: Remove Two-Child Nodes
lessons.readme:
# Remove Two-Child Nodes

Now the last case, in code. `removeTwoChildren(t)` gets a node with two children and does the lecture's three steps:

1. Find q: start at `t->left`, then go right while there's a right child. Keep a pointer `qp` to q's **parent** as you go.
2. Copy `q->info` into `t`.
3. Unlink q. q has no right child, so its parent should now point at q's **left** child (which may be `nullptr`). Then delete q.

```cpp
TreeNode* qp = t;
TreeNode* q = t->left;
while (q->right != nullptr) { qp = q; q = q->right; }
t->info = q->info;
// now unlink q...
```

Which of `qp`'s pointers points at q? Usually `qp->right`, because we got to q by going right. But there's a **trap**: if `t->left` has no right child, the loop never runs. Then q **is** `t->left`, and `qp` is still `t`:

![the trap where q is the node's own left child](courses/diagrams/a86c2139-ffbd-5d27-8fb1-9a9fb3162e12/trap.svg)

So check: if `qp == t`, set `t->left = q->left`; otherwise set `qp->right = q->left`. Lab 8's bonus tests check exactly this case, along with removing the root and removing a key that isn't in the tree.

> [!tip]
> You could also copy q's key into `t` and then call `remove(t->left, q->info)`. The recursion finds q and removes it with case 1 or 2. It's the same result, just less code.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `removeTwoChildren(t)`: replace `t`'s key with the largest key in its left subtree, then remove that node, keeping its left child linked in. Don't leak it.

The tests check the exact tree shape, so use the **largest key in the left subtree**, not the smallest in the right.

lessons.title: BST Remove Big O
lessons.readme:
# BST Remove Big O

Add up the work in `remove`:

1. Walk down from the root to the node: one path, at most h steps.
2. Case 1 or 2: change one pointer and delete. O(1).
3. Case 3: keep walking down from the node to q. That's still the **same downward direction**, so the total walk from the root to q is at most h steps. Then copy a key and unlink q in O(1).

The whole thing is **O(h)**, just like search and insert:

| Operation | Time |
|---|---|
| search | O(h) |
| insert | O(h) |
| remove | O(h) |
| traversal, count, height, copy, destroy | O(n) |

And h is between about log₂ n (balanced) and n − 1 (a chain). That's why the next lesson is about keeping the tree balanced.

One more fact the exam likes: in case 3, q is the largest key in the left subtree, so q **never has a right child**. That's why removing q is always case 1 or case 2, never case 3 again. The same goes for the other side: the smallest key in the right subtree never has a **left** child.

questions.question: What is the Big O of `remove` in a BST of height h?
In case 3, why is removing q always case 1 or case 2?
answers: q never has a left child
q never has a right child
q is always a leaf node
q is always the left child
questions.answer: q never has a right child

lessons.title: Keeping BSTs Balanced
lessons.readme:
# Keeping BSTs Balanced

A plain BST is only fast if the keys happen to arrive in a good order. Real systems can't count on that, because sorted input is common. And even a tree that starts out bushy can drift out of balance as inserts and deletes happen. So production trees **rebalance themselves**, mostly using small local rearrangements of a few pointers called **rotations**. You won't code rotations in this class, but you should know the three families:

| Technique | Trees | Guarantee | How |
|---|---|---|---|
| Strict balance | AVL, red-black | **worst case** O(log n) | rotate after every insert and delete so the height never exceeds about 2 log₂ n |
| Self-adjusting | splay | **amortized** O(log n) | each access rotates the found node up to the root |
| Randomized | treap | **expected** O(log n) | each node gets a random priority; rotations keep the priorities in heap order, so the tree looks like one built from random insert order |

The three guarantee words mean different things, and the exam can ask which is which:

- **Worst case:** every single operation is O(log n).
- **Amortized:** one search can be slow (O(n)), but a long run of operations averages O(log n) each.
- **Expected:** it depends on random coin flips, not on the input order, and is O(log n) on average over those flips.

Notice the treap borrows the heap order from the next chapter. Ideas in this course keep reusing each other.

questions.question: Which tree guarantees that **each** search is O(log n), even in the worst case?
A splay tree promises **amortized** O(log n). What does that allow?
answers: One operation can be slow, but a long run averages O(log n) each
After the first search for a key, searching for it again is O(1)
The O(log n) bound holds only when keys arrive in random order
Every single operation finishes in O(log n), whatever happens
questions.answer: One operation can be slow, but a long run averages O(log n) each

lessons.title: std::map and std::unordered_map
lessons.readme:
# std::map and std::unordered_map

Should Spartan Maps just use the standard library? It could. C++ already ships a self-balancing BST:

```cpp
#include <map>

std::map<string, int> ids;        // building name -> building id
ids["science building"] = 1;
ids["eng"] = 0;
ids["art"] = 8;
for (auto& p : ids) cout << p.first << " ";   // art eng science building
```

The loop prints the names **sorted**, whatever order they went in, because iterating a `std::map` is an in-order walk of its tree.

What the lecture says about `std::map`:

- It stores key-value pairs in **strictly sorted** key order, and you can iterate through them in that order.
- Under the hood it's usually a **red-black tree**, so its height is capped near 2 log₂ n, and search, insert and delete are **O(log n) worst case**.
- The costs: every element is a separate node allocated on the heap (memory overhead per element), and it has poor cache locality compared to a contiguous array.
- `std::set`, `std::multiset` and `std::multimap` are built the same way. A set holds keys only; the multi versions allow duplicates.

`std::unordered_map` is a different beast: a **hash table with separate chaining**, like the Hashing chapter. Lookups are O(1) on average, but it keeps **no order**, so it can't list buildings alphabetically, and finding "everything starting with sci" means looking at every key.

questions.question: Spartan Maps needs to list buildings in alphabetical order. Which container keeps its keys sorted?
What is the **worst-case** Big O of looking up a key in a `std::map` holding n keys?

lessons.title: Range Search
lessons.readme:
# Range Search

Before autocomplete, a simpler version of the same problem: list every key between `lo` and `hi`, in sorted order. Building IDs 300 to 340, say.

An in-order traversal gives sorted output, and we could keep only the keys in range. But that visits all n nodes, even when only three keys match. The BST rule lets us **prune**, skipping subtrees that can't contain a match:

- Go **left** only if `lo < t->info`. Otherwise every key on the left is smaller than `lo`.
- Visit **this node** if `lo <= t->info <= hi`.
- Go **right** only if `t->info < hi`. Otherwise every key on the right is bigger than `hi`.

The order of those three steps (left, node, right) is still in-order, so the output stays sorted.

Here's `range(t, 35, 62)`. Green nodes are output, blue ones are visited but don't match, and red subtrees are never visited:

![a pruned range search](courses/diagrams/4d72c559-658b-58c6-9825-e33f87f6b82c/range.svg)

At 30, `35 < 30` is false, so 30's left subtree is skipped. At 70, `70 < 62` is false, so its right subtree is skipped. Only 7 of the 12 nodes are touched here; in a big tree the savings are huge.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `range(t, lo, hi, out)`: append every key `k` with `lo <= k <= hi` to `out`, in increasing order. Skip any subtree that can't contain a match. The tests time many small ranges on a large tree, so visiting every node is too slow.

lessons.title: Why Prune the Search?
lessons.readme:
# Why Prune the Search?

How much does pruning save? Think about which nodes a pruned range search touches.

- The nodes on the path down to `lo` and the path down to `hi`: about **2h** nodes.
- The k nodes that are actually **in range**, since each one is output.
- Nothing else: every other subtree is skipped as a whole, at the edge of one of those two paths.

So a pruned range search is **O(h + k)**, where k is the number of results. In a balanced tree of a million keys with 10 results, that's roughly 50 nodes instead of a million.

Without pruning, the in-order walk is **O(n)** no matter how few keys match.

Lab 8's autocomplete has exactly this requirement: `startingWith` must not visit every node in the tree, and must use the BST ordering rule to skip any subtree that can't contain a key starting with the prefix. A full traversal with a filter gets the right output and still loses credit.

> [!tip]
> On the exam, when you write a pruned search, check each recursive call: "could anything down there possibly match?" If the answer is no, the call shouldn't happen.

lessons.title: Building Autocomplete
lessons.readme:
# Building Autocomplete

Everything comes together. Spartan Maps stores a `NameEntry` for every building name **and** for every abbreviation, keyed by the lowercase text, so the Engineering Building is in the tree twice: as `"engineering building"` and as `"eng"`, both with the same `buildingId`. Entries are ordered by key, so an in-order walk is alphabetical.

When the user types a prefix, `startingWith` suggests buildings whose key starts with it. Pruning works like a range search. For each node with key `k`:

- `k` starts with the prefix: it's a match. Go **left**, then this node, then **right** (matches can be on both sides).
- `k < prefix` and doesn't match: every match is bigger than `k`, so go **right only**.
- otherwise `k` comes after every match, so go **left only**.

For example, with prefix `"sci"`, the key `"ramp"` sends us right, `"zoo"` sends us left, and `"science building"` is a match.

Lab 8 adds three rules:

1. Matching ignores case. The keys are already lowercase, so lowercase the prefix with the given `lowercase` function.
2. **No duplicate buildings.** If both a name and its abbreviation match, add only the first one found, which is the alphabetically smaller key: `"sci"` before `"science building"`.
3. Return at most `limit` buildings.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `startingWith(t, prefix, out, limit)`. Append to `out` the entries of up to `limit` different buildings whose key starts with `prefix` (ignoring case), in alphabetical order of key. When a building matches twice, keep only its entry with the smaller key. Skip subtrees that can't match: the tests time many searches on a large tree.

You can add a recursive helper. `out` starts empty. `startsWith(s, p)` is given.
