lessons.title: BST Review
lessons.readme:
# BST Review

Time to practice what the exam asks: tracing a BST by hand. Draw the tree after every step, and write down which case each remove is.

Quick reference:

- **BST rule**: every key in the left subtree < node < every key in the right subtree. In-order is sorted.
- **search**: compare and go left or right, one path, O(h)
- **insert**: search, then add a new **leaf** where you fell off; duplicates do nothing. O(h)
- **remove**: case 1 leaf → parent's pointer = `nullptr`; case 2 one child → parent's pointer = that child; case 3 two children → copy in the **largest key of the left subtree** (left once, then right all the way), then remove that node, which is case 1 or 2. O(h)
- **height**: sorted inserts make a chain (h = n − 1, O(n)); balanced trees keep h ≈ log₂ n
- **pruned search**: skip subtrees that can't match, O(h + k)

lessons.title: Priority Queues
lessons.readme:
# Priority Queues

The Student Wellness Center is swamped during finals week. Students show up all day, and a nurse rates how urgent each one is. When a doctor frees up, they should see the **most urgent** student next, not whoever showed up first.

Emergency rooms and disaster crews do this with **triage tags**. The color band torn off at the bottom says how urgent the patient is (red before yellow before green), and that, not arrival order, decides who is seen next.

![three paper triage tags with black, red, yellow and green bands at the bottom](courses/diagrams/801f82b1-452b-5555-b3f7-2ddc82e0c3e9/triage_tags.jpg)
*Image: Genppy, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.*

A normal queue is first in, first out, so it's the wrong tool here. We need a **priority queue**:

| Operation | What it does |
|---|---|
| `push(x)` | add x |
| `top()` | look at the highest-priority item |
| `pop()` | remove the highest-priority item |

How fast can we make that? Try the obvious ways to store the students:

| Store them in… | push | top | pop | the problem |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| an unsorted array | O(1) | O(n) | O(n) | finding the max means checking everyone |
| a sorted array | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) | every push shifts elements to make room |

Each one is fast at one thing and slow at the other. Over this chapter we'll build a **heap**, which does push and pop in O(log n) and top in O(1). It's what `std::priority_queue` uses under the hood, and it's why Dijkstra's algorithm (later in the course) is fast.

questions.question: A priority queue always removes:
answers: The item that was added last
The item that was added first
The item with the highest priority
questions.answer: The item with the highest priority

questions.question: With an **unsorted** array, why is `pop()` O(n)?
answers: It has to sort the array first
It has to shift every item to make room
It has to scan every item to find the max
questions.answer: It has to scan every item to find the max

lessons.title: Heaps
lessons.readme:
# Heaps

A **max-heap** is a binary tree with two rules.

**Rule 1, order: every parent is ≥ its children.**

![a max-heap](courses/diagrams/94bd5748-499e-5227-a4d8-961d7414b5db/max_heap.svg)

Follow that rule down from the top and the root has to be the biggest key in the whole tree. That's all the order a heap keeps. Siblings don't care about each other: 70 and 80 could swap sides and it would still be a heap. That's less work than keeping everything sorted, and it's exactly enough to find the max instantly.

**Rule 2, shape: the tree is complete.** Every level is full except possibly the last one, and the last level fills from the **left** with no gaps.

![a complete tree next to one with a gap](courses/diagrams/94bd5748-499e-5227-a4d8-961d7414b5db/complete.svg)

The shape rule is what keeps a heap fast. A complete tree with n nodes is only about log₂ n levels tall, so walking from the root to a leaf never takes more than about log₂ n steps.

A **min-heap** is the same thing flipped: every parent is ≤ its children, so the root is the smallest.

questions.question: In a max-heap, where is the largest key?

Is this a max-heap?

```
        60
      /    \
    45      55
      \    /  \
      20  50  35
```
answers: No: it isn't complete (45 has a right child but no left child)
Yes: every parent is bigger than its children
questions.answer: No: it isn't complete (45 has a right child but no left child)

questions.question: In a max-heap with distinct keys, where can the **smallest** key be?
answers: Only at the last array index

lessons.title: Heaps in an Array
lessons.readme:
# Heaps in an Array

Here's the trick that makes heaps so practical: you don't need nodes or pointers. Number the nodes level by level, left to right, and store them in an array in that order.

![a heap with its array indexes](courses/diagrams/2ed75a0d-6cc2-54ec-b6f0-b16925fec570/indexes.svg)

Because the tree is complete, there are no gaps, and simple math finds any node's family. For the node at index `i`:

- left child: `2i + 1`
- right child: `2i + 2`
- parent: `(i - 1) / 2` (C++ integer division drops the remainder)

Check it on the picture. Index 1 holds 70. Its children are at 2·1 + 1 = 3 and 2·1 + 2 = 4, which hold 40 and 60. Index 6 holds 75, and its parent is (6 − 1) / 2 = 2, which holds 80.

> [!warning]
> Some textbooks start the root at index 1 and use `2i`, `2i + 1` and `i / 2`. This class starts at **index 0**. Mixing the two up is the most common heap bug.

## Assignment

We're building the Wellness Center's triage queue as a heap stored in a `vector<int>` of urgency scores. First, the index math.

1. [ ] Complete `leftChild(i)`.
2. [ ] Complete `rightChild(i)`.
3. [ ] Complete `parent(i)`. You can assume `i > 0`.

lessons.title: Sift Up
lessons.readme:
# Sift Up

To add a key, we have to keep both rules true.

**Shape first.** The only spot that keeps the tree complete is the next free slot: the end of the array.

**Then order.** The new key might be bigger than its parent. If it is, swap them, and keep swapping upward until its parent is bigger or it reaches the root. This is called **sift-up** (or "bubble up").

Here's `push(85)`. The key on the move is amber; the parent it's compared with is blue.

![push 85, steps 1 and 2](courses/diagrams/cd575b2c-983e-596c-8a19-1a4e0f99fa65/push_a.svg)

![push 85, steps 3 and 4](courses/diagrams/cd575b2c-983e-596c-8a19-1a4e0f99fa65/push_b.svg)

Notice that only the keys on one path, from the new leaf up to the root, ever move. Everything else stays put.

## Assignment

New students keep arriving. Write `push` so each one lands in the right place.

1. [ ] Append `key` to the end of `A`.
2. [ ] Let `i` be its index.
3. [ ] While `i > 0` and the parent's key is smaller than `A[i]`: swap them, and move `i` up to the parent.

lessons.title: Sift Down
lessons.readme:
# Sift Down

The doctor is free. Who's next? That's easy: `top()` is just `A[0]`.

Removing it is the interesting part. If we simply deleted the root, the tree would have a hole at the top. Instead:

1. Move the **last** key into the root. The tree stays complete.
2. Shrink the array by one.
3. The new root is probably too small, so **sift it down**: swap it with its **larger** child, and keep going until both children are smaller or it hits a leaf.

Here's a pop from the heap we got last lesson. 90 is removed:

![pop, steps 1 and 2](courses/diagrams/037abc8a-b824-5347-b17f-25bdd7444ddd/pop_a.svg)

![pop, steps 3 and 4](courses/diagrams/037abc8a-b824-5347-b17f-25bdd7444ddd/pop_b.svg)

**Why the larger child?** Whichever child moves up becomes the parent of the other one. If we swapped 40 with 80 in step 2, 80 would end up above 85, and the order rule would break right there.

> [!note]
> In the lecture's priority queue, `pop()` returns nothing. Read `top()` first, then `pop()`. `std::priority_queue` works the same way.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `siftDown(A, i, n)`. Only the first `n` elements count as the heap. Find the index of the largest of `A[i]` and its children (a child exists only if its index is `< n`). If that isn't `i`, swap and keep sifting from the child's index.
2. [ ] Complete `top(A)`.
3. [ ] Complete `pop(A)`: move the last key to the root, shrink the vector with `pop_back()`, then sift down from the root.

You can assume the heap isn't empty when `top` or `pop` is called.

lessons.title: Heap Big O
lessons.readme:
# Heap Big O

Both of our operations walk a single path through the tree. Sift-up climbs from a leaf toward the root; sift-down sinks from the root toward a leaf. Each step is one comparison and maybe one swap.

How long is that path? A complete tree with n nodes has about **log₂ n** levels: level 0 holds 1 node, level 1 holds 2, level 2 holds 4, and so on, doubling each time. So:

| Operation | Big O | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `top()` | O(1) | the max is always `A[0]` |
| `push(x)` | O(log n) | at most one swap per level, going up |
| `pop()` | O(log n) | at most one swap per level, going down |

Compare that with the arrays from the first lesson, where something was always O(n). A million students means about 20 swaps, not a million.

This is also why the shape rule matters. If the tree were allowed to be lopsided, a path could be n long, and we'd be back to O(n).

Why is `top()` O(1)?

lessons.title: Build Heap
lessons.readme:
# Build Heap

Sometimes all the students arrive at once: you start with an unordered array and want a heap.

You could `push` them one at a time. That works, but there's a faster way that works in place.

Every **leaf** is already a tiny heap of one node, since it has no children to break the rule. So skip the leaves and fix the parents, starting from the **last parent** and going **backward** to the root, calling sift-down on each one.

Where's the last parent? It's the parent of the last element: `((n - 1) - 1) / 2`, which is `n/2 - 1`. Everything after it is a leaf.

![buildHeap, one sift-down per step from index 4 back to the root](courses/diagrams/21f066b9-67ad-5ef9-bc30-23df252a3012/start.svg)

**Why backward?** Sift-down only works if both subtrees below are already heaps. Going from the bottom up guarantees that: by the time we reach a node, everything under it has been fixed.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `buildHeap(A)`: for `i` from `A.size()/2 - 1` down to `0`, call `siftDown(A, i, A.size())`.

Don't build it with repeated `push` calls. That gives a valid heap too, but usually a **different** array, and the exam expects the bottom-up version.

> [!tip]
> Watch the types: `A.size()` is unsigned. Write `(int)A.size() / 2 - 1` so the loop counter can go below 0 and stop.

lessons.title: Build Heap Big O
lessons.readme:
# Build Heap Big O

buildHeap calls sift-down about n/2 times, and each sift-down is O(log n). So it's O(n log n)… right?

Not quite. The tight bound is **O(n)**, because most nodes barely move.

A node can only sink as far as the levels **below** it:

| Nodes | How many | Max swaps each |
|---|---|---|
| leaves | n/2 | 0 (we skip them) |
| one level up | n/4 | 1 |
| two levels up | n/8 | 2 |
| three levels up | n/16 | 3 |
| … | … | … |
| the root | 1 | log₂ n |

Add it up: n/4 · 1 + n/8 · 2 + n/16 · 3 + … which comes out to less than n. The few nodes that can sink far (near the top) are rare, and the many nodes near the bottom can hardly sink at all.

Building with n separate `push` calls really is O(n log n), because most of the new keys land at the bottom and may climb all the way up.

lessons.title: Heapsort
lessons.readme:
# Heapsort

A max-heap always hands you the biggest remaining key. Pull them out one by one and you get the keys in order. That's **heapsort**, and the clever part is that it needs no extra array.

1. `buildHeap` on the whole array.
2. The max is at `A[0]`. **Swap** it with the last key of the heap. Now the max is in its final sorted position, at the end.
3. The heap is now one smaller. Sift the new root down, but only within the heap part.
4. Repeat until the heap is down to one key.

Here's one full pass on `[9, 7, 8, 3, 5, 6]`, and the first swap of the next one:

![one heapsort pass, then the start of the next](courses/diagrams/f4d5d5e5-3852-5efb-a9f3-22aa94d88bbb/pass.svg)

The array is split in two: `A[0..end]` is still a max-heap, and everything after it is sorted and finished.

> [!warning]
> The classic bug is sifting down with the **old** size. Then the sorted 9 counts as part of the heap again and gets pulled back up. Pass `end` as the size.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `heapSort(A)` so it sorts `A` ascending, in place. Use `buildHeap` and `siftDown`.

lessons.title: Heapsort Big O
lessons.readme:
# Heapsort Big O

| Step | How often | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| buildHeap | once | O(n) |
| swap + sift-down | n − 1 times | O(log n) each |
| **total** | | **O(n log n)** |

That's the same in the **best, average and worst** case. Unlike quicksort, no input can make heapsort slow.

**Space.** Heapsort only moves keys around inside the array. But the sift-down we wrote is **recursive**, so each call waits on the call stack, up to log n deep. That makes it **O(log n)** space as written. Rewrite sift-down as a loop and heapsort becomes O(1) space.

> [!warning]
> The Nov 12 slides said "in place: O(1) space." The professor crossed that out on Nov 17 for exactly this reason. With the recursive sift-down from class, the answer is O(log n).

**Stable?** No. The long-distance swaps (root to the end) can reorder equal keys.

In practice quicksort is usually 2 to 3 times faster because it walks memory in order, while heapsort jumps around. `std::sort` uses quicksort and switches to heapsort if the recursion gets too deep, so its worst case stays O(n log n).

lessons.title: Min-Heaps
lessons.readme:
# Min-Heaps

Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm (coming up in Graphs) always needs the **closest** unvisited spot next. That's a priority queue where *smaller* wins: a **min-heap**.

Everything flips:

- every parent is **≤** its children, so the minimum is at the root
- sift-up swaps while the new key is **smaller** than its parent
- sift-down swaps with the **smaller** child

Lab 9's `MinHeap` adds two twists, and so will we:

1. It's a class, and `pop()` **returns** the removed item (unlike the lecture's `void pop()`).
2. Popping or peeking an empty heap **throws** an exception instead of crashing.

Lab 9 also says to compare keys with only `<`, so the class works for any type that has `<`. You can always rewrite a comparison: `a > b` is `b < a`, and `a >= b` is `!(a < b)`.

## Assignment

Complete the `MinHeap` class.

1. [ ] `push(key)`: append, then sift up while the key is smaller than its parent.
2. [ ] `top()`: return the minimum. Throw `std::runtime_error` if empty.
3. [ ] `pop()`: remove and return the minimum. Throw `std::runtime_error` if empty.

Use only `<` to compare keys.

lessons.readme:
# The STL Priority Queue

In real code you won't write your own heap. C++ ships one:

```cpp
#include <queue>

std::priority_queue<int> pq;          // a MAX-heap by default
pq.push(10); pq.push(30); pq.push(20);
cout << pq.top();                     // 30
pq.pop();                             // removes 30, returns nothing
```

It's a max-heap because its default comparison is `std::less`, which feels backwards but is how it works. To get a **min**-heap, spell out all three template arguments:

```cpp
std::priority_queue<int, std::vector<int>, std::greater<int>> minpq;
```

Just like the lecture's version, `pop()` returns `void`, so read `top()` before you pop.

There are also raw heap functions in `<algorithm>` that work on a vector you own: `make_heap` (buildHeap), `push_heap` (call it **after** `push_back`), `pop_heap` (moves the max to the back; call `pop_back` **after**), and `sort_heap`. All of them take an iterator pair like `v.begin(), v.end()`.

## Assignment

The Wellness Center's dashboard wants two reports.

1. [ ] `mostUrgentFirst(scores)`: return the scores from highest to lowest, using a `std::priority_queue`.
2. [ ] `leastUrgentFirst(scores)`: return them from lowest to highest, using a min-heap `std::priority_queue`.

Don't call `std::sort`.

lessons.title: What Is a Graph
lessons.readme:
# What Is a Graph

Your team is building **SpartanMaps**: type in two campus buildings and it draws the shortest walk between them. Before we can find any route, we need a way to describe the campus to a computer.

Here's the idea. Each building or path corner is a **vertex**. Each walkway between two of them is an **edge**. That's a **graph**.

Formally, a graph is a pair **G = (V, E)**:

- **V** is a finite, **nonempty** set of vertices.
- **E ⊆ V × V** is a set of edges, and each edge is a pair of vertices.

(People also use V and E to mean *how many* vertices and edges there are. You'll see that in every Big O on this topic.)

Edges come in two kinds:

- **Undirected**: the pair is unordered, written {u, v}. You can go either way, like a walkway or a beam in a bridge truss.
- **Directed**: the pair is ordered, written (u, v), and drawn as an arrow from u to v. Think course prerequisites: Intro leads to OOP, not the other way around.

![an undirected truss next to a directed prerequisite chart](courses/diagrams/500c268b-8462-54ee-83e7-3de9e2c38cf1/kinds.svg)

Edges can also carry data. In SpartanMaps each walkway has a **weight**, its length in meters. We'll get to weighted graphs once we can walk around unweighted ones.

> [!note]
> The professor's opening example was a bridge game: joints are vertices and beams are edges. How you choose the vertices and edges decides which questions the graph can answer, so it's worth a moment's thought each time.

lessons.title: Degrees and Complete Graphs
lessons.readme:
# Degrees and Complete Graphs

Some campus spots are busy crossroads; others are dead ends. The **degree** of a vertex counts that: it's the number of edge ends touching it.

Here's a handy fact. Every edge has exactly **two ends**, so if you add up all the degrees you count every edge twice:

**sum of all degrees = 2E**

A **complete graph**, written **Kₙ**, has an edge between every pair of its n vertices. How many edges is that? Each vertex has n − 1 neighbors, so the degrees add up to n(n − 1). Every edge was counted twice, so:

**Kₙ has n(n − 1) / 2 edges**

![the complete graph K5, every vertex has degree 4](courses/diagrams/10a9e4d2-39a3-51ff-80bb-9b3506623360/k5.svg)

For K₅ that's 5 · 4 / 2 = **10**. If the graph is directed and every pair has arrows **both ways**, don't divide by 2: n(n − 1) = 20.

One more word you'll need next lesson. A **multigraph** allows **parallel edges**: more than one edge between the same pair of vertices. Two walkways from the library to the student union would be two parallel edges.

lessons.title: Euler Circuits and Paths
lessons.readme:
# Euler Circuits and Paths

SpartanMaps' first feature request is a campus tour: walk every walkway **exactly once**. When is that possible? A famous puzzle answered it in 1736.

The city of Königsberg had four land areas (A to D) joined by **seven bridges**. Locals wanted a walk that crosses every bridge exactly once and ends where it started. As a graph, land areas are vertices and bridges are edges. A and C are joined by two bridges, so it's a **multigraph**.

Here's the city in Euler's day. The river is blue and the seven bridges are orange:

![an old engraved map of Königsberg with the river in blue and seven bridges in orange](courses/diagrams/a5665e89-1cbc-5090-b04f-427461e9c13b/konigsberg_map.jpg)
*Image: Merian-Erben, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.*

The graph below keeps only what matters: which land areas each bridge joins.

![the Königsberg bridges as a multigraph](courses/diagrams/a5665e89-1cbc-5090-b04f-427461e9c13b/kberg.svg)

An **Euler circuit** crosses every edge exactly once and ends where it started. Each time the walk passes **through** a vertex, it uses two edges: one in, one out. On a circuit the start and end are the same vertex, so those pair up too. So:

- **Euler circuit**: every vertex has **even** degree.
- **Euler path** (every edge once, but start ≠ end): **exactly 2** vertices have odd degree. Start at one, finish at the other.

For a connected graph these conditions are enough, not just required.

Königsberg's degrees are A = 5, B = 3, C = 3, D = 3. That's **four** odd vertices, and a walk only has two ends to put leftover edges on. No circuit, and not even a path.

The lecture's truss is a happier story. Vertices 4 and 5 are odd, so you can trace it without lifting your pen if you start at one of them: 4 → 1 → 2 → 4 → 5 → 2 → 3 → 5.

![the truss with odd vertices 4 and 5](courses/diagrams/a5665e89-1cbc-5090-b04f-427461e9c13b/truss.svg)

answers: Yes, starting from any of the vertices
Yes, if you start at an odd vertex
No, since some degrees are even
No, since some degrees are odd
questions.answer: Yes, if you start at an odd vertex

questions.question: Königsberg builds one more bridge, between B and C. Degrees become A = 5, B = 4, C = 4, D = 3. Now:
answers: An Euler path, starting at B
An Euler path, between A and D
An Euler circuit, from any vertex
Neither, since A is still odd

lessons.title: Adjacency Matrix
lessons.readme:
# Adjacency Matrix

To store the campus in memory, the first option is an **adjacency matrix**: an n × n table where `A[i][j] = 1` if (i, j) is an edge and 0 if it isn't.

![the lecture graph next to its adjacency matrix](courses/diagrams/bdd6306d-02e2-5cc6-85fe-aee7850ad72d/matrix.svg)

Because this graph is undirected, edge 0–1 sets **both** `A[0][1]` and `A[1][0]`. The matrix is **symmetric** about the diagonal.

For a **multigraph**, a cell counts the parallel edges, so `A[i][j]` can be greater than 1. Königsberg's matrix would have a 2 between A and C.

Two things are easy with a matrix:

- **Is (u, v) an edge?** Look at `A[u][v]`. O(1).
- **Degree of u**: add up row u, so O(V). In a multigraph that still works, since a 2 counts as two edges.

The cost is space: the table always has V² cells, even if almost all of them are 0.

## Assignment

We'll keep SpartanMaps' graph code in `graph.h`. Edges arrive as a list of vertex pairs, numbered 0 to n − 1.

1. [ ] Complete `toMatrix(n, edges)`: return the n × n adjacency matrix of the **undirected** graph. For each edge {u, v}, add 1 to both `A[u][v]` and `A[v][u]`, so parallel edges count up. The tests have no self-loops.
2. [ ] Complete `degree(A, u)`: the sum of row u.

# Adjacency Lists

Most of the campus matrix would be zeros. A building connects to a handful of walkways, not to all 6,000 other points on the map. The second option only stores the edges that exist.

An **adjacency list** keeps one list per vertex: the vertices it's adjacent to. An array of size n holds the lists, so `adj[i]` is vertex i's list. In lecture each list is a linked list; in C++ we'll use `vector<vector<int>>`.

![the lecture graph next to its adjacency lists](courses/diagrams/e63b5038-187e-5b67-b449-918a4c2412a3/lists.svg)

Each **undirected** edge shows up in **two** lists, once at each end. So the lists hold **2E** entries in total for a graph with no self-loops. A multigraph repeats an entry for each parallel edge.

**Directed** graphs are simpler: edge (u, v) only goes in u's list, so `adj[u]` holds u's **out**-neighbors and there are **E** entries in all.

![a directed graph next to its adjacency lists](courses/diagrams/e63b5038-187e-5b67-b449-918a4c2412a3/directed.svg)

The order of a list is just the order the edges were added. That will matter later: DFS and BFS try neighbors in list order.

## Assignment

# Directed Graph Storage

Some campus paths are one-way: a down-only staircase, or an exit-only door. Those are **directed** edges, and both representations handle them with one rule: **`A[i][j] = 1` means an edge i → j.**

![a directed graph and its matrix, row 2 highlighted](courses/diagrams/d2ddcd33-c3de-5b46-a6cb-f209fcdcdc73/dir.svg)

So for a directed graph:

- **Row i** of the matrix lists i's **out**-neighbors. Column j lists who points **into** j.
- The matrix is **not necessarily symmetric**. Here 0 → 1 exists but 1 → 0 doesn't.
- Each edge is stored **once**, so the lists hold **E** entries.

Compare with undirected graphs, where the matrix is always symmetric and the lists hold 2E entries (with no self-loops).

> [!tip]
> To read a list entry off a matrix, go along the row and write down the column number of every 1. Row 2 above is `1 0 0 1`, so `2 → 0, 3`.

lessons.title: Adjacency Matrix or List
lessons.readme:
# Adjacency Matrix or List

So which one should SpartanMaps use? It depends on how many edges the graph has and what you ask of it most.

| | Matrix | List |
|---|---|---|
| space | O(V²) | O(V + E) |
| "is (u, v) an edge?" | O(1): look at `A[u][v]` | O(degree of u): scan u's list |
| all neighbors of u | O(V): scan the whole row | O(degree of u) |
| best when | the graph is **dense** (close to V² edges), V is small, and you check edges often | the graph is **sparse**, you often visit every neighbor (as DFS does), or vertices get added |

A matrix is simple to build and wins when you constantly ask "is this an edge?". A list wins on space and on "visit every neighbor", which is what graph algorithms do all day.

**Most real graphs are sparse**: roads, social networks, the web. So adjacency lists are the usual default.

The real SpartanMaps campus graph has V = 6,212 vertices and E = 7,945 edges. Its adjacency lists need 2E + V = **22,102** slots. A matrix would need 6,212² ≈ **38.6 million** cells, almost all of them 0.

lessons.title: DFS on a Graph
lessons.readme:
# DFS on a Graph

Now we can store the campus. Next question: starting from one building, which spots can you reach at all? That's a **traversal**: visit every vertex reachable from a start vertex, **exactly once**.

On a tree, recursion alone works, because there's only one path to each node. A graph can have **cycles** (A → B → E → F → C → A below), and plain recursion would go around one forever. So we keep a `visited[]` array and skip anything already marked.

**Depth-first search** goes deep: follow one path until you're stuck, then back up and try the next branch, like exploring a maze.

```cpp
dfs(v):
    visited[v] = true
    visit(v)                      // e.g. print v
    for each neighbor w of v
        if not visited[w]
            dfs(w)
```

DFS is naturally recursive: `dfs(w)` runs to completion before v tries its next neighbor. The call stack is DFS's stack. Here's `dfs(A)`, neighbors in alphabetical order:

![DFS steps 1 and 2](courses/diagrams/6c978319-cca8-53a8-a69a-a21156f79e74/s1.svg)

![DFS steps 3 and 4](courses/diagrams/6c978319-cca8-53a8-a69a-a21156f79e74/s2.svg)

The final visit order is **A B D E F C G**. Edge A–C (blue in step 3) is never followed, because C was already visited when A got around to it. The green edges form the **DFS tree**.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `dfs(adj, v, visited, order)`: mark v, append it to `order`, then recurse on each unvisited neighbor **in list order**.
2. [ ] Complete `dfsOrder(adj, s)`: make a `visited` vector (all false) and an empty `order`, call `dfs` from `s` once, and return `order`. Only the vertices reachable from `s` appear.

lessons.title: Tracing DFS
lessons.readme:
# Tracing DFS

The exam will hand you a graph and ask for the DFS order. Here's a reliable way to do it on paper:

1. Write the adjacency lists, in the order the question says (usually increasing).
2. Keep a call stack column. Visit the start and push it.
3. At the top call, scan its list from **where you left off** for the first unvisited neighbor. Visit it and push it.
4. If none is left, pop. You're back in the caller, which carries on scanning **its** list.

The usual mistake is step 4: after a dead end, people jump to the next vertex in numeric order instead of returning to the caller.

**DFS on a tree.** A binary tree is a graph too. Run `dfs(root)` trying the left child first, and the order is: visit the node, then go deep into the left, then the right. That's exactly **pre-order** traversal.

**Cost.** With adjacency lists, each vertex is visited once and each list is scanned once, so DFS is **O(V + E)**.

lessons.title: Connected Pieces
lessons.readme:
# Connected Pieces

`dfsOrder` only reaches what's connected to the start. Suppose the SpartanMaps data has a parking garage whose walkways were never linked to the rest of campus. Starting from MacQuarrie Hall, DFS would never see it. After a traversal, any vertex still unmarked is **unreachable** from the start.

To visit **every** vertex, the lecture wraps DFS in a loop that restarts it from any vertex not visited yet:

```cpp
depthFirstTraversal(G):
    for each vertex v in G
        visited[v] = false
    for each vertex v in G
        if not visited[v]
            dfs(v)
```

The `visited` array is shared by all the restarts. Each restart sweeps up one whole **connected piece** of the graph, so counting the restarts counts the pieces. That's one of DFS's classic uses: checking whether the campus map is all one piece.

![a graph with two separate pieces: 0, 1, 2, 3 in green and 4, 5, 6 in blue, with dfs restarted at 0 and at 4](courses/diagrams/b88cae6b-1f35-5829-8fd3-0ebcfd279e57/pieces.svg)

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `dfsAll(adj)`: try v = 0, 1, 2, … in order, and call `dfs` from each one that isn't visited yet. Return the full visit order.
2. [ ] Complete `countPieces(adj)`: return how many times the restart loop had to call `dfs`. You can assume the graph is undirected.

Use one `visited` vector for the whole function, not a new one per restart.

lessons.title: BFS on a Graph
lessons.readme:
# BFS on a Graph

DFS charges down one path. For directions we'd rather explore outward evenly: everything 1 walkway away, then 2, then 3, like a ripple in a pond. That's **breadth-first search**, and the tool that keeps the rings in order is a **queue**.

```cpp
bfs(s):
    queue q
    visited[s] = true
    q.push(s)
    while q is not empty
        v = q.front()
        q.pop()
        visit(v)
        for each neighbor w of v
            if not visited[w]
                visited[w] = true
                q.push(w)
```

The queue is first in, first out, so every vertex at distance k leaves the queue before any vertex at distance k + 1. Here's BFS from A on the graph from the DFS lesson:

![BFS steps 1 and 2](courses/diagrams/6c22ab0e-3501-543e-aead-ee8db83fd61c/b1.svg)

![BFS steps 3 and 4](courses/diagrams/6c22ab0e-3501-543e-aead-ee8db83fd61c/b2.svg)

Popping D adds nothing. Popping E adds G, and then F and G add nothing new. The visit order is **A B C D E F G**.

> [!warning]
> Mark a vertex **when you push it**, not when you pop it. If you wait until the pop, a vertex can be pushed twice: in the picture, F is a neighbor of both C and E.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `bfsOrder(adj, s)`: return the vertices reachable from `s` in BFS visit order, trying neighbors in list order. Use `std::queue<int>` (`push`, `front`, `pop`, `empty`).

lessons.title: Tracing BFS
lessons.readme:
# Tracing BFS

On paper, BFS is easier to trace than DFS, as long as you write the queue down after every pop.

1. Write the adjacency lists in the order the question gives.
2. Start with the queue `[s]` and s marked.
3. Pop the front. Go through its list in order; every neighbor that isn't marked yet gets marked and added to the **back**.
4. Repeat until the queue is empty. The pop order is the visit order.

For the lecture graph from the Adjacency Lists lesson (`0: 1 2`, `1: 0 3 4`, `2: 0 3`, `3: 1 2 4`, `4: 1 3`), BFS from 0 goes:

```
queue [0]       pop 0, push 1 2
queue [1 2]     pop 1, push 3 4
queue [2 3 4]   pop 2, nothing new (0 and 3 are marked)
queue [3 4]     pop 3, nothing new
queue [4]       pop 4
visit order: 0 1 2 3 4
```

The tie-breaker is always the same: whoever was **pushed** first comes out first, even if a smaller-numbered vertex is waiting behind it.

lessons.title: DFS and BFS Big O
lessons.readme:
# DFS and BFS Big O

Both traversals do the same total work; they just do it in a different order.

**With adjacency lists:** each vertex is marked and visited once (O(V)), and each vertex's list is scanned once. All the lists together hold E entries (2E for undirected), so the scanning is O(E). Total: **O(V + E)**.

**With an adjacency matrix:** finding one vertex's neighbors means scanning its whole row, V cells, even if most are 0. Doing that for all V vertices costs **O(V²)**, no matter how few edges there are.

| | adjacency lists | adjacency matrix |
|---|---|---|
| DFS | O(V + E) | O(V²) |
| BFS | O(V + E) | O(V²) |

On a sparse graph like a campus map, E is close to V, so lists give about O(V) while the matrix still costs O(V²). That's another reason lists are the default.

lessons.title: Fewest Hops
lessons.readme:
# Fewest Hops

BFS gives us something for free. Because it finishes every vertex at distance k before any at distance k + 1, the first time BFS reaches a vertex is along a path with the **fewest edges**.

To get the actual path, record where each vertex was discovered from: when you push w while handling v, set **`parent[w] = v`**. Then follow parents back from the target to the start, and reverse.

![the BFS tree from A with hop counts](courses/diagrams/88d15807-02fd-59f4-a40e-897e39a62249/tree.svg)

In the picture, `parent[G] = E`, `parent[E] = B` and `parent[B] = A`. Walking back from G gives G E B A, and reversing gives the route **A → B → E → G**, three hops. The green edges are the **BFS tree**: its path from A to every vertex uses as few edges as possible.

If you only need the number of hops, keep a `dist[]` array instead: `dist[s] = 0`, and when you push w from v, `dist[w] = dist[v] + 1`. A vertex that's never reached keeps `dist = -1`.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `bfsDist(adj, s)`: the number of edges on a fewest-edges path from `s` to every vertex, −1 if unreachable.
2. [ ] Complete `fewestHopsPath(adj, s, t)`: the vertices of the path BFS finds from `s` to `t`, start first. Try neighbors in list order and record `parent[w] = v` when you push w. Return `{}` if `t` is unreachable, and `{s}` if `s == t`.

`std::reverse(v.begin(), v.end())` from `<algorithm>` reverses a vector.

lessons.title: DFS vs BFS
lessons.readme:
# DFS vs BFS

Same goal, visit everything reachable once, but different personalities:

| | DFS | BFS |
|---|---|---|
| data structure | a stack (the call stack) | a queue |
| order | as deep as possible, then back up | level by level: 1 edge away, then 2, … |
| path it finds | some path, often a long one | **fewest edges** from the start |
| cost with adjacency lists | O(V + E) | O(V + E) |
| good for | mazes, cycle detection, topological sort, connected pieces | shortest hops, degrees of separation, web crawling |

Neither is "faster" in Big O. Pick by what you need: if the question is "can I get there?" or "is it all one piece?", DFS is short and simple. If the question is "what's the fewest number of steps?", only BFS promises that.

Other famous graph algorithms you may hear about: shortest paths (Dijkstra's, A* search), minimum spanning trees, max-flow, and PageRank, the original Google ranking, where pages are vertices and links are edges.

questions.question: Which traversal guarantees a path with the fewest edges?

lessons.title: The Water Jug Riddle
lessons.readme:
# The Water Jug Riddle

Graphs aren't only maps. The class activity was a riddle: you have a 3-gallon jug, a 5-gallon jug and a faucet. The jugs have no markings. Measure out exactly **4 gallons**.

Allowed moves: fill a jug to the top, empty a jug onto the ground, or pour one jug into the other until the first is empty or the second is full.

**Make it a graph.** A vertex is a **state** (a, b): a gallons in the 3-gallon jug A, b in the 5-gallon jug B. So a ∈ {0..3} and b ∈ {0..5}, which gives **4 × 6 = 24** vertices. Each move takes one state to another, so it's a **directed** edge:

| move | from (a, b) to |
|---|---|
| fill A | (3, b) |
| fill B | (a, 5) |
| empty A | (0, b) |
| empty B | (a, 0) |
| pour A → B | t = min(a, 5 − b); (a − t, b + t) |
| pour B → A | t = min(b, 3 − a); (a + t, b − t) |

The edges are directed because some moves can't be undone: emptying A takes (1, 2) to (0, 2), and no single move gets you back.

Start at (0, 0), try moves in the table's order, keep a visited list, and search until b = 4.

![the BFS path of jug states](courses/diagrams/d1f8dcf1-d62c-546d-9f70-4c1060a63730/bfs.svg)

**BFS** finds it in **6 moves**: fill B, pour B → A, empty A, pour B → A, fill B, pour B → A. **DFS** finds an **8-move** answer: fill A, fill B and empty A reach (0, 5) the long way, then the same moves as BFS. DFS actually visited fewer states this time, but only BFS guarantees the fewest moves.

lessons.title: Weighted Graphs
lessons.readme:
# Weighted Graphs

Now back to SpartanMaps for real. What's the shortest walk from **MacQuarrie Hall** (MH) to the **Event Center** (EC)?

Every walkway has a length in meters, so this is a **weighted graph**. A path's length is the **sum** of its edge lengths, and the adjacency lists now store (neighbor, length) pairs. (The lengths below are simplified for class.)

| | |
|---|---|
| MH | MacQuarrie Hall |
| P | Paseo de San Carlos |
| S | Sweeney Hall |
| F | Chávez fountain |
| R | Rec Center |
| EC | Event Center |

**The shortest path problem**: given a weighted graph where every edge length is ≥ 0, a source s and a destination t, find a path from s to t with the smallest total length.

We already have BFS. What does it find?

![the campus map: the BFS route next to the shortest route](courses/diagrams/016207b8-71d1-5228-8556-f0e652bd12ad/bfs.svg)

BFS returns **MH → R → EC**: only 2 edges, but **350 m**. The real shortest walk is **MH → P → S → F → EC**, 4 edges and **210 m**. Fewest edges isn't shortest.

BFS goes wrong for two reasons:

1. It expands in rings of **hops**, not distance.
2. It locks in each vertex the **first time** it sees it, so a better route found later is ignored.

Fix both and you get the next lesson's algorithm: pick the vertex **closest in distance** first, and allow a vertex's distance to **improve** when a better route turns up.

Which is one reason BFS fails on weighted graphs?
answers: It only works on directed graphs
It never improves a found vertex

lessons.title: Dijkstra's Idea
lessons.readme:
# Dijkstra's Idea

**Dijkstra's algorithm** finds the shortest distance from s to every vertex. It splits the vertices into two groups:

- **finished**: its distance is final.
- **unfinished**: its distance is the best route found **so far**.

Start with `dist[s] = 0` and every other `dist` at ∞. Then repeat:

1. **Finish** the unfinished vertex u with the smallest `dist`.
2. **Relax** each edge (u, v): if going through u is shorter, `dist[u] + len < dist[v]`, lower `dist[v]` and remember `prev[v] = u`.

Here it is on the campus map. Amber is the vertex just finished, green is finished, a blue circle is a distance that just improved. A blue line is the best link so far to a vertex that isn't finished.

![Dijkstra steps 1 and 2](courses/diagrams/e6c1cace-3aab-5259-be75-c61fc444f908/d1.svg)

![Dijkstra steps 3 and 4](courses/diagrams/e6c1cace-3aab-5259-be75-c61fc444f908/d2.svg)

![Dijkstra steps 5 and 6](courses/diagrams/e6c1cace-3aab-5259-be75-c61fc444f908/d3.svg)

Look at step 3. Relaxing P–S lowers S from 120 to 100. BFS would have kept the first value it saw; Dijkstra lets distances improve until the vertex is finished. After step 6 the walk to EC is **210 m**, and following `prev` back gives EC ← F ← S ← P ← MH.

For one destination, you can **stop** as soon as the target is finished. R (220) never had to be finished at all.

lessons.title: Dijkstra with a Min-Heap
lessons.readme:
# Dijkstra with a Min-Heap

"Finish the unfinished vertex with the smallest `dist`" is exactly what a **min-heap** is for. Dijkstra is **BFS with a min-heap instead of a FIFO queue**: closest first, not oldest first.

The heap holds pairs `{dist[v], v}`, keyed by the distance:

```cpp
dijkstra(G, s, t):
    for each vertex v in G
        dist[v] = ∞
        prev[v] = none
    dist[s] = 0
    pq.push({0, s})
    while not pq.empty():
        u = pq.top().vertex
        pq.pop()
        if u is finished: continue        // stale copy: lazy deletion
        mark u finished
        if u == t: stop                   // target done
        for each edge (u, v, len):
            if dist[u] + len < dist[v]:   // relax
                dist[v] = dist[u] + len
                prev[v] = u
                pq.push({dist[v], v})
```

When a vertex's distance improves, we don't dig the old pair out of the heap. We just push a new one. The old pair is now **stale**, and when it's eventually popped, its vertex is already finished, so we skip it. That's **lazy deletion**. Here's the campus run, with stale pairs struck out:

| Pop | Relax | Heap afterward |
|---|---|---|
| MH 0 | P 60, S 120, R 300 | 60 P, 120 S, 300 R |
| P 60 | **S 100**, F 210 | 100 S, ~~120 S~~, 210 F, 300 R |
| S 100 | **F 170**, **R 220** | ~~120 S~~, 170 F, ~~210 F~~, 220 R, ~~300 R~~ |
| S 120 | skip: stale | 170 F, ~~210 F~~, 220 R, ~~300 R~~ |
| F 170 | EC 210 | 210 EC, ~~210 F~~, 220 R, ~~300 R~~ |
| EC 210 | stop | ~~210 F~~, 220 R, ~~300 R~~ |

Notice the ending. We stop as soon as EC is finished, **before** relaxing its edges. R is still unfinished and the heap isn't empty, and that's fine.

lessons.title: Why Dijkstra Works
lessons.readme:
# Why Dijkstra Works

Why is it safe to call the top of the heap **finished**? Say the heap's top is `{170, F}`. Could some route we haven't explored reach F for less?

Any other route to F has to leave the finished set at some point, through an unfinished vertex. F is on top of the min-heap, so reaching **any** unfinished vertex already costs at least 170. And every edge length is **≥ 0**, so walking further can't make that route cheaper. Nothing can beat 170.

That argument leans hard on "edges are never negative". Take it away and Dijkstra can be wrong:

![a directed graph with one negative edge](courses/diagrams/10180abb-0fea-52a9-a31f-9c1b4497e3b8/neg.svg)

Edges: s → a 2, s → b 3, a → c 4, b → a **−2**.

1. Finish s. a = 2, b = 3.
2. Finish a (2). Relax a → c: c = 6.
3. Finish b (3). Relax b → a: 3 − 2 = 1 < 2, so `dist[a]` drops to 1. But a is already finished, so its edges are never relaxed again.
4. Finish c at **6**. The true shortest is s → b → a → c = 3 − 2 + 4 = **5**.

That's why Lab 9's `addEdge` rejects a negative weight with an exception.

# Dijkstra in C++ Time to write it. C++'s `std::priority_queue` is a **max**-heap by default, so ask for a min-heap with `std::greater`, the same way as in the Heaps chapter: ```cpp using P = std::pair; // {dist, vertex} std::priority_queue, std::greater

> pq; // smallest dist on top pq.push({0, s}); auto [d, u] = pq.top(); // pairs compare by .first first pq.pop(); ``` Each `adj[u]` entry is an `Edge`, a pair `{v, len}`, so `for (auto [v, len] : adj[u])` walks u's edges. **Infinity.** As in lecture, start every `dist[v]` at infinity, `INF = LLONG_MAX` (from ``). Relaxing is then just `if (dist[u] + len < dist[v])`, and an untouched vertex keeps INF. A vertex only gets relaxed from a finished u, whose distance is never INF, so the addition can't overflow. ## Assignment 1. [ ] Complete `dijkstra(adj, s)` using lazy deletion. Return a `ShortestPaths` with: - `dist[v]`: the shortest distance from `s` to v. Turn any leftover INF into **−1** just before returning. - `prev[v]`: the vertex before v on that route. It stays −1 for `s` and for unreachable vertices. Run every vertex to the end (no target here). The tests have no ties.

lessons.title: Dijkstra Big O
lessons.readme:
# Dijkstra Big O

Count what lazy-deletion Dijkstra does, with adjacency lists and a binary heap:

| step | how many times | cost each | total |
|---|---|---|---|
| initialize `dist`, `prev` | V | O(1) | O(V) |
| check an edge for relaxing | 2E (each list entry once) | O(1) | O(E) |
| push a pair | ≤ 2E + 1 | O(log V) | O(E log V) |
| top + pop a pair | ≤ 2E + 1 | O(log V) | O(E log V) |
| **total** | | | **O(V + E log V)** |

Some details behind the table:

- Edges are only checked when a vertex is finished, and no vertex is finished twice. In an undirected graph each edge sits in two lists, hence 2E.
- We push only when a relaxation succeeds, plus one push for the source: at most 2E + 1.
- With stale copies the heap can hold O(E) pairs, so a push costs O(log E). But E ≤ V², so log E ≤ 2 log V, which is **O(log V)**.

There's another version that **updates** a vertex's key inside the heap instead of pushing a new pair. Its runtime is **O((V + E) log V)**.

**Space:**

| data | size |
|---|---|
| graph (adjacency lists) | O(V + E) |
| `dist`, `prev`, finished | O(V) |
| heap, including stale copies | O(E) |
| **total** | **O(V + E)** |

lessons.title: Rebuilding the Route
lessons.readme:
# Rebuilding the Route

Distances are nice, but SpartanMaps has to **draw** the walk. That's what `prev[]` is for.

`prev[v]` is the vertex right before v on its shortest route. So start at the target and keep stepping to `prev` until you fall off the start, whose `prev` is −1. That lists the route **backward**; reverse it and you're done.

![following prev back from the Event Center](courses/diagrams/7eca9aae-e0d1-507c-b0dd-0be62b5eec6e/walk.svg)

On the campus: `prev[EC] = F`, `prev[F] = S`, `prev[S] = P`, `prev[P] = MH`, and `prev[MH] = −1`. Walking back gives EC F S P MH. Reversed: **MH → P → S → F → EC**.

It works because every piece of a shortest route is itself a shortest route. The best walk to EC goes through F, so its first part must be the best walk to F, which is exactly what `prev[F]` recorded.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `shortestRoute(adj, s, t)`: call `dijkstra(adj, s)`, then return the vertices on the shortest route from `s` to `t`, start first. Walk `prev` back from `t` with `push_back`, then reverse. Return `{}` if `t` is unreachable, and `{s}` when `s == t`.

lessons.title: Many Doors
lessons.readme:
# Many Doors

Real buildings have several doors. The shortest walk from the library to the gym starts at whichever library door and ends at whichever gym door are closest **to each other**. Running Dijkstra once for every pair of doors would work, but Lab 9 does it in **one run**:

1. Push **every** source with distance 0. Each starts with `prev = −1`.
2. Run Dijkstra as usual.
3. Stop at the **first target popped** (finished). Because the heap always hands out the closest vertex, that target is the closest one to **any** source.
4. Walk `prev` back from it until `prev` is −1. That vertex is the source door the route starts from. Reverse.

![two library doors and two gym doors, with the route from door 1 to door 7](courses/diagrams/27b6e783-1037-56c3-a8c1-674ba5cb4e97/doors.svg)

Here the library's doors are 0 and 1, and the gym's are 6 and 7. Door 1 to door 7 is 2 + 6 + 1 = **9**, which beats the best walk to door 6 (12). The result is the route 1 → 3 → 5 → 7.

Lab 9 returns a `Path` struct: whether a route was found, its length, its vertices, and its **edges**. To get those edges, the lab's `previousEdge[v]` stores the **number of the edge** that reached v instead of the previous vertex. Walking back, you take that edge's other end: if `e.v == v` it's `e.u`, otherwise it's `e.v`. Then reverse both lists. We'll use a smaller version with vertices only, so `prev` is enough here.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `closestRoute(adj, sources, targets)`. Run multi-source Dijkstra with lazy deletion, stop at the first target that gets finished, and return a `Path` with `found = true`, `length` = its distance, and `vertices` = the route from its source to it.
2. [ ] If no target is reachable, return a `Path` with `found = false` (leave the other fields at their defaults).

A vertex can be both a source and a target; then the route is just that vertex, with length 0.

lessons.title: Graph Algorithms Review
lessons.readme:
# Graph Algorithms Review

Time to practice the way the final asks: by hand, one step at a time. Write the lists, keep the stack, queue or heap in a column, and cross things off as they leave.

Quick reference:

- **degrees** add up to 2E; **Kₙ** has n(n − 1)/2 edges
- **Euler circuit**: all degrees even. **Euler path**: exactly two odd vertices, the two ends
- **matrix**: O(V²) space, O(1) edge check. **lists**: O(V + E) space, the usual default
- **DFS**: recursion (a stack), go deep, O(V + E) with lists, O(V²) with a matrix
- **BFS**: a queue, mark when pushed, fewest edges via `parent[]`
- **Dijkstra**: a min-heap of `{dist, v}`, skip finished (stale) pops, relax with `<`, stop when the target is finished, edges must be ≥ 0, O(V + E log V)

lessons.readme:
# Cutting Lumber for Profit

![rows of stacked wooden boards of many different lengths](courses/diagrams/4ed3c1f1-630f-5259-b977-410775e12627/stacked_boards.jpg)
*Image: Alex Jones, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.*

The campus Maker Space got a donation of 8-foot boards, and the woodshop club sells cut pieces at the Thursday market by the Student Union. Shoppers pay a set price for each length. Cuts are free, and they fall on whole feet:

| length (ft) | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| price ($) | 1 | 6 | 10 | 12 | 14 | 19 | 21 | 25 |

How should the club cut one board to earn the most? Selling it whole gets $25, but that isn't the best:

![an 8-foot board sold whole for 25 dollars, or cut 2+3+3 for 26](courses/diagrams/4ed3c1f1-630f-5259-b977-410775e12627/whole_vs_cut.svg)

The obvious plan is to try every way to cut and keep the best. How many ways are there? A 4-foot board has 3 marks where a cut could go, and each mark is either cut or not cut. That's 2 · 2 · 2 = 8 ways:

![all eight ways to cut a 4-foot board](courses/diagrams/4ed3c1f1-630f-5259-b977-410775e12627/four_foot.svg)

Two of them tie for the best, $12. In general an n-foot board has n − 1 marks, so there are **2ⁿ⁻¹** ways to cut it. An 8-foot board has 128. A 40-foot board has over 500 billion. Checking every option is exponential.

This chapter is about doing much better than that. The trick is called **dynamic programming**, and we'll build up to it with a function you already know.

lessons.title: Overlapping Subproblems
lessons.readme:
# Overlapping Subproblems

Before we solve the lumber problem, let's see what makes brute force so slow on a smaller example. Remember Fibonacci from Recursion? In this class the first two are both 1:

```cpp
int fibonacci(int n) {
    if (n == 0 || n == 1) return 1;
    else return fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2);
}
```

So the numbers go 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13… and `fibonacci(5)` is 8. Each call makes two more calls. Here is every call that `fibonacci(5)` makes. Blue is the first time a value gets computed; red is the same work being done again:

![the recursion tree of fibonacci(5), with repeated calls in red](courses/diagrams/e0cad926-722e-5c91-977d-57c654ba6337/fib5.svg)

Count them up:

| call | f5 | f4 | f3 | f2 | f1 | f0 | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| times | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 | 3 | **15** |

That's **15 calls for only 6 different subproblems**, f0 through f5. `fibonacci(2)` is computed three times, `fibonacci(1)` five times. The tree almost doubles at each level, so the number of calls grows by about 1.6× each time n goes up by one. That's **O(2ⁿ)**.

When a plain recursive solution keeps solving the same smaller problems again and again, we say it has **overlapping subproblems**. The cutting problem has them too: cutting 2 feet off an 8-foot board, or 1 foot and then 1 more, both leave 6 feet, so brute force works out the best way to cut 6 feet twice.

lessons.title: Memoized Fibonacci
lessons.readme:
# Memoized Fibonacci

If the same subproblem keeps coming back, don't solve it again. Write the answer down the first time, and look it up after that. That's **memoization**: the natural recursion, plus a cache.

The lecture keeps the cache in an `unordered_map` from n to fib(n), passed by reference so every call shares it:

1. Base case first: `n <= 1` returns 1.
2. **Check the cache.** If n is in it, return the stored answer.
3. Otherwise compute it the normal way, **save it** in the cache, and return it.

Here's `fib(5)` with a cache. Each value is computed once (blue). The second time f3 and f2 are asked for, the map already has them (green), so those calls return right away with no children. A repeated base case (gray) returns 1 right away too:

![the call tree of memoized fib(5): 9 calls, two of them cache hits](courses/diagrams/a21ef050-0e40-51f5-b268-8acab1bd98bb/memo5.svg)

Fifteen calls drop to nine, and the gap grows fast: fib(40) needs about 330 million plain calls but only 79 memoized ones.

> [!note]
> The lecture's version uses `unordered_map<int, int>`. We use `long long`, because fib(80) is about 3.8 × 10¹⁶ and overflows an `int`.

**Dynamic programming** is the general strategy: solve each distinct subproblem once and store its answer so it can be reused instead of recomputed. Memoization is one way to do it, the top-down way.

## Assignment

The woodshop club's pricing app starts with a warm-up. Complete `fibMemo(n, memo)` in `dp.h`. `fib(n)` is already written for you and calls it with an empty map.

1. [ ] If `n <= 1`, return 1.
2. [ ] If `memo` already holds `n`, return the stored value without recursing. (`memo.count(n)` is 1 if it's there.)
3. [ ] Otherwise compute `fibMemo(n - 1, memo) + fibMemo(n - 2, memo)`, store it in `memo[n]`, and return it.

The tests call `fib(80)`, which must finish within 2 seconds, and they also hand `fibMemo` a map that already has an entry, to make sure you use it.

lessons.title: Memoization Big O
lessons.readme:
# Memoization Big O

Why does memoized Fibonacci get so fast?

With the cache, each `fib(k)` from 0 to n is **computed once**. After that, asking for it again is a single O(1) map lookup. Every computed value makes at most two calls, so the whole run makes about **2n − 1** calls: 9 for fib(5), 11 for fib(6).

| | Plain recursion | Memoized |
|---|---|---|
| calls for fib(5) | 15 | 9 |
| time | O(2ⁿ) | **O(n)** |
| extra space | O(n) call stack | **O(n)**: the map plus the call stack |

That's the deal dynamic programming makes: **trade a little memory for a lot of time.** We keep n stored answers, and in return the running time drops from exponential to linear.

> [!tip]
> On the exam, if a question asks why memoization helps, the answer is that each subproblem is solved only once and then reused, not that it "makes recursion faster" in general.

lessons.title: Bottom-Up Fibonacci
lessons.readme:
# Bottom-Up Fibonacci

Memoization starts at the top, fib(n), and recursion works its way down to the base cases. You can also go the other direction: start from the **smallest** subproblems and fill a table upward, so that every value you need is already there when you need it. That's **bottom-up** dynamic programming, also called tabulation. No recursion at all, just a loop.

For Fibonacci the table is a vector `f` where `f[i]` is fib(i). Both base cases are 1, and every other entry is the sum of the two before it. Here it is filling up for n = 5. The amber cell is being filled; the blue cells are the two it reads:

![filling f[2] and f[3]](courses/diagrams/9022d233-a82a-58b8-bd9d-dd55c53b4d2f/fill_a.svg)

![filling f[4] and f[5]](courses/diagrams/9022d233-a82a-58b8-bd9d-dd55c53b4d2f/fill_b.svg)

The loop runs n − 1 times and the table has n + 1 entries, so this is **O(n) time and O(n) space**, the same as memoization. There's no call stack to grow, though, so a big n can't overflow the stack.

## Assignment

Complete `fibTable(n)` in `dp.h`. Don't recurse.

1. [ ] Make a `vector<long long>` with n + 1 entries, all 1. That covers `f[0]` and `f[1]`.
2. [ ] For `i` from 2 to n, set `f[i] = f[i - 1] + f[i - 2]`.
3. [ ] Return `f[n]`.

> [!warning]
> n can be 0. A table made with `n + 1` entries has only `f[0]` then, so don't write to `f[1]` yourself. Starting every entry at 1 avoids that.

lessons.title: Top-Down or Bottom-Up
lessons.readme:
# Top-Down or Bottom-Up

You've now seen both ways to do dynamic programming:

| | Top-down (memoization) | Bottom-up (table) |
|---|---|---|
| shape | the natural recursion, plus a cache | a loop that fills a table |
| starts at | the big problem, fib(n) | the smallest subproblems, f[0] and f[1] |
| solves | only the subproblems it actually reaches | every subproblem up to n |
| stack | grows with the recursion depth | none |
| Fibonacci | O(n) time, O(n) space | O(n) time, O(n) space |

Either one counts as dynamic programming, because either one **solves each distinct subproblem once and stores the answer**. That's what separates DP from plain recursion. Memoization is not a different technique from DP; it's one way of doing it.

For bottom-up, the important question is the **order**: fill the table so that whatever entry you're computing only reads entries that are already done. For Fibonacci that's just left to right.

Memoization is the top-down way to do DP

lessons.title: The Rod Cutting Recurrence
lessons.readme:
# The Rod Cutting Recurrence

Back to the lumber. The lecture calls this **rod cutting**. Here's the idea that turns 2ⁿ⁻¹ options into a short table.

Every way of cutting a j-foot board has some **first piece**, of length i (from 1 up to j, where i = j means selling it whole). After that piece, what's left is a (j − i)-foot board, and we want the **best** we can do with it. So:

**best[0] = 0**
**best[j] = max over i = 1..j of ( price[i] + best[j − i] )**

The answer for a big board is built out of the best answers for shorter boards. That's called **optimal substructure**. And those shorter boards come up again and again, which is the overlap. So fill a table bottom-up, starting from 0 feet. Here it is with the lecture's prices. The amber cell is being filled, and the blue cells are the `best[j − i]` values it reads:

![best[1] and best[2]](courses/diagrams/b9337211-ae09-5de5-8241-89cf4f79d45d/rod_a.svg)

![best[3] and best[4]](courses/diagrams/b9337211-ae09-5de5-8241-89cf4f79d45d/rod_b.svg)

At j = 4 there's a tie: 12 + 0 (sell it whole) and 6 + 6 (2 + 2) both give **$12**, just like the list of all 8 ways showed. Carrying on to 8 feet:

| j | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| price[j] | 0 | 1 | 6 | 10 | 12 | 14 | 19 | 21 | 25 |
| best[j] | 0 | 1 | 6 | 10 | 12 | 16 | 20 | 22 | **26** |

best[8] = 26: the 2 + 3 + 3 cut from the first lesson, $1 more than selling it whole.

questions.question: With the lecture prices and best[0..4] = 0, 1, 6, 10, 12, what is best[5]?
New prices: 1 ft $2, 2 ft $5, 3 ft $8, 4 ft $9. What is best[4]?

lessons.title: Rod Cutting in C++
lessons.readme:
# Rod Cutting in C++

The recurrence turns straight into two loops. The outer loop picks the board length `j` we're solving, from 1 up to n. The inner loop tries every first piece `i` and keeps the best total:

```
best[0] = 0
for j = 1 .. n:
    for i = 1 .. j:
        best[j] = max(best[j], price[i] + best[j - i])
return best[n]
```

When the inner loop reads `best[j - i]`, it only ever looks at lengths **shorter** than j, and those were all filled in on earlier passes of the outer loop. That's the bottom-up order doing its job.

`price` is indexed by length, so `price[3]` is what a 3-foot piece sells for, and `price[0]` is 0 and never used.

## Assignment

The club wants a price list for any board length. Complete `rodCut(price, n)` in `dp.h`.

1. [ ] Make a table `best` with n + 1 entries, all 0.
2. [ ] Fill it bottom-up with the two loops above.
3. [ ] Return `best[n]`.

You can assume `price` has at least n + 1 entries and every price is positive. The tests include a 40-foot board, which must finish within 2 seconds, so trying all 2³⁹ cuts won't do. `std::max` is in `<algorithm>`, already included.

lessons.title: Rod Cutting Big O
lessons.readme:
# Rod Cutting Big O

Count the work in `rodCut`. For each length j, the inner loop tries j first pieces, and each try is O(1): one addition and one comparison.

1 + 2 + 3 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2 tries in total, so the time is **O(n²)**. The table has n + 1 entries, so the extra space is **O(n)**.

| Approach | 8-foot board | 40-foot board | Big O |
|---|---|---|---|
| try every cut | 128 options | over 500 billion | O(2ⁿ) |
| bottom-up DP | 36 tries | 820 tries | O(n²) |

Same answer, and the difference is the whole point of the chapter: the brute force rebuilt "the best way to cut the rest" from scratch every time, and the table works each one out once.

lessons.title: Which Cuts to Make
lessons.readme:
# Which Cuts to Make

`rodCut` says the best 8-foot board earns $26. The club also needs to know **where to cut**.

When the inner loop finds a new best for length j, remember which first piece gave it, in a second table `first[j]`. Then walk back from n: take a piece of length `first[n]`, and what's left is `n - first[n]` feet, whose best first piece is already stored too. Keep going until nothing is left.

Here are both tables for the lecture prices. When two first pieces tie, the loop keeps the one it found first, because it only updates on a strictly bigger total:

![the best and first tables for an 8-foot board, the walk back from 8 highlighted, and the board cut into 2, 3 and 3 feet](courses/diagrams/20db9a54-9144-5356-b928-2ac44130f5a9/walk.svg)

From 8, the first piece is 2 feet, leaving 6. From 6, the first piece is 3, leaving 3. From 3, sell the last 3 feet whole. The cuts are **2, 3, 3**, worth 6 + 10 + 10 = $26.

This "store the choice, then walk back" pattern works for most DP problems: the table of best values tells you **how much**, and the table of choices tells you **how**.

## Assignment

Complete `bestCuts(price, n)` in `dp.h`. It returns the lengths of the pieces in a best way to cut an n-foot board.

1. [ ] Fill `best` like in `rodCut`, and also fill `first[j]` with the first piece that gave the best total.
2. [ ] Walk back from n, pushing each piece length onto a vector, until 0 feet are left.
3. [ ] Return the pieces. For n = 0, return an empty vector.

Any order of pieces is fine, and when several cuts tie for the best, any of them is fine. The tests check that the pieces add up to n feet and earn as much as `rodCut` says is possible. Every price is positive.

lessons.title: Requirements for Dynamic Programming
lessons.readme:
# Requirements for Dynamic Programming

Fibonacci and rod cutting both gave in to DP. What do they have in common? The lecture lists the requirements:

1. **Optimal substructure.** A best solution is built from best solutions to smaller subproblems. The best 8-foot cut is one first piece plus the best cut of what's left.
2. **Overlapping subproblems.** A plain recursive solution solves the same subproblems again and again. Fibonacci recomputed f2 three times in fib(5); brute-force cutting re-solves short boards constantly.
3. **Usually an optimization problem**, a min or a max. There may be several best solutions, and we only want one of them.

That last point showed up already. A 4-foot board earns $12 either whole or as 2 + 2:

![a 4-foot board earns 12 dollars whole or cut 2+2](courses/diagrams/a372dbb1-72f6-5fc1-b22c-935eb98bfa76/tie.svg)

DP finds the best **value**, $12, and hands back one cut that earns it.

> [!warning]
> Overlapping subproblems is what makes DP worth it. Merge sort also splits a problem into smaller ones, but its two halves never overlap, so there's nothing to store. That's plain divide and conquer, not DP.

answers: Its running time is O(n²) in the worst case
It isn't correct on every possible input array
It doesn't use recursion anywhere in its code
Its halves never overlap, so nothing is reused
questions.answer: Its halves never overlap, so nothing is reused

answers: Nothing, because the answer isn't unique
The cut with the fewest pieces only
Every cut that earns the best price
The best price and one cut that earns it
questions.answer: The best price and one cut that earns it

lessons.title: Greedy Coin Change
lessons.readme:
# Greedy Coin Change

Down the hall from the Maker Space, the Engineering building has a vending machine that gives change. It wants to hand back as **few coins** as possible.

![a pile of US pennies, nickels, dimes and quarters](courses/diagrams/fa76f884-ea80-50bd-b7d5-aeee8b398ab9/us_coins.jpg)
*Image: Elembis, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.*

You already know how to do this without thinking: take the **biggest coin that fits**, subtract it, and repeat. For 65 cents with US coins (25, 10, 5, 1):

![greedy change for 65 cents: 25, 25, 10, 5](courses/diagrams/fa76f884-ea80-50bd-b7d5-aeee8b398ab9/us65.svg)

That's a **greedy algorithm**: at each step, take the option that looks best **right now**, and never go back to reconsider it. There's no table and no trying of alternatives, so greedy algorithms are usually simple and fast. Here it's one pass over the coin types.

For US coins, biggest-first always gives the fewest coins. Nobody needs to check every combination.

You've seen a greedy algorithm already: **Dijkstra's**. At each step it finishes the closest vertex that isn't finished yet, and never revisits that choice. With non-negative edges, that choice is always safe.

The catch is that greedy only works when the best-looking choice is always part of some best answer. The next lesson breaks it.

What makes an algorithm **greedy**?
answers: It tries every combination and keeps the best one
It stores the answer to every one of its subproblems in a table
It takes the best-looking choice now and never reconsiders
It splits the problem in half and recurses on both
questions.answer: It takes the best-looking choice now and never reconsiders

lessons.title: When Greedy Fails
lessons.readme:
# When Greedy Fails

A student club puts its own token machine in the Student Union, with tokens worth **1, 3 and 4**. A drink costs 6 and you pay with a 12, so the machine owes you 6. Greedy takes the biggest token that fits:

![greedy gives 4+1+1 but 3+3 uses fewer tokens](courses/diagrams/f2e07ce3-79f8-53e5-8e68-263a67ccd13d/tokens6.svg)

Taking the 4 looked great, but it left 2, which costs two 1s. Greedy never goes back, so it's stuck with 3 tokens when 2 would do.

What went wrong is that the best answer for 6 doesn't have to start with the biggest token. It might start with **any** token. That's exactly the rod-cutting situation: the first piece could be any length, so try them all and use stored answers for the rest.

**best[0] = 0, best[a] = min over coins c ≤ a of ( 1 + best[a − c] )**

DP gets 2 here. Greedy is still right for US coins, but you have to prove it for each coin system, and for many systems it simply isn't true.

> [!tip]
> To show greedy fails, one counterexample is enough. Try amounts just above the biggest coin.

questions.question: Coins {1, 5, 8}, amount 10. How many coins does largest-first greedy use?
Coins {1, 7, 10}, amount 14. Greedy uses how many coins, and what's the fewest possible?

lessons.title: Fewest Coins
lessons.readme:
# Fewest Coins

Let's put both approaches side by side in code.

**Greedy** walks the coins from biggest to smallest and takes each one as many times as it fits.

**DP** fills `best[a]`, the fewest coins that make amount `a`, from 0 up. For each amount it tries every coin as the last one used:

![the fewest-coins table for tokens 1, 3, 4 up to 6](courses/diagrams/c7061b3b-0caf-527d-a9d8-a3bda9f09f9b/table.svg)

Same pattern as rod cutting: max became min, and "price of the first piece" became "one more coin". The time is O(amount · number of coin types).

## Assignment

Complete both functions in `dp.h`. `coins` is sorted from **largest to smallest** and always contains 1, so every amount can be made.

1. [ ] `greedyCoins(coins, amount)`: return how many coins biggest-first uses.
2. [ ] `minCoins(coins, amount)`: return the fewest coins possible, using a bottom-up table `best[0..amount]` with `best[0] = 0`. For each amount, start from a value bigger than any real answer (like `amount + 1`) and take the min over every coin that fits.

Both return 0 for an amount of 0. The tests make change for 100,000, so `minCoins` must not try every combination.

lessons.title: Greedy vs. Dynamic Programming
lessons.readme:
# Greedy vs. Dynamic Programming

Greedy and DP are **quiz-style only** on the final: know the ideas and be able to trace them, no code.

| | Greedy | Dynamic programming |
|---|---|---|
| each step | take the best-looking option **now**, never reconsider | try every choice, using stored answers to subproblems |
| speed | usually fast, often a sort plus one pass | slower: it fills a table |
| correct? | only if the best local choice is always part of a best answer | whenever there's optimal substructure |
| examples | US coin change, Dijkstra, activity selection | Fibonacci, rod cutting, coin change with any coins |

**Activity selection** is a classic where greedy *does* work, if you pick the right rule. The Student Union has one study room and these requests: A 9–12, B 10–11, C 11–13, D 12–15, E 13–14. Fit in as many as possible. The rule that works is **always take the request that finishes earliest** among those that still fit (a request may start exactly when the last one ends):

![activity selection: B, C and E are taken, A and D are rejected](courses/diagrams/cd31c66e-0d5e-55d6-9039-657f07ca8a34/rooms.svg)

B, C, E: three meetings, and no schedule fits more. Taking the one that **starts** earliest instead would grab A (9–12), then D, and stop at two.

> [!note]
> The Nov 24 lecture (DP & Greedy, Day 2) is the last new material and comes after the slides this course was built from. When it's posted, check both halves: compare its rod-cutting solution with this chapter, and add any new greedy examples or clicker questions to your notes sheet.

lessons.title: Dynamic Programming Review
lessons.readme:
# Dynamic Programming Review

The final asks about DP and greedy in quiz style, so practice the traces by hand. Draw the table, fill one cell at a time, and write each `max(…)` or `min(…)` out.

Quick reference:

- **DP** = solve each distinct subproblem once and store the answer. Needs **optimal substructure** and **overlapping subproblems**; usually a min or max problem.
- **Top-down** = recursion + cache (memoization). **Bottom-up** = a table filled from the smallest subproblem.
- Fibonacci, f(0) = f(1) = 1: plain recursion makes 15 calls for fib(5), O(2ⁿ). Memoized: 9 calls (2n − 1), O(n) time, O(n) space.
- Rod cutting: 2ⁿ⁻¹ ways to cut; **best[j] = max over i of price[i] + best[j − i]**, O(n²) time, O(n) space.
- **Greedy** = best-looking choice now, never reconsidered. Right for US coins, Dijkstra (non-negative edges), and activity selection by earliest finish. Wrong for coins like {1, 3, 4}.

lessons.title: Final Review: Classes and Polymorphism
lessons.readme:
# Final Review: Classes and Polymorphism

It's the week before the final. Your study group has a room on the fifth floor of King Library, a stack of scratch paper, and one plan: go through the whole course once more, topic by topic, in the style of the exam. Every lesson in this chapter is a short refresher and then a few questions with new numbers. Anything you miss goes straight onto your notes sheet.

We start where the class started, with classes and inheritance. That was 10% of the midterm, and it was a single "what prints?" question. The rule that decides it:

| The function is… | Which version runs? | Decided at |
|---|---|---|
| `virtual` in the base | the **object's actual type** | run time (dynamic dispatch) |
| not virtual | the **pointer's or reference's type** | compile time |

A base-class pointer or reference that refers to a derived object is the whole trick. Read each call, ask "is it virtual in the base?", and pick the class from the table.

Two more rules that show up as true/false:

- A **pure virtual** function (`= 0`) has no body and makes the class **abstract**. You can't create an object of it, only point to derived ones.
- A base class that will be deleted through a base pointer needs a **virtual destructor**, or only the base part gets destroyed.

> [!tip]
> On paper, write the output one call at a time. The usual mistake is reading the object's type for every call, including the non-virtual ones.

questions.question: A class declares `virtual double area() const = 0;` and nothing else. What is true?
answers: You cannot create an object of it
Every object of it has area 0
It cannot be used as a pointer type
Its `area` is picked at compile time
questions.answer: You cannot create an object of it

lessons.title: Final Review: Pointers and Memory
lessons.readme:
# Final Review: Pointers and Memory

Pointers and dynamic memory were 23% of the midterm, the second biggest topic. Most of it comes down to four ideas.

**Where things live.** Local variables and parameters are on the **stack** and disappear when the function returns. Anything made with `new` is on the **heap** and stays until you `delete` it.

**Match the forms.** `new` goes with `delete`, and `new[]` goes with `delete[]`. Mixing them is undefined behavior.

**Leak.** You lose the last pointer to a heap block before deleting it. The block can never be freed.

**Dangling pointer.** `delete` frees the block but doesn't touch the pointer. It still holds the old address. Any other pointer that was copied from it is dangling too.

Here's a tiny trace you can do on paper:

```cpp
int* p = new int(4);    // heap block #1 holds 4
int* q = p;             // q points at block #1 too
p = new int(9);         // heap block #2 holds 9
delete q;               // block #1 freed; q now dangles
delete p;               // block #2 freed; p now dangles
```

Nothing leaks here, because each block was deleted exactly once, through some pointer. Drop the `delete q;` line and block #1 leaks.

![stack pointers p and q with arrows to heap blocks after lines 2, 3 and 5 (dashed red = dangling), and how a leak looks](courses/diagrams/2d2be138-d919-594e-b382-65a20233dcf4/trace.svg)

> [!warning]
> Setting a pointer to `nullptr` after `delete` is your job. `delete` never does it for you.

answers: Both of them, until main returns

lessons.title: Final Review: Loop Analysis
lessons.readme:
# Final Review: Loop Analysis

Algorithm analysis was the biggest share of the midterm, 25%. Most questions gave you code and asked for the tightest Big O. The rules:

| Pattern | Count | Big O |
|---|---|---|
| loop to n with an O(1) body | n | O(n) |
| two nested loops to n | n · n | O(n²) |
| inner loop runs `j < i` | 0 + 1 + … + (n − 1) = n(n − 1)/2 | O(n²) |
| inner loop runs a constant 100 times | 100 per outer step | drop the constant |
| `i *= 2` or `i /= 2` | log₂ n steps | O(log n) |
| each call makes k ≥ 2 recursive calls, n shrinks by 1 | about kⁿ calls | O(kⁿ) |

One pattern fooled a lot of people. When the outer loop doubles and the inner loop runs **i** times, the work is 1 + 2 + 4 + … + n, and that sum is **2n − 1** when n is a power of 2. It's O(n), not O(n log n). The same thing happens when the outer loop halves from n: n + n/2 + n/4 + … + 1 is also under 2n.

> [!tip]
> Don't multiply the loop counts blindly. When the inner count depends on the outer variable, add up the actual counts.

lessons.title: Final Review: Linked Lists and Recursion
lessons.readme:
# Final Review: Linked Lists and Recursion

**Linked lists** were 15% of the midterm. The costs come down to one question: do you already have a pointer to the node you need?

| Singly linked list | Cost | Why |
|---|---|---|
| insertFront, removeFront | O(1) | head is right there |
| insertBack, no tail pointer | O(n) | walk to the end first |
| insertBack, with tail | O(1) | tail is right there |
| removeBack, even with tail | O(n) | you need the node **before** tail |
| insertAfter a node you hold | O(1) | relink two pointers |
| size(), if it walks the list | O(n) | counts every node |

That last row hides inside loops. `for (i = 0; i < list.size() / 2; i++)` calls a walking `size()` on every pass, so the loop is O(n²), not O(n).

**Recursion** was 16%. Every recursive function needs a **base case** that stops, and every call must make **progress** toward it. The professor's fast power halves n each call:

```cpp
long power(long x, int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 1;
    long half = power(x, n / 2);
    if (n % 2 == 0) return half * half;
    else return x * half * half;
}
```

`power(2, 10)` calls with n = 10, 5, 2, 1, 0: five calls, so it's O(log n). Integer division is what makes the odd case work: 5 / 2 is 2.

questions.question: A singly linked list keeps `head` and `tail`. Which operation is still O(n)?
How many calls to `power` does `power(2, 20)` make, counting the first one?

lessons.title: Final Review: Stacks and Queues
lessons.readme:
# Final Review: Stacks and Queues

Stacks and queues were 11% of the midterm, spread over four small questions.

**Postfix.** Operands go straight to the output; operators wait on a stack. To **evaluate** postfix, push numbers, and when you hit an operator, pop two, apply it (the **second** pop is the left operand), and push the result.

`6 2 3 + * 4 -` → push 6, 2, 3 → `+` makes 5 → `*` makes 30 → push 4 → `-` makes **26**.

**Circular array queue.** The class version keeps `f`, the index of the front, and `r`, the index of the **next free slot**. Both move forward with `% N`.

![a circular queue of 8 slots drawn as a ring and as an array, holding 4 items that wrap past the end](courses/diagrams/6da7b73d-d5de-5b3f-9dae-ad665c003b6e/ring.svg)

| | Formula |
|---|---|
| size | `(N - f + r) % N` |
| empty | `f == r` |
| full | size is `N - 1` |

In the picture, (8 − 6 + 2) % 8 = **4** items: p, q, s, t. The `+ N` keeps the subtraction from going negative when the queue has wrapped.

> [!warning]
> An N-slot array holds only **N − 1** items. If it held N, a full queue would have `f == r`, which looks exactly like an empty one.
