lessons.title: Final Review: Searching and Hashing
lessons.readme:
# Final Review: Searching and Hashing

Halfway through the afternoon, the study group turns to the material after the midterm. None of it has been tested on an exam yet, so expect plenty of it on the final.

| Search | Needs | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| sequential | nothing | O(n) |
| binary search | a **sorted** array | O(log n): about 10 checks for 1,000 items |
| hash table | a good hash function | **O(1) average**, O(n) worst |
| balanced BST | keys with `<` | O(log n), and keeps them in order |

**Linear probing** by hand: compute the home bucket, and if it's taken, try the next one, wrapping around. With h(k) = k mod 10, inserting 15, 25, 35 puts them in buckets 5, 6 and 7. Then 16 starts at 6, finds 6 and 7 taken, and lands in **8**.

**Deleting** from a probing table writes a **tombstone**, not an empty bucket. An empty bucket would stop later searches too early and hide keys stored past it.

**Load factor** α = items / buckets. As α grows toward 1, probe runs get longer, so tables grow before they fill.

questions.question: Fastest **average** lookup by key, when you never need the keys in order:
h(k) = k mod 10, linear probing, empty table. Insert 42, 52, 13, 62. Where does 62 land?
Why does deleting from a linear-probing table write a tombstone?
answers: Tombstones lower the load factor of the table
It makes every later insert O(1) in the worst case
The hash function changes after any delete happens
An empty bucket would stop later finds too early
questions.answer: An empty bucket would stop later finds too early

lessons.title: Final Review: Sorting
lessons.readme:
# Final Review: Sorting

The lecture versions decide every row of this table, so copy it onto your notes sheet as is.

| Sort | Best | Average | Worst | Extra space | Stable |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bubble (lecture) | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | yes |
| Selection | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | no |
| Insertion | **O(n)** | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | yes |
| Merge | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | **O(n)** | yes |
| Quick | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | **O(n²)** | O(log n) stack expected, O(n) worst | no |
| Heap | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(log n) stack | no |

The rows people miss:

- The lecture's bubble sort has no early exit, so even sorted input costs n(n − 1)/2 comparisons. Only **insertion sort** is O(n) on sorted input, and only the shifting version with early exit. The swap-based `sort_list` from the analysis lectures always runs its inner loop to i, so it's O(n²) even when sorted. Read the loop before you quote a best case.
- Quicksort with the **last element** as pivot hits its worst case on input that's **already sorted**: every partition peels off just one element.
- Heapsort's sift-down from class is recursive, so it uses O(log n) stack. It's O(1) only with a loop.

questions.question: A sorted array goes into quicksort with the last element as the pivot. Run time:
Which lecture sort runs in O(n) on input that is already sorted?
You need a stable sort that is O(n log n) even in the worst case. Which one?

lessons.title: Final Review: Trees and Heaps
lessons.readme:
# Final Review: Trees and Heaps

**BSTs.** Search and insert walk one path, so they're O(h), where h is the height: O(log n) if the tree is balanced, O(n) if it's a chain (insert keys in sorted order to get one).

**Remove** has three cases: a leaf just goes; a node with one child is replaced by that child; a node with **two** children takes the key of the **largest key in its left subtree**, which is then removed from down there. That's the class rule. The smallest key on the right also gives a valid BST, but it's the wrong answer on this exam unless the question asks for it.

![a BST with root 50; 30 has children 20 and 40, 20 has right child 25, 40 has left child 35](courses/diagrams/cf55a1d2-6d86-59ca-8dfe-6232c11be463/bst.svg)

**`std::map`** is a balanced BST: O(log n) worst case, and it iterates in sorted order. `std::unordered_map` is a hash table: O(1) average, no order.

**Heaps** live in an array with the root at index 0. For index i, the children are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and the parent is (i − 1) / 2.

lessons.title: Final Review: Graphs and Dijkstra
lessons.readme:
# Final Review: Graphs and Dijkstra

**Storage.** An adjacency matrix takes O(V²) space and answers "is (u, v) an edge?" in O(1). Adjacency lists take O(V + E) space, which is far less for sparse graphs. In an undirected graph the degrees add up to **2E**, and a complete graph on n vertices has n(n − 1)/2 edges.

**DFS and BFS** both run in O(V + E) with lists. DFS goes deep first (recursion or a stack); BFS goes level by level with a queue and finds the path with the **fewest edges**. Both try neighbors in **list order**, so the order of the lists decides the answer.

**Dijkstra** is BFS with a min-heap: always finish the unfinished vertex with the smallest distance, then relax its edges. It needs every edge to be ≥ 0. The lecture's version runs in O(V + E log V).

![an unweighted graph on A to F, and a weighted graph on S, A, B, T](courses/diagrams/0100da7a-d30c-541e-9583-85c0cf88a12c/graphs.svg)

For the weighted graph: S finishes at 0, then B at 1. Relaxing B's edges improves A from 4 to 1 + 2 = 3. A finishes at 3, which improves T from 7 to 4. The shortest S to T path is S, B, A, T, with length **4**.

lessons.title: Writing C++ on Paper
lessons.readme:
# Writing C++ on Paper

The study room has a whiteboard, and that's the right tool for this lesson. Part of the final is writing C++ by hand, with no compiler to catch you. Code that "basically works" on paper often loses points to the same few slips. Practice by rewriting a function from memory after you pass its code lesson, then check it against this list.

## Checklist

1. [ ] **Empty input.** What happens when `head` is `nullptr`, the array has 0 items, or the tree is empty? Handle it first.
2. [ ] **One item.** Removing the only node must leave both `head` and `tail` as `nullptr`.
3. [ ] **Every `new` has a `delete`.** Removing a node means saving a pointer to it, relinking, then deleting it.
4. [ ] **Pointer parameters that change.** If a function must change the caller's `head` or `root`, take it by reference: `Node*& head`.
5. [ ] **Every path returns.** A non-void function needs a `return` on every branch.
6. [ ] **Loop bounds.** `<` or `<=`? Check the first and last pass by hand.
7. [ ] **Base case first** in every recursive function, and every call makes progress toward it.
8. [ ] **Pass big things by `const&`.** A `vector` or `string` you only read shouldn't be copied.

The functions worth writing out once more: list insert, remove and reverse; the rule of three; the postfix calculator; the circular queue; binary search; linear-probing insert and find; insertion sort, merge and partition; tree height, node count and traversals; BST search and insert; sift-up and sift-down; BFS and DFS.

lessons.title: Your Notes Sheet
lessons.readme:
# Your Notes Sheet

You get **one 8.5" x 11" sheet, handwritten, both sides**. That's not much room, so don't copy the course onto it. Write down what you can't rebuild quickly under pressure: formulas, tables, class conventions and the traps you fell for in these reviews.

![a notes sheet: before-midterm topics on the front, after-midterm topics on the back](courses/diagrams/4a7aae56-7d1e-5183-8580-f804a0cef559/sheet.svg)

A layout that works: the midterm topics on the front (blue), and everything after the midterm on the back (green).

## What to write

1. [ ] The **Big-Oh definition**, word for word, and how a proof picks c and n₀.
2. [ ] Two sums: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2, and 1 + 2 + 4 + … + n = 2n − 1 for n a power of 2.
3. [ ] The **virtual** rule: object's type if virtual, pointer's type if not.
4. [ ] The linked list cost table, and the circular queue formulas with f, r and N − 1.
5. [ ] The **sorting table** from the sorting review, lecture versions.
6. [ ] The class rules: BST remove uses the largest key on the **left**; heaps start at index 0.
7. [ ] Dijkstra's steps, and its O(V + E log V).
8. [ ] The DP recurrences for Fibonacci and rod cutting, and one coin system where greedy fails.

> [!tip]
> Writing the sheet is studying too. The act of choosing what fits is what makes you remember the rest.
